## §W3 · EXPANSION WAVE 3 — the FULL-JOURNEY wave, and the eight measured gaps beside it (Ian, 2026-09-07)

Ian: *"let us now extend the numbers of our trajectories, I want you to determine first"* -> *"add also the
trajectories for full journeys, diverse, for my platform"* -> *"we still have to expand and extend the
journeys."* So the wave was **determined before it was designed**: every count below is a gap measured in
the registry as it stood at the close of wave 2, and the largest direction is the one the program was
thinnest on.

### What the determination found (measured read-only, 2026-09-07)

| Axis | What 2,437 rows actually held |
|---|---|
| **Whole journeys barely existed** | **9 rows crossed >=3 pages and none crossed five.** 171 rows used journey words; 117 of them walked a single page. |
| **Cast in the wrong verticals** | The platform hosts **Manila Electronics Assembly, Lucena Pharmaceutical Mfg., Baguio Textile Mills, Dela Cruz Delivery Fleet, Ramos Jeepney Line, Tan Delivery Vans** - and the registry held 1 electronics row, 0 textile, a few pharma, against 307 vehicle and 37 power-plant rows. |
| **Content pages had one row each** | 54 learn articles: 1 row apiece, all Usability; **52 with zero F, A and I.** 60 calculators: 47 at one row; **59 lacking F, 59 lacking A, 60 lacking I.** |
| **The critic had graded them once** | 31 root pages on the full rubric; **146 pages on a single dimension** (CV1, anon CTA activation): 53 learn, 47 calculators, 48 function files. |
| **Edge functions** | 6 with no row at all, 56 with exactly one. |
| **Shared components** | 17 root scripts named in no row - `connectivity-widget.js` ships on 33 pages. |
| **Cells never walked** | Per root page: new-user 18 · returner 18 · tablet-768 18 · deep-link 18 · anon 27 · search-arrival 37 · qr-print 33 missing. 102 of 546 page x layer cells empty. |
| **Lifecycle lenses** | mic/camera denied 1 · second hive 7 · year-2 aging 10 · leaving 10 · two tabs 21 · export->import 23 · notification storm 25 · release skew 30. |

### The nine directions, and the honest arithmetic

**1,502 new rows seeded in one change: 2,437 -> 3,939 in scope, and the headline dropped to 61.9% the same
day** - the same discipline as every prior wave (the denominator moves once; the generator does the
arithmetic; a hand-typed number fails the `trajectory-registry` gate).

| Code | Direction | Rows | How the count was derived |
|---|---|---|---|
| **W3-JN** | **Full diverse journeys** | **724** | 32 archetypes x the platform's own cast x four tiers (below) |
| W3-LN | Learn articles to full UFAI | 156 | one row per missing dimension per article |
| W3-CL | Calculators to full UFAI | 178 | one row per missing dimension per calculator |
| W3-FN | Edge-function contracts | 186 | 62 functions x refusal / degradation / documented job |
| W3-SC | Shared components as subjects | 56 | 14 scripts x four UFAI lenses, each on three host pages |
| W3-PG | Persona · device · entry gaps | 55 | the cells a root page had never been walked in |
| W3-LC | Lifecycle lenses | 64 | 8 thin shapes x 8 surfaces each |
| W3-AR | Empty page x layer cells | 79 | one row per empty (page, layer) where the layer applies |
| W3-DF | Wave-2 deferred carry-over | 4 | what the last wave found and named as deferred |

The plan estimated ~1,539; the seeder **measured** 1,502. The difference is where an estimate met the
registry: the persona-gap roster came out at 55 rather than 129 because arrival cells that only ever reach
a sign-in door were excluded (the deep-link lens that once graded the same door 24 times), and the empty
page x layer roster came out at 79 rather than 60. `tools/seed_expansion_wave3.py` is the one place that
decides the size, and `validate_trajectory_registry.py` derives its expected ids from it.

### W3-JN - what a journey row is

One whole story: a named person (or a **role pair**, because a two-sided journey owes one side each), cast
in one of the six hives or as a hive-less operator or an anonymous arrival; a device, a language, a moment
in the hive's life, and a condition. It crosses **>=4 pages and >=3 layers**; tier D crosses **>=8 pages,
>=5 layers and three moments**.

| Tier | What varies | Rows |
|---|---|---|
| **A** base cast | every archetype x every vertical it applies to · phone · English · today | **130** |
| **B** device + language | each again on a desktop, and Filipino-first on both devices | **381** |
| **C** overlays | condition x3, moment x2, entry x2, assistive x2, tablet/kiosk | **197** |
| **D** whole lifetimes | a hive's year, a worker's career, a machine's life, a part, a listing, a project, a vehicle | **16** |

The 32 archetypes span the platform's own stages: **acquire** (onboard to first value, alone-then-not,
stranger-to-member, new hire, locked out) · **operate** (breakdown to close-out, the PM month, the
AI-assisted day, the supervisor's week, two hives one person, safety incident, one spare part, the brief
arrives) · **maintain** (sensor to work order, predicted risk, one machine's life, the energy audit, an
engineering project, typhoon season) · **comply** (audit season, the founder's month-end, benchmark to
decision) · **trade** (shortage to shelf, hire a specialist, a deal goes wrong, money in and spent) ·
**grow** (the knowledge loop, the portable portfolio) · **integrate** (the machine client, the vehicle
owner's month) · **degrade** (the same day degraded, leaving).

### The instrument, and the three faults it had before it had any findings

`tools/prove_full_journeys.mjs` walks each story's ordered path in one context and grades three rails: the
**transition** (the next surface is reachable from this one and arrives as itself - never that a control was
clickable), the **identity** (hive, role and name survive every hop), and the **effect** (each archetype
declares a JOIN along its own chain, read *as the person*, so a chain proven only by both ends existing is
not proven).

Its first run reported six failures out of six, and **all three causes were the instrument**:

1. **The nav hub is a closed drawer, and a closed drawer is not an absent one.** The hub is
   `visibility:hidden` until opened, so a visibility filter across the page read *"no way onward at all"* on
   every hop of every journey. A hub link now counts whether or not the drawer is open; only the page's own
   links must be on screen to count as its own thread.
2. **A thread read on a page you did not ask for is not that page's thread.** Three fleet casts could not
   sign in, every step bounced to `index.html`, and the walk cheerfully counted the landing page's links as
   five journey threads - the deep-link lens grading the sign-in door, one layer along. A step that did not
   arrive now contributes no thread evidence at all.
3. **The platform's own table, not mine.** The chain for the breakdown journey counted `anomaly_alerts`,
   which holds zero rows in every hive; `alert-hub.html` reads **`v_alert_truth`**. Six hives whose alert
   page renders a full screen were reported as *"the chain is empty here."*

And one real setup gap: the three fleet accounts had no recoverable password, so the fleet journeys could
not be walked as authenticated people at all. Their local fixtures were given the same test credential the
plant hives already use - a local, reversible seed change, made rather than spoofing a session, because a
walk that fakes its identity is the *probe's-persona-was-an-admin* failure in a new costume.

### Three of the six hives could not LIVE the stories, and that is a seeding job

The first J2 walk ("breakdown to diagnose to close-out") found the plant hives whole - six of six steps
arriving, the identity held across every hop, the chain reading 27 to 36 rows as the person - and the three
fleet hives **empty**: Dela Cruz Delivery Fleet, Ramos Jeepney Line and Tan Delivery Vans held vehicles and
**zero logbook entries**. They were seeded as a vehicle registry, never as an operating fleet, so more than
twenty archetypes had nothing to be true about in half the platform's own verticals.

Missing data is a seeding job, never a blocker. `tools/seed_fleet_history.py` writes eight believable jobs
per fleet - oil changes, brake pads, an alternator that stopped charging mid-route, an LTO roadworthiness
pre-check - **against the units each fleet already owns** (a 2026 Ford Ranger XLT, a 2023 Toyota HiAce
Commuter, a 2019 Nissan LEAF), reported by that fleet's own supervisor, every row marked and reversible with
`--revert`. Verified through the product's own read path: a fleet supervisor's PostgREST token returns them.

**It took three attempts, and the two failures are the lesson.** The seeder wrote 0 rows twice and said so
quietly, because the helper swallowed the error that named the cause: `logbook.date` is NOT NULL with no
default, and `status` is a CHECK over `Open/Closed/Resolved` - **"Completed" was my word, not the table's**.
The same vocabulary error the whole wave keeps finding, this time in a seeder rather than a lens.

### What the threads between pages actually look like

`tools/report_journey_threads.py` classifies every readable hop the walks have taken - the page carries the
next one in its OWN body, it is reachable only through the shared drawer, or there is no way onward at all.
A hop is counted only if its page arrived and finished rendering, because a thread read on a page that
bounced says nothing about the page it was supposed to be.

Across the first 61 readable hops:

| | hops | share |
|---|---|---|
| the page's own link | 14 | 23% |
| the nav drawer only | 35 | 57% |
| no way onward | 12 | 20% |

**Four pages never carried their own onward link at all** - logbook (14 hops), asset-hub (12), shift-brain
(8), pm-scheduler (7). Every move from them requires opening the drawer. That is not a defect; each page
works and the drawer is one tap away. It is a design observation with a number on it: **a journey where four
fifths of the hops need shared chrome is a set of tools rather than a path**, and the places where a person
is most likely to want the next surface - the alert they just read, the PM they just planned - are exactly
where the page says nothing about where to go next.

**One caveat, stated because the number would otherwise be read as worse than it is.** Most of these hops
were walked BEFORE the nav-mode repair, while a supervisor's drawer was missing Analytics, the Alert Hub and
Reports - so the two dominant *no way onward* pairs (`pm-scheduler -> analytics`, 5, and
`alert-hub -> asset-hub`, 4) are partly that defect rather than a missing link. The report now says so, and
the pairs are re-measured on walks taken after the repair. **A count taken across a fix is two counts.**

### THE WAVE'S FIRST PRODUCT DEFECT: every supervisor navigated with a worker's menu

The journey walks kept reporting *"1 hop(s) have no way onward at all"* on hops whose pages were fully
rendered and settled - `pm-scheduler -> alert-hub`, `pm-scheduler -> analytics`. Unlike the thin readings,
that finding **survived every correction to the reader**, which is what made it worth chasing.

The nav hub was identical on all four pages checked (31 KB, 17 links) and contained **neither
`alert-hub.html` nor `analytics.html`** - while `nav-hub.js` plainly declares both, tagged
`roles: ['supervisor']`. The person walking was a supervisor.

**The mechanism.** `getMode()` reads `wh_nav_mode`; if it holds a valid mode it wins. Otherwise `_defaultMode()`
derives one from `wh_hive_role` **and persists it**. The first page anybody meets renders the hub while nobody
is signed in - so the derivation ran with no role, returned `field`, stored it, and the stored value won for
ever after. Measured live, both by the ordinary arrival and by a control that signed in first:

| | role | stored mode | hub links | Analytics | Alert Hub | Reports |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | supervisor | **field** | 17 | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |
| after | supervisor | supervisor | **24** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

**Why no per-page test could see it.** Every one of those pages works when you arrive by URL. The defect is
not on a page; it is in the thread between pages. This is precisely the class the full-journey wave was built
for, and it was invisible to 2,437 rows of per-page work.

**The repair keeps the original intent** - *"existing users with an explicit choice keep it"* - by recording
WHY a mode was stored (`wh_nav_mode_src`: `chosen` | `derived` | `guess`). A chosen mode is never touched; a
mode guessed before the role was known is re-derived when the role arrives. Locked by
`tools/prove_nav_mode.mjs` (gate `nav-mode`) with teeth in both directions, because a repair that hands
everyone the supervisor menu is a worse defect than the one it fixes: a worker still gets the tight field
set, and a supervisor who chose Field keeps Field.

**The class worth carrying:** a value derived from identity, cached before identity is known, and never
re-derived. Whenever a default is computed from who somebody is, ask when it is first computed - and if that
can happen before they are known, record whether it was a guess or a decision.

### W3-LN's Internal-Control lens, and a warning the critic sweep needs before it runs

A learn article is the front door for a stranger with no account and no reason to trust it, so it owes
sources and a freshness statement. Measured across all 54: **54 name sources or the authority behind them
(DOE, IEA, DOLE, PSA, ERC, PSME…) and 54 say how fresh they are.** Gate `learn-provenance`.

**Only 2 of 54 carry a `.wh-source-chip`, and that is deliberately NOT a finding.** No generator emits one
for learn pages; the two that have it picked it up during other work on those specific articles. The chip is
a product-surface convention, and prose that says *"According to the Department of Energy"* with a dateline
serves the same reader need on a page that is mostly prose.

**This matters for the wave that comes next.** The critic program is scheduled to grade all 53 learn articles
on the full rubric, and the rubric's `E3` dimension looks for exactly that chip. Run as-is, it will return
**51 failures for a chip those pages were never designed to have** - a rubric-fit problem wearing the costume
of 51 defects, and the largest single block of false findings this wave could still produce. **Fixed in the rubric, before the sweep ran.** `E3` now asks whether a READER can check the claim, and on
an article accepts the sentence: a page under `/learn/` that names its sources or the authority behind
them AND states its freshness scores the dimension in full, while every product surface still owes the
chip. `rubric-parity` stays green (102 prose / 102 spec). The 51 findings were prevented rather than
triaged - which is the cheaper half of the same lesson, and the only half available before a sweep runs.

Recording it before the sweep runs is the cheap half of the lesson this whole wave keeps re-learning:
**a checker meeting a page type it was not written for produces confident nonsense at scale.**

### W3-CL's Internal-Control lens: all 60 calculators cite their standard, and the seventh vocabulary catch

An engineering calculator's number goes into a drawing, so it owes a citation an engineer can actually look
up. Measured from the generated pages: **60 of 60 cite a standard with the number they would open it at** -
`ASHRAE 62.1:2022 Ventilation Rate Procedure`, `ISO 22400-2`, `IEEE 18-2012`, `PEC 2017 Art. 4.50`,
`Philippine Plumbing Code §P-1101`, `CTI STD-201`. Standing gate `calc-citations`.

**That number moved twice before it settled, and the route is worth keeping.** It read 60, then 11, then 60:

| pass | verdict | what was actually being measured |
|---|---|---|
| first | 60/60 name standard AND clause | the clause half matched **HTML tag names** - `<section a…`, `<article c…`, the words *"table t"* - because the pattern allowed a letter after the keyword. Right answer, wrong reason. |
| second | 11/60 name a clause | tightened to demand a digit, which was correct - and then demanded the literal words *Table* or *Section*, which is **my** convention, not an engineer's |
| third | 60/60 cite specifically | the real question: does the citation carry the number you open the book at? `ISO 22400-2` and `ASHRAE 62.1:2022` do; a bare "ASHRAE" would not |

**A live read is what exposed the first pass.** The browser, reading rendered text, found no clause where the
static check found sixty - and a tag is invisible to one instrument and a citation to the other. **When two
instruments disagree, the disagreement is the finding**; here it cost an hour and produced a checker that
knows the difference between markup and a reference.

And the second pass is the more familiar failure: correcting an error by over-correcting into my own
vocabulary, which is the same move this wave has caught seven other times wearing seven other costumes.

Getting there took one more correction of the kind this wave keeps making. A first pass demanded an acronym
followed immediately by a digit and reported that **17 calculators named no standard at all** - the septic
tank, the grease trap, the storm drain, water treatment, the boilers. Reading four of them refuted it in one
line each:

| calculator | what it actually cites | why the pattern missed it |
|---|---|---|
| septic tank | **Plumbing Code §P-1101** | Philippine plumbing code, not an NFPA-style acronym |
| storm drain | **DPWH Blue Book**, Rational Method | a national agency and a method, not a numbered standard |
| water treatment | **PNS 1998 / PNSDW** | Philippine National Standards |
| boiler steam | **ASME BPVC Section I** | BPVC is letters; the pattern demanded a digit |

**The pages the checker accused were the ones most correctly localized.** A checker that only knows
NFPA/ASHRAE/ISO shapes will always flag a Philippine platform's plumbing and sanitary work first - which is
the whole vocabulary lesson, arriving through the front door of a wave built to avoid it. The gate now knows
the National Plumbing Code, the PSME Code, PNS, PNSDW, DPWH, DENR DAO, PD/RA numbers, BPVC, and the named
methods (Rational, Hazen-Williams, Darcy, Manning, Colebrook).

### W3-SC's Internal-Control lens, answered from the sources - and deliberately not called a finding

The shared-component wave asks whether a shared piece ever keeps one person's state where the next person
inherits it. That is answerable from the sources before any browser opens: of 13 storage writes across the
shared scripts, **3 carry an owner in the key and 10 do not.**

Most of the ten are device-scoped by design and no leak at all - a session id, a signup source, a retry
counter, a told-you-once flag, the analytics consent (which belongs to the browser, not the person). Three
are different in kind: `wh_voice_lang_pref`, `wh_voice_brevity` and `wh_voice_journal_persona` are personal
choices, and the sign-out path clears only `wh_last_worker`. On a shared plant tablet - a cell this wave
walks on purpose - the next person inherits the previous one's voice language, brevity and AI persona.

**It is recorded as a candidate, not a finding, and the counter-argument is why.** The platform already
treats `wh_lang`, the interface language, as a device preference, and nobody would call that a leak; voice
language is the same shape. The one that is genuinely personal is the AI persona. A static read cannot settle
whether these should follow the device or the person - that is a product judgement, and the walk plus Ian's
call decide it.

Saying so costs nothing and protects the wave's credibility: **a night that caught a dozen of its own false
findings should not spend that credit on a design question dressed as a defect.**

### W3-FN opened, and the probe that timed out before the platform did

The function wave asks three things of each of the 62 edge functions: it must refuse a caller holding a real
token for another hive (with a sentinel from that hive absent from the reply), degrade legibly when its
dependency is down, and answer its documented shape to somebody who actually calls it.

Its first run reported three functions that *"never returned - a hang is not a degradation a person can
read"*. **The platform bounds those calls; my prober did not wait for the bound.** `_shared/ai-chain.ts`
wraps every provider call in `AbortSignal.timeout(60000)` and allows one jittered retry pass before degrading
to `"{}"` - a worst case of about two minutes, by design. The prober gives up at 35 seconds, so *"the call
never returned"* was the probe abandoning it, reported as three functions hanging.

Corrected: a timeout in the prober is **not evidence** when the source shows a bounded provider call with a
degradation path, and remains a finding when nothing in the source bounds it at all. Re-run, `agentic-rag-loop`
passes all three lenses and `ai-eval-runner`'s timeouts are reported as unreadable rather than as hangs - six
false findings prevented in eight functions.

**The rule this adds to the wave's collection: a probe's patience must exceed the platform's own.** A
timeout shorter than the system's declared bound cannot distinguish "it hung" from "I left".

### A page that is WAITING is not a page that failed

`analytics-report.html` was read still-thin in **4 of 4** walks that touched it - the highest rate of any
page - and each time the walk recorded *"never finished rendering, wait ran out"*. Reading the page settles
it: the report is built only when somebody presses **Generate**. Its resting state is a small, action-first
shell around that button, and 527 characters is the design rather than a failure.

That is the third distinct way this wave's render floor has been wrong, and the pattern in all three is the
same: **a size threshold is a proxy, and every proxy eventually meets a case it was not written for.** First
it called load-thinned pages "leads nowhere"; then it called a two-phase load "almost nothing"; now it called
a deliberately compact page "never finished".

The rule is no longer size alone. A step is thin only if it is **short AND offers nothing to do** - three or
more of the page's own visible controls means the page is complete and waiting for a person, not broken. The
settle loop uses the same test, so the walk stops spending its whole budget on a page that finished in a
second.

### What the journey wave costs to walk, measured rather than hoped

At the throughput this host actually delivers - about two and a half minutes per whole story, once the
session is cached, the chains are read up front and only one walk runs at a time:

| tier | journeys | browser time |
|---|---|---|
| A base cast | 130 | ~5.4 h |
| B device + Filipino | 381 | ~15.9 h |
| C overlays | 197 | ~8.2 h |
| D lifetimes | 16 | ~0.7 h |
| **all four** | **724** | **~30 h** |

That is the honest size of W3-JN, and it is why the runner is built the way it is: one archetype at a time,
a lock that refuses a second drive, a wait for the stack before each archetype, a re-walk of any run that
lost it, and banking after each archetype rather than at the end. **A thirty-hour walk that has to restart
from zero after a wedge is not a walk; a thirty-hour walk that banks every six journeys is a queue.**

The order is deliberate: tier A first, because it is the only tier where every archetype-and-vertical pair
appears exactly once - it is the map. B, C and D are the same stories under a different device, language,
moment or condition, and they are worth most once the base cast is known to hold.

### The re-walk confirms the fix, in the only way that counts

`J1` was re-walked after the nav-mode repair, and the measurement it was queued for came back clean: **zero
hops with no way onward, in every hive.** Before the repair, `J1` and `J2` reported dead hops on
`pm-scheduler -> alert-hub` and `pm-scheduler -> analytics` - the two surfaces the supervisor's drawer was
missing. After it, `W33` (Baguio Textile Mills) and `W34` (Dela Cruz Delivery Fleet) walk all six steps,
keep the identity and read their chain, and pass.

That is the loop closing on itself: a journey walk found a defect no per-page test could see, the repair was
verified in three directions and locked behind a gate, and **the same walk re-run is now the evidence that
the fix worked** - not an argument that it should have.

The rows that still hold in that batch hold for reasons of the moment rather than of the product: two casts
met `WH_DB_TIMEOUT` from a local auth server under load, and one story arrived at 1 of 6 pages while a
62-function contract sweep had the host. Both are the contention this wave has now made structurally
impossible - every browser prover takes a single shared slot before it launches, so the suite's concurrent
gates queue instead of racing. **The findings from before that lock are about the lock's absence.**

### A fix invalidates the evidence taken before it

The nav-mode repair changed what a supervisor's drawer contains, so every hop the walks measured toward
Analytics, the Alert Hub or Reports **before** that repair is stale: those hops read `none` for a reason that
no longer exists. `J1` and `J2` are queued for a re-walk on that basis alone - `W35` (Ramos Jeepney Line) was
held for exactly one finding, *"1 hop has no way onward at all"* on `pm-scheduler -> alert-hub`, and that hop
is precisely what the fix restored.

This is a small discipline with a sharp edge: **a repair does not only change the product, it expires a
subset of the measurements taken against it.** The queue now carries the re-walk explicitly rather than
leaving those rows held against a defect that is gone, and `tools/report_journey_threads.py` prints the same
caveat above its census so the number is never read as current when half its hops predate the fix.

### RETRACTED: content waits behind identity

The section below was recorded as *"a correlation across six pages plus a mechanism, not a proven cause"* and
marked for re-check on wider data. **The wider data refutes it.** Measured across every walk so far - 12
pages with three or more readable reads each, counting how often each was read still under the render floor
against how many sequential identity round-trips it makes:

| page | read thin | reads | identity hops |
|---|---|---|---|
| analytics-report | 100% | 4 | 4 |
| pm-scheduler | 67% | 18 | 6 |
| inventory | 50% | 6 | 4 |
| asset-hub | 35% | 20 | 6 |
| alert-hub | 21% | 14 | 5 |
| **logbook** | **0%** | **24** | **9** |
| analytics | 0% | 15 | 2 |

The median identity-hop count is **4 for the pages that read thin at least half the time and 4 for the pages
that never do** - and `logbook`, with the most identity hops of any page measured, never read thin once in
24 reads. The mechanism was plausible, the six-page table was convincing, and the relationship is not there.

**What survives:** some pages consistently need longer than the walk's budget on this host, and which pages
those are is stable. Why is still open, and the honest place to answer it is a quiet host, not a wider regex.

**What this cost, and why it was cheap:** the claim was hedged when it was written, so retracting it is a
paragraph rather than a retraction of banked evidence. **A finding recorded with its confidence attached can
be withdrawn; one recorded as fact has to be defended.**

### The journeys' first substantive finding: content waits behind identity

Across every J1 and J2 walk, the same pages were repeatedly caught still empty and the same pages were always
full - and the readings were identical to the character, which is the signature of a reader arriving before
the page fills rather than a page that is broken. The question worth asking is *why those pages*.

Counting the identity round-trips each page makes before its first data call answers it:

| page | `auth.getSession` | `restoreIdentityFromSession` | `validateHiveMembership` | how the walks read it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| analytics | 1 | 1 | 0 | always full (5,120 chars) |
| alert-hub | 2 | 3 | 0 | usually full (4,995) |
| shift-brain | 1 | 2 | 2 | mixed (914 - 3,928) |
| logbook | 3 | 2 | 4 | usually thin (916 - 1,196) |
| asset-hub | 2 | 2 | 2 | usually thin (609) |
| **pm-scheduler** | **3** | **1** | **2** | **never filled inside a journey** |

`pm-scheduler`'s `init()` is the clearest case: it awaits `restoreIdentityFromSession`, then
`auth.getSession`, then `validateHiveMembership` - three sequential round-trips - before anything asks for a
PM. When the local auth service is slow (and on this host it is: the walks also collect `WH_DB_TIMEOUT` on
sign-in), the page holds at its shell with nothing to read.

**This is an Adaptability finding, not a bug.** Each await is individually correct - the page must know who
is asking before it shows a hive's work. What a person meets is the compound: the more identity hops a page
makes in sequence, the longer it shows them an empty screen with no explanation, and the ordering is the same
whether the walk is fast or slow. The candidate improvements are to overlap the data read with the identity
check where the read is already hive-scoped and RLS-protected anyway, or to say *"checking your access"*
rather than showing an empty page.

**Stated honestly: this is a correlation across six pages plus a mechanism, not a proven cause.** It is
recorded as the journey wave's first substantive candidate and is re-checked on a quiet host, where a page
that still will not fill is the page's problem and one that fills is the host's.

### W3-AR pre-sorted, and the sixth narrow search

The 79 empty (page, layer) squares were sorted before walking by asking each page's source whether it shows
any evidence of the layer it owes. Reading the page ALONE said **fifteen** layers were absent outright - ten
of them rate limiting, on achievements, analytics-report, audit-log, founder-console, integrations,
marketplace-admin, pm-scheduler, project-manager, project-report and skillmatrix.

All ten load `utils.js`, which carries twenty-two rate-limit references and the central `whAiErrorMapper`.
Counting each page **plus the scripts it loads** - which is what a page IS to the person using it - the
absent count falls to **zero**: all 79 squares have something to grade, and the walk decides what a person
actually sees.

That is the sixth time in one session that a search scoped to where I expected the answer produced an
accusation the platform did not deserve: the nav drawer, the alert table, the settle gap, the function
callers, the article call-to-action, and now the shared error handler. **Shared chrome is part of the page**
- the rule was already written down after a page-floor walk counted the hub's buttons as the page's own, and
it needed applying to a static scan too.

### W3-LN's first finding, and the false one it nearly was

The learn wave's Functionality lens asks whether the tool an article sends you to opens and does the job the
article promised. Asked statically across all 54 articles, the first answer looked damning: **only 6 of 54
link to any of the platform's 60 free calculators**, while all 54 funnel to a sign-up. That is a real
measurement and it was about to become a finding for 48 rows.

Matching each calculator-less article to its nearest calculator is what refuted it. Of 48 articles, **one**
produced a confident match, and that match was wrong (an FMEA bottling-line worked example paired with a wire
sizing calculator). The overlap is absent because the articles are practice guides - FMEA, lock-out/tag-out,
shift handover, CMMS-versus-spreadsheet - and the calculators are engineering sizing tools. *"An article
should link to a calculator"* was my expected shape, not the platform's; the articles name the surfaces they
are actually about, and they link to those (analytics 9, logbook 7, asset-hub 5, pm-scheduler 5).

**What survived is small, exact and worth fixing: three articles offered a reader nothing to DO but sign up**
- `best-free-cmms-software-philippines`, `workhive-vs-maintainx-comparison`, and
`workhive-vs-upkeep-free-cmms-comparison`. All three are the comparison articles somebody reads *while
deciding*, which is exactly where a thing to try is worth more than a form. Each now closes by naming two
free calculators that need no account, beside the sign-up rather than instead of it. Re-measured: **zero**
articles offer nothing but the sign-up.

The pattern is the night's pattern, one more time: **a measurement that indicts 48 surfaces is a hypothesis
about my vocabulary; the one that indicts three is a finding.**

### The reading that was stable, reproducible and wrong

`pm-scheduler.html` read **493 characters** on every hive, on every run, loaded and quiet alike. That
stability is what made it convincing: the walk's render floor had been calling thin steps "unreadable, blame
the host", and a number that repeats exactly is not a host. So the floor was split - a step still showing
skeletons is unreadable, a step that settled clean and is still thin is a **finding about what the person was
shown** - and this one was about to be written up as a defect.

Opened alone, with a longer wait, the same page renders **2,617 characters** of real content. It paints its
shell in under a second, holds still while its PM list is in flight, and only then fills. The settle loop was
waiting for the text to stop changing, and the text had stopped changing - in the gap between the shell and
the answer.

**Two rules came out of it, and both are now in the instrument.** A page is not settled while it is still
asking: the walk requires no REST or RPC read in flight, and none for 1.2 seconds, before it believes a
reading. And **reproducibility proves the reader is consistent, never that the reading is true** - "the same
493 in every hive on every run" is exactly what a systematically early reader produces.

The same pass found the identity oracle passing any step whose hive key was EMPTY (`!hive || hive ===
expected`) - which is precisely the state a page leaves behind when it revokes a member and drops to solo
scope. The one page that can throw a member out would have read as *identity kept*. It compares against the
expected value now, never against "or nothing".

**And the sign-ins were the throughput problem.** Every story re-authenticated, so a wave of 724 journeys
meant 724 sign-ins against a local auth server that answers `WH_DB_TIMEOUT` when this host is busy - walks
failing because the probe asked the same question 724 times, not because the platform refused. The session is
minted once per person-and-hive and replayed as storage state, which is also what a real person carries from
one page to the next. With that and the settle loop, a whole story costs about two minutes instead of seven.

### The host is part of the instrument

This box has ~0.3 GB free of 7.8 GB with the Supabase stack running. Two node jobs at once produced a docker
engine returning 500, a `docker exec` that never came back, and a six-journey walk **frozen at zero CPU with
no output and no error** - because `execSync` waits for ever by default. Every shell-out in the wave-3
provers now carries a timeout and a kill signal, and the walks run one at a time. The stack recovered on its
own the moment the browser load stopped, so nothing was restarted: the evidence said "starved", not "broken".

## §LX · The LAYER-UX wave — what a person FEELS when a layer misbehaves (Ian, 2026-09-06)

Ian: *"we have to expand the trajectories more to those uncharted, uncovered, unexplored... I want it more to improve
the UFAI UI UX for every Full Stack SaaS Layer I have"*, and *"those layers that have less trajectories, we have to
make more for those."* He chose the framing (**what the person feels**, not whether the layer is internally correct)
and the size (**exhaustive across all 13 layers**).

**THE AXIS DID NOT EXIST UNTIL THIS WAVE.** Rows have carried a `layers` field since the P-program, but only the
seeder ever wrote it: on 2026-09-06 it was populated on **704 rows and empty on 725** — every T, VP, VD and VM row,
which is to say every persona journey, the half of the program most about what a person experiences. A per-layer
number over half the rows is not a number. `tools/backfill_trajectory_layers.py` closed that: every row now names
the layers its journey crosses, multi-tagged the way the field already worked (597 rows carried more than one
before the backfill). 95 of the 725 matched no rule and took the stated default `["F"]`; the script prints that
count on every run so the default can never quietly become the answer.

**WHY HOSTING IS THE POINT.** The same day, a walk found the repo shipping Cloudflare `_headers` and a
`netlify.toml` to a **Vercel** host, which reads neither — so no security header had ever been served in production
and `/_fixtures/` answered 200. There were 1,429 trajectories and not one asked what the deployed origin actually
hands a person. Hosting held 38 rows after backfill and was the least-WALKED layer of all, 18 of 38.

**THE DEFICIT, AND THE HEADLINE MOVING.** With every row tagged, the generated header could state the gap against a
90-row target: CI 15 (+75) · L 31 (+59) · LB 33 (+57) · H 38 (+52) · RL 45 (+45) · S 66 (+24). `tools/seed_layer_ux_wave.py`
seeded those **316 rows** at `specced`, and the headline dropped from **91.4% of 1,377 to 74.3% of 1,693** the moment
they landed. That drop is the honest direction and the generator computes it — the same discipline as the tightening
earlier the same day, which moved the number 64.6% → 49.9% when "closed" began requiring the right instrument.

| Layer | Lens — each row is this sentence on one surface |
|---|---|
| **CI** CI/CD | a release lands mid-session and the page changes under you · a feature arrives half-on · a migration ships ahead of its screen · you cannot say which version broke · a rollback takes your unsaved work |
| **L** Logs | the error you hit leaves no trace · "something went wrong" where the log knew exactly what · nothing to quote to support · your failure reached nobody |
| **LB** Scaling | past twenty people the page slows and never says so · the list stops paginating · the export carries less than the screen · two of you act at once and one loses silently |
| **H** Hosting | a feature dead in prod because the origin sends no header · a link that 404s in prod and opens for its author · a redirect that loses what you arrived with · an asset re-downloaded every visit |
| **RL** Rate limits | refused without being told when to return · someone else spent your hive's limit · your retry makes it worse and nothing warns you |
| **S** Security | refused in a way that tells you nothing, or too much · you can see it but must not act, and the page does not say which |

**THE WALK ORDER AND ITS INSTRUMENTS** follow §LW.1 — the lens picks the instrument, and a layer with no MCP is a
queue item, not an excuse. Thinnest first: **CI** (github MCP + the gate suite), **L** (sentry + grafana, the outside
witnesses), **H** (raw-http against the deployed origin — `tools/prove_prod_headers.mjs` already exists — plus a
**Vercel MCP to connect**), **LB** (postgres MCP for query cost as a hive grows, playwright for what the page does,
**k6 to install** for the local load tier), **RL** (a raw-http burst plus postgres for the bucket), **S** (the
`tenant-refusal` gate built this wave). Two MCPs to connect proactively — **Vercel**, and bringing **chrome-devtools**
live for the caching lenses — and one tool to install, **k6**.

#### ★THE WAVE WAS SEEDED 297 ROWS TOO WIDE — non-production subjects, descoped (Ian, 2026-09-30)

**production** page"* — and violated anyway, because the seeder took `served_pages()` wholesale. It put **297 rows
onto 11 surfaces no customer persona ever visits**, and `validate_auto_discovery.NON_TOOL_PAGES` had named every one

archival, never in nav"**; `design-system.html` carries Ian's own 2026-07-17 ruling *"internal tool page, NOT
family"*; `llm-observability`, `agentic-rag-observability`, `validator-catalog` and `status` are admin/devops
