`tools/prove_double_fire.mjs`'s write-holding shim installed before any page script: every mutating request counted
and HELD in the page, so nothing landed. Each write flow is the prover's own (lifted verbatim, one source): reached the
way a person reaches it, its submit pressed, then pressed again while the first write was in flight.

**Measured.** Every graded write held at one on two presses and showed it was busy: logbook Save Entry, the seller's
Save Changes, the change order, the report send and contacts, inventory Save Part and Confirm Use, the skill exam,
alert dismissal, the FMEA save, the companion send, hive's Leave, the marketplace post, the resume save, community post
and reply, all three PM-scheduler writes, shift-brain's re-run, the vehicle create, Platform Actions' triage, both
day-planner saves. Writes a cast is not offered were said, not passed: logbook's asset registration and shift-brain's
Weibull fit for these workers, the landing page's updates form (shown only to visitors), and the two retired pages
(founder console, Marketplace Admin - its actions moved to Platform Actions, which held). The retry half: utils.js
re-sends GET only, so the platform never repeats a write; a person's retry after a lost reply is
`refresh-retry-dedup`'s.

**Found and fixed.**
- **A second Leave Hive could start while the first was in flight.** A leave is an awaited audit row then the delete;
  the menu item stayed live, so a second tap and its confirmation ran performLeave again - a second member_left row, a
  delete that removes nothing, and "you have NOT left" over a leave that worked. Teeth: with the guard switched off in
  the page, answering the second confirmation fired a second write (1 -> 2); with it, no second confirmation, 1 write.
  One leave at a time now, the item reading "Leaving...".
- **The prover graded less than it claimed.** "Send Reports" now asks before sending to an address outside the hive,
  so the prover's flow opened the dialog and graded nothing on the platform's one irreversible send; it answers the
  confirmation as the sender would and grades PASS. The marketplace post flow starved its own page by holding read RPCs
  sent as POSTs (530 characters rendered); they are named and let through. Six flows were added (vehicle, post, seller
  edit, admin approve, Platform Actions triage, hive leave, the updates form).

**Locked.** `double-submit-lock` keeps the hive leave anchors (the binding scan cannot see an inline confirm-then-write
handler; removing the guard fails it), `refresh-retry-dedup`, and `cb_double_fire` with the new flows.

### §SL.8 Walk 8 — A4 slow reads: the client asked every timed-out read four times, and pages waited, went blank or walled in silence (2026-10-19)

**The ask.** "The platform must show a skeleton, time out, and say how fresh the data is when this page's reads are
slow." 30 pages, each as its row's cast at phone-390 and desktop-1280, in a service-worker-blocked context with fetch
patched before any page script: every data read answered 5 s late (the wait judged at 1.8 s, the freshness once the
reads had landed and stayed quiet), then every data read hung with the platform's own timeout knob set to 6 s (judged
once every hung read had been given up, five samples over five seconds). A timeline probe (every 2 s for 75 s) was used
where one moment could not tell "speaks late" from "never speaks".

**Measured.** All 30 pass at both widths under the final code: a wait said at 1.8 s, nothing still loading once the data
landed, the freshness said (or, behind an access wall, no figures to date), and a failure sentence once the timeout gave
up with nothing left claiming to load. design-system makes no data reads. analytics' two empty lines under hung reads
are true - its figures come from the analytics function's server-side reads, which the browser hang never reaches, and
the database agrees (0 parts transactions in 30 days, 0 quality readings on all 8 assets).

**Found and fixed.**
- **The client asked every timed-out read four times.** supabase-js 2.110 retries a rejected GET three more times (1, 2,
  4 s apart) unless the rejection is named AbortError, and the shell's timeout aborted with a TimeoutError. Measured:
  v_hives_truth asked at 0.3, 7.3, 15.3 and 25.3 s on three pages; marketplace's counts took 62 s. At the production
  45 s timeout a dead backend held every read 3 min 7 s, per link of every chain. A REST timeout now reaches the client
  as an AbortError with the same WH_DB_TIMEOUT message (every timeout test still matches); a refused connection keeps
  its quick retries. Pages now say a read failed within one timeout.
- **The settle pass knew one skeleton spelling.** community's pre-JS feed and leaderboard shapes (.skeleton) shimmered
  for the whole 75 s under "part of this page could not be loaded". A container of nothing but empty shapes now gets the
  same "could not load this section" card, only while a service is still failing, never inside a composite skeleton.
  The pass also knows "Checking...", hides a settled line's own shapes (skill-matrix), tells pages the reads failed
  (report-sender's contacts card stopped "checking"), and drops a chip's "Checking" clause ("Read failed · Checking").
- **Wait states that came too late.** resume painted nothing in its form until its identity and role reads answered (63 s
  blank with reads hung); its skeleton now comes first, and after a failed load no section says "Nothing here yet." under
  "this is a loading problem, not an empty resume". ai-quality shows its skeleton before its first read.
- **Gates that showed nothing, or the old page.** The two admin pages that hide the whole document while the admin check
  runs (agentic-rag and LLM observability) were a blank screen; they say "Checking your access..." now. Marketplace Admin
  showed its moderation tiles as bare dashes to everyone until the answer; it holds them back behind the same line.
- **Could not ask is not "no", twice more.** An unanswered hive lookup walled a solo owner with "Supervisor access only"
  (integrations) - now "Your access could not be checked" with Reload. A role check that could not be asked walled in
  silence; plant-connections and integrations now say the wall is the role this device last saw. The hive lookup and
  the role check carry the third answer (whStartupHive .unread, _whRoleUnread). A walled worker's page no longer paints
  a figures line over the wall.
- **Lines with nothing behind them.** project-report's chooser listed live projects and statuses with no source line (it
  has one now). analytics told a hive with 8 PM assets "No PM assets or scope items found." - it says no scope items
  were due in the period.
- **The instruments were wrong eight times before the pages were.** The shared failure vocabulary every prover imports
  matched only a straight apostrophe, so the platform's own "Couldn’t load ..." read as silent (and the walk generators
  read node's output in the Windows codepage, which garbled the apostrophe set anyway). The walk also counted a Retry
  label, a failure sentence that mentions loading, inert content behind a retired overlay and a labelled skeleton
  SPECIMEN as waiting, and missed a gate card outside main. Each was corrected before its page was judged.

**Locked.** `slow-read-honest` holds the shell fixes (the timeout fails once; every skeleton spelling settles; Checking;
wh:reads-failed; the third answers; the pending-line inert exemption), 22 page anchors, the restored sentences and the
curly apostrophe - 11 mutation tests, each failing it. `skeleton-labelled`, `waiting-is-spoken` and `skeleton_resolves`
keep the live floor.

### §SL.9 Walk 9 — AV2 offline queue and sync: the queue drained in key order, a part's ledger entry was lost, and a resume's "will sync later" never did (2026-10-20)

**The ask.** "The platform must queue what this page writes while offline and sync it once, in order, when the network
returns." 33 pages, each as its row's cast at phone-390 and desktop-1280. Every write flow the three provers carry for
the page (prove_offline_queued's captures, prove_offline_refusal's online-only writes, prove_double_fire's flows -
lifted verbatim; a verb scan where none covers the page) reached online, then the network cut (context offline,
navigator.onLine false, the offline event) and the control pressed: HELD (queued, told, and on return sent once per
queued item with the queue emptied), REFUSED (nothing queued, told it needs a connection, nothing sent later) or not
offered. Every write a queue sent on return was answered in the page, so nothing landed. Then the ORDER probe: two items
through each registered queue, the first with the LATER key.

**Measured.** All 33 pass at both widths under the final code. HELD and synced once, in order: logbook entries (form
and wizard), inventory parts and uses, skill targets, FMEA modes, community posts, PM completions, day-planner items,
progress logs, the resume. REFUSED in the platform's own sentence: every approval, money, role, AI and compute action
walked. Eleven pages offer no write to their cast (read-only pages, two retired pointers, a worker's wall).

**Found and fixed.**
- **The queue drained in KEY order.** offline-queue.js and logbook's own queue read getAll(), which IndexedDB orders by
  key, and the keys are random UUIDs: made 1 then 2, synced 2 then 1 - server-stamped times then showed a person's two
  offline posts swapped. Both stamp queued_at at enqueue (a re-queued row keeps its place) and drain by it.
- **A part's ledger entry was fired at a dead network.** Adding a part offline queued the part, while its opening stock
  entry - the ledger the stock figure is mirrored from - and its audit row were sent and lost. Offline Use and Restock
  fell back to an absolute stock write plus a ledger insert, both lost, under "This part did not save... try again".
  Now an item may name its own table (the entry and audit row wait behind the part) and the atomic Use/Restock
  functions queue as themselves (allowlisted per queue). A refused replay is checked against the row it writes: the
  staged-stock guard refused a replayed deduct before the unique check could - proven against the real database, the
  landed deduct was recognised and nothing moved twice.
- **Resume's "will sync later" never synced.** Reconnecting only toggled a banner, and the next load preferred the older
  cloud copy, so the next keystroke overwrote the offline work. An offline save is now marked pending, backed up on
  reconnect ("Your offline changes are now backed up to your account.") and preferred on load.
- **Five online-only actions fired at a dead network.** Project-manager's change order (it blamed the change-order
  number), analytics' risk recompute ("Recompute failed. Try again shortly."), shift-brain's re-run (it told a supervisor
  to "Run npx supabase functions serve" - in production too), the hive's focus and the Weibull fit now refuse before
  sending; the re-run's planner-unreachable sentence is a person's.
- **The provers had rotted in two places.** The hive-intent flow only knew the first-run prompt (a hive that already
  chose a focus reopens it from its chip); the Weibull flow toggled the reliability workbench open and then shut again.
  Both fixed in tools/prove_double_fire.mjs. The walk's own instrument was wrong seven times first (recorded in the
  instrument family): Playwright selectors read as absent, offline chrome read as a refusal, a kept report dialog
  answered as a confirmation, among them.

**Locked.** `offline-sync-in-order` (20 anchors, 8 mutation tests) holds the queue order, the per-item table and the
allowlisted function op, the landed-replay check, inventory's queued companions and atomic calls, resume's sync, the
five up-front refusals and the absence of the developer command; `offline-queued`, `queue-drain`, `offline-write-guard`
and `offline_queue_confirm` keep the live and static floor. Open, not this layer's: inventory-ledger-reconciled reads 16
historical ledger rows (2026-06-23 to 2026-09-10) whose chain does not add up - data that predates this walk.

### §SL.10 Walk 10 — AV3 degraded mode: a blocked live channel froze 9 of 11 pages, and four lines still said they were live (2026-10-20)

**The ask.** "The platform must keep this page current by polling when the live channel is blocked or down, and say
that it is not live." 14 pages, each as its row's cast at phone-390 and desktop-1280. A control load with the realtime
websocket allowed records what the page says when it IS live; then the page loaded with the websocket closed the moment
it opened (a plant firewall's shape) and watched for 12 s + 70 s: every data read after the channel failed timed and
grouped into rounds (a poll is a round of reads repeating with nobody touching the page), and every visible word and
source line read. A page whose channel belongs to one thing is opened on it, as a person does (asset-hub subscribes only
for an open asset).

**Measured before the fix.** 9 of the 11 pages with a live channel never read again: a teammate's log entry, a used
part, a completed PM, a posted reply, a new listing, an earned badge - none arrived for the whole visit. Only alert-hub
and platform-actions moved, on their own 60 s refreshes. Four lines still claimed to be live: project-manager and hive
"updates automatically", community "ONLINE NOW" over a presence list nobody could fill, and audit-log "Live updates on"
for what is a 30 s poll with no channel at all. The shared helper that degrades to polling (whRealtimeSubscribe) had no
adopters: every page subscribes through rtConn(), which only painted a connection state; hive and community re-read
after a DROP, but with the socket closed from the start nothing ever subscribed, so nothing re-read.

**Found and fixed.**
- **rtConn carries the fallback.** rtConn(onState, ms, opts): when the channel cannot JOIN (CHANNEL_ERROR, TIMED_OUT or
  no answer in `ms`), opts.reload - the page's own live-change handler - runs on whPoll (paused while the tab is hidden)
  until the channel is SUBSCRIBED. CLOSED is a page removing its own channel and never starts a poll. Every subscribing
  page now names what it keeps current; four that merged pushed rows themselves got a quiet re-read of their own
  (achievements' level changes, logbook's teammate-entry count, marketplace's new listings, founder-console's inbox).
- **The page says it.** _whLiveState: the source line's "updates automatically" becomes "live updates off - checks for
  changes every N s" (renderSourceChip says the same for a line drawn again while live is off, and it comes back when
  every channel joins), and one information-toned notice - "Live updates are off on this connection, so this page
  checks for changes every N seconds. Your work is not affected." - with no Reload, because a reload cannot open a
  firewall. "Not live" was first written into a line that opens "Live ·" (a live read): it read as a contradiction, so
  the clause names the updates, not the data.
- **hive and community** (the shared backfill) run the same refetch every 60 s while no channel can join - their
  whole-page refetch is 11 and 15 reads, alert-hub's own cadence for a board left open - and stop when one joins.
  Community's presence says "Not shown while live updates are off on this connection." under "Who's online".
- **audit-log** polls by design: its source line and footer now say "refreshes every 30 s". alert-hub and
  platform-actions keep their 60 s refreshes and now say so when their channels cannot join.
- **founder-console is retired**: it opens no channel and claims nothing (walked). Its inbox code was proven for the day
  it is restored by un-retiring it in the walk (the overlay's id renamed as it parsed - a route that rewrote the document
  hung every read even with an unchanged body, so the route was the instrument's fault): re-read at +19 s and +49 s, the
  notice shown; its empty inbox no longer promises "real time".
- **The instrument, twice:** reference-repaint-focus typed into marketplace-admin's search behind its retirement overlay
  (inert; checkVisibility does not see occlusion) and called the lost focus a defect - a walled control is now n/a like
  an absent one; and refusal-has-a-sentence pinned the exact Reload line, widened to accept the live-notice condition
  while keeping the refused member's.

**Measured after.** All 14 at both widths: every page with a channel re-reads on its own (30 s for single-region
reloads, 60 s for whole-page refetches and the self-refreshing boards), says it is not live and how often it checks,
and nothing still claims live updates. Cost while degraded is one to 15 reads a round, only while the tab is visible;
with the channel joined nothing polls (idle-network unchanged).

**Locked.** `live-off-polls` (42 anchors, 12 mutation tests) holds rtConn's poll and its CLOSED rule, the source-line and
notice wording, the backfill's minute, every page's named fallback, a generic ban on a bare rtConn() handed to a channel,
and the four corrected lines; `realtime-backfill`, `realtime-blocked-socket`, `realtime-degradation-honest`,
`realtime-channel-cleanup`, `idle-network` and `reference-repaint-focus` keep the live floor.

### §SL.11 Walk 11 — AV4 reload once, never loop: a flapping network reloaded pages on every reconnect while the database was down (2026-10-20)

**The ask.** "The platform must recover this page with at most one reload, never a loop." 24 pages, each as its row's
cast at phone-390 and desktop-1280. Every reload guard on the platform lives in sessionStorage - per tab - so every
probe is a FRESH tab from the cast's signed-in storage, and documents are counted as main-frame navigation requests (the
skew heal stops the stale document before DOMContentLoaded, so counting DCL hid the very reload being measured). The
only honest test of a guard is a fault the reload cannot fix: clean (exactly one load - a false heal reloads every
visitor); the skew heal STUCK (every utils.js, the refetch past the cache too, is yesterday's); the stored hive lost at
every document start; a worker change after every load (the page under the service worker); and the database
unreachable while the network flaps offline/online every 3 s for 35 s, then the database back and one more reconnect.

**Measured before the fix.** The three guards built for this held on every page: the skew heal refetched once, reloaded
once and stayed; the hive recovery reloaded at most once; the worker handoff reloaded once and its 60 s guard held the
second change. The FLAP looped: public-feed and logbook reloaded on every reconnect - 12 loads in 35 s, for as long as
the flapping lasted - and llm-observability's "could not check your access" card reloaded every ~10 s (the client's 7 s
back-off, then the next flap). The cause is one shape in two places: a failed read's Retry is very often
location.reload() (the settle pass's own and a dozen pages'), and the unattended-screen auto-retry (T126) re-ran it on
every 'online'; and five admin pages plus the offline fallback reloaded on every 'online' outright. 'online' is about
the Wi-Fi, not the database.

**Found and fixed.**
- **A reconnect asks the database first.** whServerAnswers: one HEAD on a public view, its own 5 s budget, one in flight
  at a time; any answer under 500 is an answer. The auto-retry round re-runs nothing until it answers.
- **A retry that reloads is an automatic reload**, allowed once until the page has loaded clean (whAutoReloadAllowed and
  a 20 s clean-load reset - the skew heal's own rule), so a wall display recovers from a 9:00 blip and again from a
  14:00 one, but never ping-pongs. A person's own Retry press is never limited.
- **whReloadWhenBack** is the one reconnect reload (ask first, reload once): agentic-rag-observability, founder-console,
  llm-observability, marketplace-admin and platform-actions use it, their skew-heal blocks name it, and the offline
  fallback asks the site before its own reconnect reload, once a minute at most.
- **Removed from the active hive** (hive.html reloads unconditionally into recovery): walked with the cast's membership
  marked kicked in the local database for the walk and restored after - one reload, then recovery seated his other hive
  in place; recovery excludes kicked memberships, so it cannot re-seat the hive it left.
- **The instruments, twice:** this walk first counted DOMContentLoaded and missed the very reload it was for (the skew
  heal's window.stop() ends the stale document before DCL) - documents are navigation requests now; and skew-heal-live
  read index.html at 1280 as "14 of 14 missing" because it counted the reload's navigation REQUEST while the old,
  stopped document was still the one being read - it now waits for a document whose own navigation entry says reload.

**Measured after.** All 24 at both widths: clean 1 load; stuck 2 (one refetch); hive lost 1; worker change 2; the flap
1 load and no reload while the database is down, then at most one reload when it answers (project-manager, inventory,
asset-hub, index, community, pm-scheduler, shift-brain, dayplanner, llm-observability, platform-actions), and every
failed read cleared on its own.

**Locked.** `reload-once` (23 anchors, 11 mutation tests, and a generic ban on a bare reload-on-online) holds the
database question, the once-until-clean guard and its reset, whReloadWhenBack on the five pages, the offline fallback's
probe, and the three guards that already held; `auto-read-retry` now also proves no retry while the database is out of
reach, the retry once it answers, and the automatic reload allowed once.

### §SL.12 Walk 12 — C2 period, window and as-of: a 14-day count said "this week", and running totals read as this period's (2026-10-20)

**The ask.** "The platform must state which period, window or as-of date every figure on this page belongs to." 155
pages (27 production, 9 founder, 119 public), each as its row's cast at phone-390 and desktop-1280, settled, scrolled to
its last element with every `<details>` opened. Every visible FIGURE - a number stating a quantity, not a date, a time,
an identifier (an asset tag, a standard's number, a code line reference), a step counter or a control's label - read
with its OWN statement (its sentence, its tile, the heading over its card; never a qualifier borrowed from another card)
and its per-figure reveal, and the page's own as-of read (its Sources line, or a guide's dated byline).

**The rule the receipts apply.** A figure passes when its period is stated beside it or in its reveal, or it is a
worked example, a sample or a benchmark, or a record's own value (a part's quantity, a listing's price) or a count of
what exists now - both answered by the page's as-of. A running total or a windowed figure must name its window. Every
figure the rule could not place was read and given its reason in the banker (a regulation's number, a threshold, a
duration that is itself the window) - none was a measurement missing its time.

**Found and fixed.**
- **pm-scheduler counted 14 days and said "this week".** The view counts due-soon over the next 14 days (or within
  500 km on a meter) and the tile says "(14d)", but the line under it said "N assets need PM this week", the verdict
  said "due this week" and "to schedule this week", and the figure registry said "seven days". All say the next 14
  days now. Its compliance figure names which window it is: the SMRP figure over the rolling 90 days, or - when that
  read is unavailable - the share of assets on track right now.
- **Running totals read as this period's.** logbook's "Jobs closed out 2274 of 2277" counts every entry ever logged
  (now "Jobs closed out, all time", the team strip too); community's "Posts" and "Community XP" (now "so far"); the
  provider tier's "jobs done" (now "so far").
- **analytics said "over the period" and never named it.** Its eleven tile figures carry the window the reader picked
  ("The last 90 days, rolling to now"), and the two forecasts say they count forward from today.
- **The reveals said where a figure came from and never when.** All 88 registered figures carry a period ("Now:
  counted when the page loaded", "The last 7 days, rolling to now", "All time: ...", "Today's brief: the 6 AM
  snapshot"), the reveal card shows it as a Period row, and render_figure_sources.py refuses an entry without one.
- **design-system's specimens** show numbers (27 open jobs, an MTBF of 6.4d) that are samples; the page says so and the
  gallery carries `data-wh-sample`.
- **What was already right, and the instrument that first missed it:** hive's value strip sits under "what this hive
  has delivered so far"; index's counters under "Hive Activity Today"; status's targets under "SLO targets (28-day
  window)"; analytics and the readiness gate state "computed <time>"; 119 public pages carry a dated byline (seven in
  ISO form). The walk's first readings borrowed a byline's year for unrelated figures and counted asset tags, hex
  colours and line references as figures - proximity, identifier and byline rules fixed each before any receipt.

**Locked.** `period-stated` (16 anchors, every tile figure checked, 9 mutation tests) holds the reveal's Period row,
the registry's periods, analytics' windows, pm-scheduler's 14 days and compliance window, the running totals' "all
time" and the specimens' sample mark; `figure-sources-written` refuses a registry entry without a period.

### §SL.13 Walk 13 — C3 time on exports and prints: a printed page said nothing about when, and two stamps named the load time (2026-10-20)

**The ask.** "The platform must stamp what this page prints or exports with the time and the period it covers." 88
pages (27 production, 7 founder, 54 public), each as its row's cast at phone-390 and desktop-1280, prepared as a person
would where the printable thing must first exist (asset-hub's asset opened, analytics-report generated, project-report
opened on a project - one was seeded locally for a hive that had none). Each page printed the way the browser prints
(beforeprint, then the print media query) and the text that would reach paper read; every Export, Download, CSV, Save
as PDF and Print control pressed (window.print stubbed so no dialog holds the walk) and its file, popup or printout
read - one level into a dialog it opens (the resume's Preview & Export) and onto a report page it opens.

**Measured.** A page printed with Ctrl+P (or Share, then Print, on a phone) carried no time and no period: the screen's
"as of" line sits in the collapsed Sources area, and only logbook and audit-log had a print header - which wrote
"Printed:" with the time the page LOADED, so a printout made after lunch named the morning. The CSV exports stamped
"Exported: Oct 20, 2026, 02:55 PM" and never said which clock; the skill matrix and project exports never said what
period they covered; the analytics report printed "Report Date: Oct 20, 2026" and asset-hub's reliability report
"Generated: Oct 20, 2026" - a day, never the moment - and the reliability report named its 365-day window only deep in
its body.

**Found and fixed.**
- **One print stamp, written at the moment of printing**, in utils.js (app pages) and wh-feedback-fab.js (public pages),
  guarded to one per page: the page's title, the hive and who printed it when signed in, "Printed: <date, time> PHT",
  and "Covers:" - a guide's latest dated byline (Updated before Published), "a calculation from the inputs shown" on a
  calculator, or the moment the page's figures were last read (utils.js now records it on every good read; each
  figure's own window prints beside it, SL C2). A layout with its own header (the project report's cover) marks it
  `data-wh-print-own` and keeps it. logbook's and audit-log's load-time stamps are gone; the shared one fills their
  element. Every served page loads one of the two scripts (promo-poster, printed as artwork, excepted).
- **The exports name their clock and their period**: "Exported: ... PHT" on the seven formatted stamps; the skill matrix
  export says "Covers: levels and targets as they stand at the export time; badges earned all time"; the project export
  carries the project's own period.
- **The reports print the moment**: analytics-report's cover gains "Generated: <date, time> PHT" (and its sign-off the
  time); asset-hub's reliability report prints its generation time and "Covers: corrective events of the last 365 days".
- **Named, not stamped:** asset-hub's QR tag (a physical label, no figure to date); the resume's CV (its periods are the
  roles it lists; its creation time is in the PDF's own properties - measured); project-manager's and analytics' report
  buttons hand off to the report pages, walked on their own rows.
- **The instrument:** a glyph in a control's name ("⇩ CSV") defeated name matching - controls are clicked by a tag the
  scan sets; a control that says "print-ready" only in its title was missed; the walk's text slicing cut an emoji in
  half and the result receiver crashed writing the lone surrogate (it now escapes non-ASCII).

**Locked.** `print-export-stamped` (9 stamp anchors in each of the two scripts, 11 page anchors, every served page loads
a stamp script, no load-time stamp may return; 9 mutation tests) and `period-stated` hold it.

### §SL.14 Walk 14 — LB2 query cost: what a page reads must stay on an index as the platform grows (2026-10-20)

**The ask.** "The platform must keep this page's queries on an index as its tables grow." 34 pages (27 production, 7
founder), each as its row's cast at phone-390 and desktop-1280: an init script recorded every REST and RPC request the
page made, and each was matched to the read in the LB2 inventory (the page's own db.from / db.rpc chains and the shared
scripts it loads: 424 reads, 111 RPC calls) whose SQL had been EXPLAIN ANALYZEd as the same cast, RLS on, after its tables
were grown from their own rows inside one rolled-back transaction (50k-130k rows on the history tables, ~100x the hives,
people and assets). A row banks only when every read is on an index at that size and every RPC's statements are too
(auto_explain, nested).

**Measured.**
- 42 reads on 16 pages, the worker drawer and compute_hive_readiness read a growing table end to end for want of an
  index - 20261020000001 adds the 19.
- The rest were SHAPES no index could serve: `is_mine` / `to_me` / `from_me` were per-row SECURITY DEFINER calls (the
  seller's listing count 1.1 s at 56k listings, its inquiries 0.5-1.0 s at 30k); my_service_provider_ids() was an OR
  around a hashed subplan (all 7,007 providers, and every balance that asks it); v_service_provider_truth and
  get_hive_trade_peers aggregated the whole platform before the page's filter; founder_dau_series called
  is_platform_admin() 33,922 times (6.3 s); the founder's credit totals summed every ledger entry (2-4.7 s at 13k).
- Under all of them, **225 of 365 policies compared against a bare auth.uid()**. Under RLS that comparison cannot become
  an index condition (the call is inlined per row and is not leakproof), so every "my hives" check read ALL of
  hive_members - 2,625 rows removed to keep one, 3.5 ms, against 0.037 ms with `(select auth.uid())` - and the planner,
  costing each check at a full read, hashed whole tables (12,423 PM assets, 10,302 inventory items) to answer a page
  about one hive. The inventory had grown hive_members to 2,626 rows, under the 5,000-row line that marks a grown table,
  so the one table every policy reads never showed as a full read.
- Home's companion follow-up read was missing from the inventory (nav-hub.js injects companion-launcher.js at run time;
  the inventory read only script tags). Four retired pages make only the shell's start-up lookups, each on an index.

**Found and fixed** - 20261020000003_lb2_read_shapes.sql, each piece proven to leave every reader's rows as they were
(`tools/prove_rewrite_equivalence.py`: every account + anon + a signed-in stranger, row fingerprints before and after in
one rolled-back transaction, the edge rows a rewrite could treat differently seeded; a structural proof that 359 of the
365 policies are byte-identical once the wrap is undone, the other 6 data-proven), and measured on all 576 distinct
inventory reads before and after, each run twice, the warm run compared:
- the reader's own listings and inquiries come from SECURITY DEFINER sets scoped to auth.uid(), asked once
  (`id = ANY(ARRAY(SELECT my_listing_ids()))`) - the reader cannot SELECT auth_uid (column grants), so the views cannot
  compare it themselves;
- my_service_provider_ids() is a UNION of its two arms with a new idx_service_providers_auth_uid; v_service_provider_truth
  counts per provider (LATERAL); get_hive_trade_peers narrows its badges to the hive's active members; the analytics
  admin policy asks is_platform_admin() once;
- the credit totals are KEPT: an AFTER trigger on the (append-only) ledger keeps one row per entry type, following
  UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE too; an admin reads them, anyone else sums their own accounts on the account index;
- achievements' Recent activity reads my_recent_xp() - each of the person's names, its own 30 newest on
  idx_xp_log_worker - checked row for row and in order against the direct read for every account;
- every policy asks auth.uid() once (480 calls, 225 policies, 125 tables, regenerated from the database as the
  migrations built it, loop-made policies included); the PM-asset and inventory-item policies and the two FOR ALL write
  policies that ask them take the reader's hives (and the supervisor set) as one array, so the hashes the planner builds
  from them come from an index.
- Measured, not assumed - and dropped: the scope-item read policy rewritten as a correlated EXISTS (proven equivalent)
  ran per row for every row the write policy rejected (day planner 52 -> 519 ms), and the one-array form on every
  inventory policy before the auth.uid() wrap made single-row lookups 3-9x slower. The first proposal for the PM scope
  policy (key it on the scope item's own hive) was caught by the prover showing 4 accounts 6 extra rows.
- Two things that look like the fix and are not, now written into the migration's header: inlining
  `l.auth_uid = auth.uid()` into an invoker view (permission denied for the reader), and CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW without
  restating `security_invoker` (the options list is replaced, even by an empty one).
- **Still known, not walked:** the service-request and broadcast views (marketplace.html:4311, marketplace-seller.html:
  2264/2265 - RLS-only OR scoping), the area-presence aggregate (marketplace.html:5304), community's keyword search
  (`title ILIKE '%x%'`, community.html:3110) and report-sender's fallback read (an unordered LIMIT the planner now serves
  with an early-stopping scan). None was made by a walk; each is an LB follow-up.
- **The instrument:** the harness crashed the database once - calling a function a reader cannot EXECUTE from a
  superuser session that SET ROLEs down segfaults PostgreSQL 17.6 (the real path refuses cleanly); the prover now asks
  the catalogue first. A check that parsed nothing reported "same" (a boolean renders `true`, not `t`) and a psql
  variable named in mixed case was never set - both now fail loudly.

**Locked.** `query-indexes` holds the 20 indexes and their page reads, and now the shapes: each object's last definition
in supabase/migrations keeps its measured shape (a later migration that brings the old one back is a red), no policy may
compare against a bare auth.uid() and no later migration may add one, the kept credit totals reconcile with the ledger on
every run, and 13 shape probes (views EXPLAINed, functions called with auto_explain) stay off full reads at grown size;
28 self-test checks.

### §SL.15 Walk 15 — L2 the change trail: who changed what, in words, on every path that makes the change (2026-10-21)

**The ask.** "The platform must leave a readable trail of who changed what on this page." 21 pages, each as its row's
cast at phone-390 and desktop-1280: the page's own change function (or its control, pressed as a person presses it, its
confirm and prompt answered) made one real change to a probe seeded per viewport on the local stack, and the database was
read for the trail it left - the actor bound to the signed-in account, the action in words through the one vocabulary,
the thing's own name. A two-party record must carry who and when itself and appear in no hive's trail; a person's own
row must be readable by nobody else in their hive.

**Measured.**
- The trail had two vocabularies and neither was whole. The hive board kept its own 74-entry map; audit-log.html - the
  page whose whole job is the trail - printed the action code with its underscores opened up ("amend closed logbook
  entry"); 10 of the 46 actions stored locally had words on neither (supervisor_password_reset 71 rows, soft_delete_post
  57, edit_listing 30, edit_seller_messenger 25, restore_post 19 ...). The gate that owned the vocabulary read 12 named
  pages: community, marketplace-seller and the supervisor-reset edge function, where those writers live, were never read,
  and it never asked what was stored.
- Shared changes with NO trail: an API key created or revoked, an integration's endpoint or credentials changed, a report
  recipient added or removed, a project item renamed, reassigned or moved on, a PM task added, an RCM strategy written,
  an FMEA mode added, a shift plan published or archived, a service request moved on, a provider's areas or availability
  changed, the hive's focus set. Closing a logbook entry was trailed from the logbook and not from the day planner; a
  member who deactivated vanished from the roster; clearing an alert's hive-wide "seen" was announced and not trailed.
- Trails that named nothing: RCM and FMEA approvals and deletes stored the id as the name, Alert Hub stored the dismissal
  key ("risk:Pump-01"), community's pin / flag / visibility / delete / restore stored no name and no target column, and
  a report row named the post's AUTHOR where its words ("Reported post") named the post.
- Trails of changes the database refused: community's moderation, Asset Hub's deletes, report-sender's recipient
  removal (the recipient left the list and kept RECEIVING REPORTS) and platform-actions' listing and seller decisions all
  checked only `error` - and a refused update or delete matches zero rows with no error.
- Platform decisions in the wrong place: platform-actions wrote every admin decision into the OPERATOR'S OWN hive trail
  (the only hive hive_audit_log let it write), where an unrelated hive's supervisors read it under an id; a top-up
  recorded when it was decided and not who; a listing's moderated_by and a published plan's published_by were whatever
  name the browser sent.
- The walk found two more. A logbook close through the edit form wrote two rows in one second (the page's edit row and
  the database's new close row). And the day planner, when its own save was REFUSED, rolled the item back and said "the
  item is as it was" while it closed the linked logbook entry for the whole hive anyway - the close ran beside the save,
  never after it (measured as Gloria Tan; the refusal came from a seed of mine with a category the page's own contract
  rejects, which is how a valid save would fail on a refusal, a conflict or a network fault too).

**Found and fixed.**
- One vocabulary: utils.js WH_AUDIT_ACTIONS / whAuditLabel / whAuditView - 101 actions with words, glyph and tone, and
  the name as it should be SEEN (never a bare id, never the actor's own name again). The hive board's map is deleted,
  audit-log.html renders through it (colour by tone, words in the filter, a `what_happened` column in its CSV, and the
  voice-driven actions its export had left out). The board's per-action colours had been dead code - a signed-off
  amendment meant to show amber showed grey; the tone reaches the glyph now.
- 20261021000001: audit_shared_change() on 13 tables, for the events a person decides and never the bookkeeping beside
  them (an API key's call counter, an integration's sync status, a provider's live position): add_/change_/remove_<thing>,
  the thing's own name, the changed column NAMES and - for a state column only - its new value, so the words can say
  "Turned off API key" or "Published shift plan"; no free-text value (an integration's token is one of the columns), and
  a save that changed nothing writes nothing. NOT attached where a page already trails the change (community's
  moderation, the hive rename), nor to marketplace inquiries (a two-party conversation: a hive row would show a buyer's
  message to supervisors its own policy keeps out). close_logbook_entry on every path; deactivation trailed before the
  name is erased; a top-up stamps verified_by, feedback triaged_by / triaged_at; platform decisions go to
  platform_audit_log (read by platform admins only) and show on platform-actions as Recent decisions; moderated_by and
  published_by are bound to the account.
- Pages: every trail row names its thing and is written only after the database confirmed the change (community x5,
  Asset Hub x3, Alert Hub x4 including the new "cleared seen" row); report-sender puts back a recipient whose removal was
  refused; platform-actions confirms each decision; a pure logbook close records once; the day planner closes a linked
  entry only after its own save landed or was queued - re-walked with a refused save: no logbook write, the entry still
  Open, no trail row, and "the item is as it was" true.
- Two covering instruments were wrong and fixed on the way: marketplace-economy E4 read a review policy's old vocabulary
  (seller_name, replaced by the account binding in 20261008000062), and lifecycle-cells read "platform admins only" as an
  ungated page (it knew only "admin only").

**The instrument.** The probe seeder's first run wrote "the platform · Added project" into a real hive's trail - a
system insert IS the platform's act, but a seed is scaffolding - so every seed now runs with triggers off. The banker's
first JSON reader took only lines starting with `[` or `{`: every count it asked (a platform decision leaking into a hive
trail, another member reading a private row) parsed as null and could not fail. It reads the value now, and both checks
were shown to bite: a supervisor reads 2 of a worker's assistant verdicts, 0 of their profile.

**Locked.** `change-trail` (live, rolled back, as a real supervisor, author, leaver and admin; 4 static + 10 live
mutants) and `audit-trail-coverage` (5 layers - lifecycle changes trailed; every action any writer can produce AND every
action stored in either trail has words; both readers render through the one vocabulary and the CSV carries the words;
names, not ids; 7 mutants). Banked 21/21 CLOSED: 14 changes read back as words with their thing and the signed-in
person; a buyer's inquiry and an assistant verdict carry who and when on the record and appear in no hive's trail; the
home page and the resume change only the person's own row; a solo owner on integrations is refused up front; two retired
consoles send nothing; audit-log.html reads the walk's own rows as words.

### §SL.16 Walk 16 — L3 usage events: what a page was used for, counted under an identity the database decided (2026-10-21)

**The ask.** "The platform must record this page's use as events someone can count." 31 pages, each as its row's cast at
phone-390 and desktop-1280 (signed out for the visitor's page): the page loaded once under a session named for the walk,
its main use was made once, and analytics_events was read for that session - one page view for the load, one event for
the use, bound to the right account, hive and name - and the operator's rollup was read for the count.

**Measured.**
- 30 of the 31 pages recorded a visit and nothing else. The table's own migration (20260513000000) promised that
  "feature pages ALSO emit feature_use"; only resume.html ever did. 268,353 events locally, 268,207 of them page views:
  the operator could count VISITS per page (founder_page_heatmap) and never what a page was used for.
- A count by person or hive was a count of claims. bind_analytics_events_submitter() returned early for a request with
  no auth.uid(), so an ANONYMOUS insert kept whatever account it sent - anyone could log events as anyone - and for
  everyone the hive and the name were whatever the device remembered: a stale hive, a remembered name.
- The operator's usage card printed "People today -" every day: founder_dau_series returns {day, dau, events} and the
  card read .count / .value, from the LAST row - the last day anyone came, not today.

**Found and fixed.**
- 20261021000002: the binder decides who, which hive and what name - a visitor (role anon) keeps no account, hive or
  name; a member gets their own account, a hive only while an ACTIVE member of it, and their own name (the rule the
  trail's actor binding uses); every event's props keep only short plain values under keys that cannot carry a person or
  their words. founder_feature_use(p_days) counts every non-page-view event by page and action, with signed-in ACCOUNTS
  and signed-out SESSIONS apart (one "people" figure would add an account to a browser tab), as the caller - so only a
  platform admin's read sees anything - over a partial index of use events.
- utils.js whUse(db, action, props): one feature_use per use, called where the use is CONFIRMED (a refused save is not a
  use; a queued one cannot leave an offline device either), props screened again on the way out. 127 confirmed-use sites
  across the 31 pages - posts, replies, reactions, best answers and moderation; alerts seen, handled, snoozed, put back;
  FMEA modes and RCM strategies; parts used, restocked, added; entries logged, edited, closed; PM tasks, completions and
  assets; projects, change orders and item moves; listings opened, watched, submitted, edited; inquiries sent and
  answered; reports generated, exported, printed, sent; handovers, stages, lessons, exams; and for read-only pages the
  deliberate read (a phase opened, a section chosen, the details opened). resume's own resume_* events count by name.
  whUseThen waits for the row (at most 1.5 s) where the page reloads right after the use (ph-intelligence, plant
  connections); whUseLink records a link that IS the use before it leaves. The operator's usage card now lists what
  each page was used for, and "People today" reads today's row.
- The walk found five more, each fixed and re-walked:
  - The shared remembered-tab helper restored a chip by CLICKING it, so the seller profile recorded "section opened"
    275 ms into a load nobody had touched. whAutoRememberTabs and whAutoRememberFilters now replay inside whReplay,
    and whUse records nothing while a replay runs (re-walked: one press, one event).
  - My own edit left `onclick="setPhase('diagnostic', true)\"` on analytics' four phase tabs. Every tab threw
    "Invalid or unexpected token" when pressed. scripts-parse compiled only `<script>` blocks, so it now also compiles
    every inline on* handler in the markup, with a mutant for this case.
  - Two pages are LOCKED for their cast's hive: ai-quality below Stair 2 and ph-intelligence below Stair 3. There the
    Maturity Stairway gate is the whole page. The shared gate now records its one in-page act ("how the stairway
    works", stairway_explained) and its way forward (the stairway link, recorded before it leaves).
  - A hive-less owner is not refused on integrations: the page offers them the vehicle wizard ("Supervisor access only
    ... the vehicle wizard above is yours to use"), and a vehicle added is now their use.
  - Writes that matched no row and still said "saved". Each now reads its row back and says so:
    - the hive focus;
    - a seller's inquiry reply and close;
    - a project's status, delete and item status;
    - a shift plan's archive.
    A blocked handover print window is now told.

**The instrument.** Four lessons:
- The scope checker (tools/check_whuse_scope.mjs) hung for minutes on the smallest page. The repo's acorn is 7.4.1,
  which loops forever on `ecmaVersion: 'latest'`.
- An HTML comment that MENTIONS `<script>` opened a false match that swallowed the real script after it. Both are
  fixed, and a script that does not parse fails the run.
- The walk's session name outlived its page, so the next row's sign-in page view was filed under it. The tag is
  cleared after each viewport, and the banker counts only the row's own page.
- Every check in the banker was shown to bite: the first walk's double "section opened" is refused, and a walk judged
  as the wrong cast is refused on account and hive.

**Locked.** `usage-events` checks:
- static: utils' screen, return and replay guard; all 31 pages' uses plus the shared gate's; no person in props; the
  refused-update read-backs; every client in scope; the binder and the rollup; the operator card; one page view per
  load;
- live, rolled back, as a visitor, a member and an admin: a forged account, hive and name each dropped or bound to the
  truth; the rollup counts accounts and sessions apart, and only for an admin;
- self-test: 8 static mutants and the scope mutant, and 7 live mutants.

`scripts-parse` now covers inline handlers. Banked 31/31 CLOSED. Each page recorded one page view and one use at both
widths, bound to its cast (Jun with no hive, the visitor with no account), and founder_feature_use counted it:
- three pages count a locked or gated state's own act;
- two pages that reload count two loads;
- the two retired consoles count their visit and no use.

The walk's 151 events, its probes and the 14 trail rows they left were removed after banking.

### §SL.17 Walk 17 — L4 the sentence a person saw is logged: what the page SAID when it failed, beside the code (2026-10-21)

**The ask.** "The platform must log the sentence this page showed a person when something failed, not only the code."
32 pages, each as its row's cast at phone-390 and desktop-1280 (signed out for the visitor's pages). The failure was
induced at the network, the way an outage or a refusal reaches a page:
- a page that writes had every write after load answered 403 with Postgres's own 42501 text naming the table, then its
  main use made as a person makes it;
- a page that reads had every read answered 500 from the first request.

client_errors was then read for the window: a row whose sentence is the one on screen, under the right identity.

**Measured.**
- client_errors held 390 rows. 383 were the uncaught net (uncaught-error 189, unhandled-rejection 194); the other seven
  were sign-in-unavailable and offline-drain notes.
- No row anywhere held what a person was told. A refused save, a list that could not load and an access check that
  could not be asked logged nothing: the pages showed their sentence and moved on.
- whLogError, the one logger, kept the error's technical message. The four sentence makers (whWriteError, whReadError,
  whFnError, whAiError) returned the sentence and logged nothing.
- The pages' own toasts lived in six differently named hosts (#toast, #dp-toast, #hive-toast, #toast-container,
  #wh-toast, #wh-auth-toast), and one was created only on first use.
- The identity on a row was the device's claim: hive and name came from what the device remembered. A visitor's row
  could only be one of the two uncaught contexts.

**Found and fixed.**
- 20261021000003: client_errors keeps `shown`, the sentence (400 characters at most), and `code`, the SQLSTATE, HTTP
  status or error name. A BEFORE INSERT binder decides who, which hive and what name, the rule L3's events use:
  - a visitor keeps no account, hive or name, and their told-* row is admitted;
  - a member gets their own account, a hive only while an ACTIVE member of it, and their own name. A member's row
    naming a hive they had left was REFUSED by the old check, so the failure was lost; now it is kept, without the hive.
- utils.js whTold(kind, sentence, err) logs one row per sentence per load, with the code and the technical message
  beside it. A sentence told before the page has a client waits for one, for up to 10 s. Every shared teller calls it:
  - the four sentence makers;
  - the failure notices (session, permission, connection, hive), never the update or live notices;
  - the inline list error and the access-check sentence;
  - a watcher that reads every page's toast hosts, including one added later and an id-less role=alert, and logs what
    the shipped classifier calls a failure. "Undo" is never logged on its own; a toast that only informs is not logged.
- The walk found seven more, each fixed and re-walked:
  - **The refusal itself was shown in Postgres's words.** My first batch sent a SHORTENED refusal message, and the
    shared sentence hid it. Sending Postgres's real one ("new row violates row-level security policy for table ...")
    showed it verbatim: the raw-Postgres filter knew constraint and syntax errors, not RLS or grant refusals. It does
    now. resume's cloud save printed the same words through its own "Could not save to cloud: " prefix; it now uses
    the shared sentence: "Not backed up to your account ... It is saved on this device."
  - **Inventory queued a refusal and then said it was submitted.** Any insert error went to the offline queue, which
    replayed it and printed "submitted for supervisor approval" over a part the database had refused. A probe part was
    actually created by a replay, and its push notification queued. Now only a network-shaped error is queued; a refusal
    takes the part back and says "The part was NOT saved".
  - alert-hub created its toast host on first use, after the watcher had looked. The watcher now watches the body for
    hosts that appear later.
  - Reading a toast host per child would have logged a lone "Undo". A host is read whole, except the stacking
    container, which is read per toast.
  - The shared notices and the pages' list and access sentences were not logged: skillmatrix's matrix, the retired
    consoles' access gates and platform-actions' cannot-ask gate.
  - The assistant's rating said "Not recorded - try again." and its greeting said the records could not be reached;
    neither was logged. Both are now.
  - The classifier: a lowercase "not" in an information toast, "refused by", "is unavailable" and "what went wrong"
    (a feedback prompt) read as failures; a conflict, a block, offline and no-change sentences were missed. 14 fixed
    cases hold it.

**The instrument.** Three lessons:
- The write failure was switched on AFTER load, and the phone width's refused resume save left a pending cloud sync.
  The desktop width's load replayed it BEFORE the switch, so the walk created a resume for Isidro Suarez, who had none.
  It was removed after banking. A page that replays pending writes on load must be failed from the first request, or
  its replay read and cleaned.
- The receipt's 120-character floor exists to catch the sign-in wall. With every read refused, the Founder Console's
  whole page is its 107-character access sentence, with the admin still signed in. A step whose condition is a told
  failure now arrives when it carries that sentence, matched to its logged row, and kept its identity, as a held
  load's step already did.
- Every L4 page's told text was collected as it showed (toasts come and go) from toasts, live regions and inline errors,
  and the page's own text was kept, so a row's sentence is matched to what was on screen, not to what the code says.

**Locked.** `told-failures-logged` checks:
- static: whTold records the sentence, its code and once per load, and holds an early sentence; the four makers, the
  notices, the list error and the access sentence log; every L4 page's toast host is read; the shipped classifier
  answers 14 cases; RLS and grant refusals are Postgres-shaped; the seven walk fixes hold; the migration binds;
- live, rolled back: a member's row with another name and a foreign hive is kept and bound to the member; a visitor's
  told row is admitted with no identity and any other context is refused; the binder is enabled;
- self-test: 6 static and 2 live mutants.

Banked 32/32 CLOSED. Every page logged at least one told row at both widths whose sentence was on screen, bound to its
cast (a visitor: no account), and no sentence was shown in Postgres's own words. The walk's 122 told rows, its 133
events, its probes, the resume and the outbox row were removed after banking.

### §SL.18 Walk 18 — LB1 row caps: every list is paged or capped, and says when more exists than it shows (2026-10-21)

**The ask.** "The platform must page or cap every list on this page and say when more exists than it shows." 33 pages,
each as its row's cast at phone-390 and desktop-1280, at rest on the local stack's seeded volume. A few pages show their
capped list only after a press (the resume's auto-fill, the hive board's closed disclosures and its Load More, the seller
console's inquiries tab), and the walk made it. Every list read was taken off the network: its source, the cap it asked
for and the rows that came back. The page was then read for what it said.

**Measured.**
- The 33 pages made 241 capped list reads. 47 said nothing past their cap. 85 had "more" wording somewhere near them,
  not necessarily for that list. 97 carried a note, 23 of them "cap-ok: rows only", which meant "no total is painted",
  never "nothing is hidden".
- Against today's data 58 caps BIT, among them:
  - alert-hub showed 20 of 64 signature alerts;
  - plant-connections' gateway audit showed 50 of 164;
  - hive's logbook analytics read 2,000 of 7,700 entries, under a note that said "never truncates".

**Found and fixed.**
- utils.js whMoreNote is the one sentence after a capped list: "Showing the 20 newest of 64 alerts.", or "... There are
  more." when there is no total. It offers a 44px way to the rest, and removes itself when nothing more exists.
- Every capped read now carries one disposition:
  - more-said: it probes one row past its cap, or counts, and the page says so;
  - paged:<fn>: a Load-more control calls <fn>;
  - cap-ok[cols]: sized live under half its cap. A stream may not be cap-ok, because local data cannot see
    production's volume;
  - window-ok[Nd], in-list[cols], or exact-count:<var>.
- 20261021000004: the resume's figures come from the whole logbook (my_logbook_summary, logbook_synced_machines), not
  from its newest-300 slice.
- The gate learned to see all the reads:
  - It used to end a read 900 characters on. Marketplace's grid read put its `.limit(PAGE_SIZE)` past that window, so
    8 reads on 7 pages were invisible, 5 of them with no disposition. Reads are now followed link by link, through a
    wrapper's paren and a ternary group.
  - It now traces queries built in steps (`let q = db.from(...)`; `await q.limit(N)`): achievements' re-read and
    dayplanner's plant-PM rail. A binding is visible only inside its own block.
  - A cap no read reaches now fails.
- Dead caps: eight chains carried two caps where only the last is sent (alert-hub 200/10, asset-hub 200/1 and its
  repeated 50, dayplanner, marketplace ×2, pm-scheduler 1000/500). Inventory's in-chain 1000 was overridden by a 2000
  chained after its role ternary. Each read now has one cap, the one it means.
- Caps INSIDE functions: hive's board (feed 40, PM feed 20, old WOs 5, pattern alerts 5, benchmarks 5 and 10, audit
  50), index's dashboard (open jobs 5, risks 5, low stock 100) and the platform reply average (a sample of 500) are
  declared with the page function that says each one, read live from the function definitions.
- **The parts rail was the 24 smallest UUIDs.** get_marketplace_parts_for_my_assets capped itself at 24, and DISTINCT
  ON (l.id) forced `ORDER BY l.id`. The rail showed an order no person can read and never said that more matched.
  20261021000007:
  - EXISTS replaces the join: a part stocked twice had listed its listing twice;
  - newest first;
  - the cap moves to p_limit (clamped 1..500), and the page probes 24 + 1, says "Showing the 24 newest matching parts.
    There are more." and offers "Show more matching parts".

  Proved in a rolled-back transaction with 30 matches:
  - a probe of 25 returns 25, newest first;
  - 30 rows are 30 distinct listings, with one part stocked twice;
  - the default is 24, and 0 is clamped to 1;
  - a non-member gets 0.
- dayplanner read the OLDEST 1,000 planner items. It now reads the newest, and a 1,001st row says more exist.
- The marketplace's inquiries panel, the seller console's listings (500 + 1) and wallet ledger (3 + 1), and the seller
  profile's replies now probe and say more. The console's "PLATFORM AVG" says "(up to the latest 500 replies)".
- **The walk found one more: a seller's public profile showed a signed-in visitor their OWN slice of the seller's
  record.** "Inquiries Replied" and "Avg Reply" were computed from the inquiries, and RLS shows a person only the
  conversations they are party to. David Velasco, signed in, saw "0 replied · None yet" about Bryan Garcia, who has 2
  replies and a 172-hour average. A signed-out stranger saw "– · 172h". The Quick Reply badge needs 5 replies under 4
  hours, so it could reach no visitor but the seller's own trading partners.
  - 20261021000008 marketplace_seller_reply_stats returns the reply count and the average over the seller's whole
    record: the formula of the public response_time_h, two aggregates, no row. Anon may run it, as declared in
    `definer-doors`.
  - The profile reads it for every visitor. Its 50-row cap and its "50 most recent" note are gone, because nothing is
    capped any more.
  - Walked live: the stranger and signed-in David both see "2 · 172h", "Average over all 2 of this seller's replies",
    and the page's only read is the aggregate.

**Gates the work sharpened.**
- `rpc-argument-consistency` read canonical_registry.json, whose miner kept a function's FIRST argument list forever.
  It found 13 drifts: 12 functions the stale registry did not know, and the parts rail's new p_limit. The miner now keeps
  the latest definition's signature, which corrected 32 recorded signatures (inventory_deduct's p_job_ref, the search
  functions' match_owner, the semantic searches' p_limit).
- `reference-pages-uncapped` knew only the literal "cap-ok:", so LB1's dispositions read as 6 undisclosed caps. It now
  reads them, the probe's `more ? 'latest 20'` badge, and an ellipsis-cut string. The last was alert-hub's
  `name.slice(0, 79) + '…'`, red before LB1 began.
- `figure-sources-written` checked that each figure's read exists in the database, never that the page makes it. Its
  own generated block names every read, so a page-level check would always have passed. A figure's read must now be in
  the page's code or a script it loads, with comments and the block set aside. Moving the profile back to the RLS view
  is caught.

**The instrument.** The walk template records a table function's rows (a top-level array) as an inner read, so a
function that caps itself is held to its sentence like the board's arrays.

**Locked.** `list-caps-say-more`:
- static S0–S10: every cap traces to a read, a step-built read is attributed, one cap per chain, the dispositions and
  their proof, whMoreNote, exact-count, and the declared inner caps;
- live V1–V3: cap-ok and window-ok sized under half their cap, in-list unique indexes, every inner cap declared and
  every declaration still capping;
- self-test: 15 static and 3 live mutants.

**Banked 33/33** at `locking`. Each full read matched its own sentence:
- achievements: "latest 30 events; older events are not listed here";
- alert-hub: "the 10 most recent past briefs";
- hive: "the newest activity" and "the 5 most severe active pattern alerts. There are more.";
- logbook: "Load More";
- report-sender: "the 5 most recent of 61";
- resume: "938 documented maintenance jobs" beside its 301-row slice.

### §SL.19 Walk 19 — LB3 a thousand rows: the page stays responsive with a thousand rows in its longest list (2026-10-21)

**The ask.** "The platform must keep this page responsive with a thousand rows in its longest list." 76 pages, each as
its row's cast, at phone-390 with the CPU slowed 4x (a mid-range phone) and at desktop-1280. Every list read was answered
from a pool of 1,000 rows built from the cast's own rows (a function's inner cap respected). Each list was then grown the
way a person grows it - its own Load more, press after press - until it held a thousand rows or the control was gone,
the main thread was left to settle, and the page was measured:
- B1: every interaction answered within 200 ms (INP "good");
- B2: no single long task over 200 ms after the rows arrived.

**Found and fixed, in the order the measurements forced.**
1. Every "show more" rebuilt the whole list. whRenderRows (utils.js) appends a grown list, patches a few changed rows
   in place (carrying focus) and replaces anything else; long lists render their rows with content-visibility:auto.
   Eleven handlers on ten pages moved onto it; rows are bound once; searches wait for the typing to pause.
2. The instrument was most of the reading. A CPU profile of the walk (booked by stack: injected script = instrument)
   put ~230 of 299 profiled seconds in the walk's own Playwright text locator and list scan. The walk now finds its
   control with one cheap in-page pass and books any long task containing its own work to itself.
3. The page-guide chip (learn-link.js, on every page) read a rect for every control on every mutation - inside
   content-visibility rows, which forces their layout: report-sender's 500 contacts became one 2.1 s task. It now
   passes over rows the browser is skipping before reading any rect.
4. The same chip drove itself: it showed itself to measure, hid again, and answered its own style writes - 360 writes in
   3 s of a page at rest, a long task every frame with a thousand rows (146 s of the logbook walk). It now measures from
   a remembered box, skips its own writes, tests the chip where it is, leaves at once (nine hit tests under it) and
   returns at most four times a second.
5. Alert-hub's 60-second refresh replaced the settled feed with a 5-row skeleton every minute: a reader lost their
   place, and every alert was rebuilt. The skeleton is now latched to the first load, as the brief card's already was.
6. whFmtDate built a new Intl formatter per date (toLocaleString); one formatter per shape is kept (3,740 dates
   compared, 0 differences, ~1/38 the cost).
7. nav-hub's dialog stand-down and the Sources area scanned the document on every attribute change / every appended
   row; nav-hub now answers a dialog at once and everything else four times a second, and the Sources area ignores
   bursts that carry nothing it mirrors.
8. Lazy rows broke figure marking. innerText of a row the browser is skipping is "", so on inventory only the first two
   quantities became tappable (2 of 8 sampled). The first repair asked each row whether it was skipped
   (checkVisibility), which computes that row's styles: 4.9 s of the walk. Anything inside a long list is now judged
   by its textContent (whitespace folded), the same answer on screen or off: 20 of 20 marked, no style computed.
9. The chip threw away its remembered controls whenever a label rewrote its words ("Showing 40 of 1,004 parts" swaps
   a text node), and re-queried the whole page - 3.8 s of the inventory walk. It now drops them only when an element
   outside a list is inserted or removed. The overlay Back-dismiss did the same for every class change on the page
   (1.4 s, each part's figure marked was one); it now answers only an overlay's own class.

10. The chip's instant check forced the page's layout. Traced at 390, one logbook Load More frame was 411 ms, 182 ms of
    it the chip: its nine hit tests forced the layout of the rows just appended (119 ms), and each walked a thousand rows,
    since a content-visibility row is its own paint layer. The check now runs after the frame's own layout, from a
    ResizeObserver on the chip (observing it afresh asks for exactly one report, after layout and before paint). It asks
    only about the elements just inserted, one rect per long-list row. A scroll queues the full pass and settles it the
    moment the scroll ends (scrollend). Probed live at 390: a button inserted under the chip saw it lift clear within
    the frame; a row appended under it, with the full pass held off, saw it go down within 33 ms; a button far away
    left it up; after a scroll it covered no control.
11. The chip's control scan read the controls inside dialogs: the logbook's two pickers (role="dialog", closed) held
    1,500 of them, each style-checked on every pass. A dialog's controls never matter to the chip: while one is shown it
    stands down, and while it is closed they are hidden. The scan leaves them out.
12. The Sources area ran its layout-reading pass (21 hit tests at the foot of the screen) after every class or style
    change on the page. It now counts a change only on an element that holds one of its carriers, anchors or slots (a
    remembered set, one lookup a change), or on a fixed control at the foot of the screen. Inside a long list's row
    nothing is fixed to the screen, so a row's changes count only for a carrier.
13. The logbook's search folded seven fields of every entry on each pause in the typing. Each entry's words are now
    folded once and kept until they change, joined by a control character no search contains. 21 queries over all
    31,257 logbook rows, accented and not: 0 differences. (The filter was ~1 ms a thousand entries either way; the
    traced 753 ms search was not this, see the measurement note.)

14. Every logbook and inventory card slid in each time the list drew it (.entry-card / .part-card carried the
    entrance): each search, filter, Load More and reload. A trace of a logbook Load More frame put ~180 ms in rendering
    (Layout 63, PrePaint 38, style 25, intersection checks 21, hit tests 19, Paint 13 ms) with the chip at ~1 ms. On a
    bare page of 1,000 cards at 390 with the CPU 4x slower, a 20-card append cost ~26 ms of rendering; with the
    pages' slide-in on every card, ~245 ms over the animation - each moving card made the browser re-check every
    content-visibility row's place on every frame. The motion standard (review-animations: list renders happen tens of
    times a day, "remove or drastically reduce"; the craft floor: "one authored moment, not one identical entrance")
    gives the answer: only the entry or part a person has just saved slides in, under the platform's arrival class
    (.new-entry, as hive's feed and community's posts already do), with an opacity-only fade for reduced motion. Gate
    long-list-render R14 holds it for every row drawn through whRenderRows.

15. The skill matrix drew its radar in the same task as the grid and cards. Chart.js read its container's size while
    everything just written was still un-laid-out, and so laid the page out on the spot: one 311 ms task on load, 125 ms
    of it that size read, and every press of a target's +/- paid the same inside the press. The radar now draws after
    the frame (renderRadarSoon), when the size is already known, and a run of presses in one frame draws it once.

16. The founder's feedback list built a date formatter per card and drew its 100 cards in one pass. One formatter is
    kept, and the cards draw through whRenderRows as a long list (content-visibility), so the cards below the screen
    are not laid out until a person scrolls to them.

17. Analytics drew every queued Plotly chart in one animation frame: one 723 ms task, 622 ms of it newPlot. Each chart
    now draws in a frame of its own, so the browser paints and answers between them. The first chart also paid for
    compiling Plotly (~570 ms on a bare page at 390 with the CPU 4x slower, against ~120 ms for each chart after it).
    The page now draws one throwaway chart off screen while its snapshot read is in flight. The first version purged
    that chart before Plotly's margin pass had run, which raised `_redrawFromAutoMarginCount` at both widths (the
    walk caught it). It is now purged when newPlot's promise settles.

18. The day planner's open-items sidebar drew all thousand cards in one task, and each card searched the whole schedule
    for the items linked to it. The schedule is now indexed by logbook id. The sidebar draws 50 cards through
    whRenderRows, says "Showing 50 of N open items, newest first", and grows by 50 under "Show more open items". At 390
    the sidebar sits behind its own toggle, so the walk opens it with a tap before it grows the list.

19. **A fresh browser is not a returning person.** The long tasks left on skillmatrix and platform-actions were almost
    all the browser's own Layout (185-430 ms) on DOMs of 600-2,000 elements. A settled full relayout of skillmatrix
    costs 8 ms. Traced with Blink's font and layout categories on, skillmatrix's 184 ms layout after its rows arrived
    held:
    - 94 ms shaping text in 101 blocks;
    - 16 ms building a Poppins face that arrived mid-render (135 text nodes invalidated "Fonts changed").

    On a returning visit (the page opened once first) the same layout cost 22 ms for the same 265 of 659 objects, with
    3 ms of shaping. Platform-actions went from 224 ms to 25 ms for 435 objects, and its shaping from 133 ms to 9 ms.
    The walk's long layouts were the glyph caches and font files of a browser that had never drawn the platform's
    text. That cost belongs to the first page a person opens, and it is the same with one row or a thousand.

    From batch wn the walk measures a **returning visit**: the page is opened once with the cast's real rows (pool off),
    then measured with the thousand rows. The rows arrive only on the measured visit, so none of their work can land
    before its window. The 64 rows banked before were measured on a first visit, the harder condition, and their
    receipts say so by omission. Each later receipt names the returning visit.

    The first-visit font cost is a platform finding, not LB3's. Google's stylesheet arrives after the first paint, so
    `display=optional` has no `@font-face` to hold back, and each Poppins weight replaces the fallback mid-render. This
    is the same mechanism as logbook's 0.112 phone CLS. Its fix: a self-hosted Poppins whose `@font-face` sits in a
    local stylesheet, with the weights the first paint uses preloaded.

20. The hive board's roster drew every member while it was folded. The board function answers all of a hive's
    members, and the roster built a card for each (about 10 elements) behind its "Show": a 10,418-element page at a
    thousand members, built after the rows arrived and seen by nobody. The roster now draws 50 members through
    whRenderRows as a long list, says "Showing 50 of 1,000 members, in the order they joined.", and adds 50 under
    "Show more members". The walk opens the roster with a tap and grows it through that control. The walk's control
    finder now prefers the "show more" beside the longest list; it used to take the first on the page, and on hive the
    feed's came first.

21. **Tier badges vanished in any big list, silently.** loadWorkerTiers put every name in one `in.()` list, and its
    callers pass whole lists: a hive's roster, community's feed authors, leaderboard and replies, achievements' top
    list, marketplace's sellers. On the local gateway, 200 names made a 4.4 KB URL (200) and 400 names an 8.7 KB URL
    (414 URI Too Long). The catch turned the 414 into "no tiers", so every avatar showed the lowest tier. Each name is
    now asked once, 50 to a request (a worker holds at most 8 achievement rows, so a request stays far under the API's
    row cap), and the answers are merged. The roster asks only for the members it draws.

22. **The same 414 was a class: a lookup by every key a page listed.** A UUID is about 39 bytes of URL, so about 200
    ids pass what the gateway accepts. Of the platform's 60 `.in()` lookups, these built their key list from what the
    page listed:
    - pm-scheduler: every asset id into its scope and completion reads. A plant of a few hundred assets read no PM work
      at all, and the scheduler said there was nothing to do.
    - project-manager: every project id into its two rollups. Every card read 0% with 0 items, and no project carried
      its late work.
    - hive: the members' names into the legacy-feed fallback, the team-stock fallback and the once-a-session logbook
      backfill (a write that stamped nothing).
    - community: every post on screen into reply counts and reactions.
    - achievements: up to 500 names into the standings, which also could not hold 12 domains per member past 41
      members.
    - index: the solo owner's PM completions. Marketplace: the saved-listings sheet. Integrations: a large import's
      rollback.

    The banked pm-scheduler and project-manager walks had timed pages that silently skipped this work. They are
    re-walked.

    utils.js gains **whInChunks**: keys de-duplicated, 100 a request, at most 4 in flight, rows in order, counts
    summed, the first error kept (unit test, 18 cases). The lookups above ask through it; each piece keeps its read's
    own order and cap, and the pieces are sorted together where order mattered. Achievements asks 40 names a request,
    so 40 x 12 domains stays under its 500-row cap. Lookups that cannot grow (one person's memberships, one asset's
    links, a page capped at 60) say so where they stand: `in-list-bounded: <why>`.

    The walk now records every call the stack refused, and a 414 fails the row. It had passed key lookups through to
    the database unseen. The walk's pool also turns one person's memberships into 500 copies of the same hive id, so
    those lookups now ask each hive once.

23. Analytics' list filters ran in the keystroke's own task. Typing into a list's filter at 390 with the CPU 4x slower
    took 472 ms to paint: each keystroke read the text of every row, revealed the hidden rows, and laid out every match.
    Now:
    - the filter waits for the typing to pause;
    - each row's text is read once;
    - at most 50 matches are shown, and the note says "Showing the first 50 of N matching rows. Keep typing to narrow
      it."

    Gate R4 could not have caught it: it reads a box by its id and a handler by what it re-renders, and these boxes
    have no id and only hide rows. **R15** holds every box that searches or filters, however it is named, to run after
    the typing pauses.

24. Community's Load More erased the reply counts of every earlier post. Each press asks the reply counts of its 20 new
    posts, and the count started from an empty map, so every post loaded before lost its count. The feed is
    virtualised: a card more than 1,500 px from the screen collapses to a stub and is drawn again on the way back. So
    after any Load More, scrolling back up showed "0" replies on posts that had them, and the unanswered tally counted
    every earlier post as unanswered. Only the posts asked about are counted afresh now.

25. **On a returning visit, the shared chrome was most of what each press cost.** Profiled at 390 with the CPU 4x
    slower, inventory's 82 presses and the logbook's 49 spent more in two shared passes than in drawing their rows:
    - The page-guide chip (learn-link.js) re-queried every control outside the long lists. Each press replaces the
