      list's "Showing N of M" note, a new element outside the list, and that threw the remembered controls away
      (pageControls 5.0 s on inventory). The remembered controls now follow what is inserted: the new element's own
      controls are added (one query over that element), a removed one is passed over when the pass meets it, and the
      set is rebuilt only once removed ones pile up. Gate R11 now holds this, with a mutant.
    - The Sources area re-ran its full pass on every press (2.6 s of `elementsFromPoint` and 1.3 s of document-wide
      queries on inventory). Each press scrolls to the list's end, which brings the area back within reach. Its 21
      hit tests at the foot of the screen walk every paint layer under each point, and each long-list row is one. The
      sample of how far the fixed controls reach up is now kept until a control at the foot of the screen, the window
      or the column changes. The area coming within reach runs only that room pass, never the full one. New gate R16,
      2 mutants.

    The rows' own drawing (whRenderRows) was 2.1 s of inventory's walk.

    Measured again, both passes still ran on most presses, so a probe recorded the stack behind every hit test and
    every long-selector query during the presses. It named the triggers, which the profile could not:
    - Inventory's figure marking gives each stat number a `role` on every press (19 in two presses), and the chip
      rebuilt its controls on ANY role change. Now only a role that makes a dialog rebuilds them; any other role
      change adds the element if it has become a control.
    - The guide chip is itself a fixed control at the foot of the screen, and it moves itself twice a press. Each move
      re-ran the Sources pass and its 21 samples. The Sources observer now passes over the chip's own style changes.
    - The 21 samples now ask `elementFromPoint` for the top element rather than `elementsFromPoint` for the whole
      stack, which visited every row's paint layer. At phone speed a sample fell from ~1.5 ms to ~0.15 ms (42 samples, 6 ms).

    After those, the probe saw no whole-page control query during the presses, and the gate holds all three.

26. Three shared observers searched every node a chart drew. Plotly inserts and restyles hundreds of SVG nodes per
    chart, and the Sources observer (26 ms of an analytics chart frame), the toggle-state observer (8 ms) and the guide
    chip's observer each looked at every one. An SVG drawing holds no source line, no toggle and no control, so all
    three now pass over mutations inside one.

27. The hive roster's "Show more members" read the roster again. The board's payload is consumed once, so a re-read
    went to the direct query, which is capped at 500. A press in a thousand-member hive would have shrunk the roster
    and the total it states. The roster as read is now kept, and Show more only draws 50 more of it (renderRoster).
    prove_hive_at_scale's live half now takes the size it is given. At 64 members the roster drew 50, said "Showing 50
    of 64 members", grew to all 64 through its own control, and its count matched the database.

28. A note written into a row's template was copied into every row. Inventory's part card carried three HTML comments
    inside its template (about 1.5 KB of design notes a card), and pm-scheduler, alert-hub and asset-hub carried more.
    Each comment is one more node in every row, parsed, kept and traced by the collector, which a thousand times over
    was not free. The notes now live as JS comments beside their templates. New gate R17 holds every row drawn through
    whRenderRows to carry no HTML comment. Its scanner follows template literals and the `${...}` inside them to find
    where each call really ends. R14 had looked 1,500 characters past the call for the row's class, and a note moved
    above a template's return pushed the class out of that window; R14 now uses the call's own extent too.

29. The browser walked every row to choose what to hold the screen to. On each frame that changes layout, the browser
    picks a scroll anchor - the element whose position it keeps still - by walking the scroller's content in order,
    and a long list's thousand rows were all candidates. The browser's own frame timing (Long Animation Frames) put
    three logbook presses near a thousand rows at 208 / 256 / 192 ms to paint at 390 (CPU 4x); with the rows out of
    that choice (`overflow-anchor:none`), 152 / 176 / 136 ms. But a probe found the cost of taking them all out: the
    list itself became the anchor, so a row above the screen that changed height - a row patched in place - pushed
    what was on screen down by exactly its change (300 px for a row 300 px taller; 0 before). The rows now stay out
    except those the browser is drawing: utils.js marks a row when it starts drawing it and unmarks it when it stops
    (`contentvisibilityautostatechange`, an attribute, because every page's observer answers class changes), and a
    marked row is a candidate again. Timed alone at the foot of 920 rows (20 rows appended, laid out, taken away, laid
    out; the fastest of 9 interleaved rounds at full CPU speed): every row 6.6 ms, no row 3.8, drawn rows only 3.7. The
    mark matched what the browser drew exactly (14 drawn, 14 marked), and a row 300 px taller moved nothing on screen.
    New gate R18, 4 mutants (every row back in, no row in, the mark never set, the mark set as a class).

30. Two shared passes ran inside the press's own frame. The guide chip's full pass (learn-link.js) and the nav hub's
    quarter-second pass (nav-hub.js) were scheduled from the press's mutations into a frame callback, which runs
    before that frame paints: 33-41 ms and 14-16 ms of each press at phone speed (traced near a thousand rows). Both
    now hand the pass from the frame callback to a task, which runs once the frame is painted; a dialog appearing
    still stands the hub down before its first paint, and the chip still gets out of a control's way at once (its
    instant check runs after the frame's layout). New gate R19, 3 mutants.

31. The instruments read a tenth of every long list. The rows the browser skips have no innerText, and the page's
    innerText leaves them out too: on the live logbook at 390, `document.body.innerText` held the words of 2 of Bryan
    Garcia's 20 entries. 91 instruments read a long-list page's text with innerText (68 registered gates and 23
    driven by other tools, across the 15 pages that draw a long list), so from the day the rule shipped each saw
    the first screen of a list, and a "must not appear" check passed over the rest of it.
    `tools/lib/long_list_text.mjs` now gives them two ways to read every row:
    - `ALL_ROWS_DRAWN`, installed on every context a text prover opens, draws every row (proven: 20 of 20);
    - `PAGE_TEXT` puts the skipped rows' words back without changing the rendering (20 of 20). It is for a walk
      that also times the page: lx_walk's LB verdict judges long tasks.
    A sweep that times first and reads afterwards (family_rubric_sweep) draws the rows once its LCP and CLS
    readings are taken. Installed by codemod in 87 files and by hand in 4: a one-statement
    `(await browser.newContext()).newPage()` gets it on the page, and the MCP walk bodies carry a marked inline copy.
    Verified live with every row drawn: stored-text-escaped 36/36 and shared-handover pass. New gate
    prover-reads-whole-list (9 mutants) derives the pages from the code, holds every such instrument to install the
    script on as many contexts as it opens (or to read through PAGE_TEXT), and holds the helper to the class utils.js
    skips rows in.

32. **The day planner parsed every card's hidden body on every press.** A press's window, broken down (the walk's new
    trace mode `press`: every main-thread task inside the three slowest clicks, with its script, rendering and
    collector time), held the click handler's 50-85 ms of CPU at 390 (CPU 4x). Of that, 23-54 ms was parsing the fifty
    new cards' markup, and each card's body - the problem, its badges, "+ Place on Schedule" - is hidden until the
    card is opened. Then came the rendering frame (42-59 ms), and in the slowest press a 13 ms major collection.
    - The body is now drawn only for the SELECTED card. A tap selects the card, and its key carries the selection, so
      the card is redrawn with its body before selectLogbookItem opens it.
    - The header's six inline styles are classes.
    - Each card's key is kept per item instead of re-serialised for every card on every press.
    After: handler 25-27 ms, parsing 6-8 ms, the thousand cards 9,584 elements instead of 14,584, slowest press 126 ms
    (152-256 across the three walks before). Checked at 390: a tap opens a card with its body, a second tap closes it
    and drops the body, a tap on another card moves it, Enter opens it; the Done/Missed/Scheduled badges and a done
    card's dimming compute the same colours and opacity as the inline styles did. New gate R20, 2 mutants.

33. **The logbook re-serialised every entry it had drawn on every Load More.** whRenderRows' default key is the whole
    row as JSON, built for every row on every call. The logbook's slowest traced press held a 19 ms major collection
    inside its click. whRenderRows gains `immutable: true`: a page that REPLACES a changed row (never edits one in
    place) keeps each row's default key with the row (a WeakMap). The logbook sets it - its entries change only by
    replacement (a spread of the old entry, the offline copy, the edit). Checked live: an entry replaced the way the
    page replaces one redraws its card alone (the next card stays the same node), a render with nothing changed keeps
    every node, Load More appends 20. New gate R21, 3 mutants (the kept key bypassed, the opt-in removed, a listed
    entry written in place).

34. **Project-manager built every card's HTML on every press to compare it.** Its grid was keyed `'html'`, which
    whRenderRows' own note reserves for short lists, and its card carried an HTML comment - one more node in every
    card. R17 never saw the comment, because the card builder (pcardHtml) is passed by name and R17 read only the
    call's own templates. The grid now keys on exactly the fields the card shows. That key also sees the rollup
    fields the page writes onto projects in place: checked live, a `_pct` written in place redraws its card alone
    ("77% done", the other three kept). R17 now follows a row builder a call passes or calls in its code (never a
    name in template text, such as an onclick handler), reading each builder's extent on comment-blanked source: on
    the raw page, an apostrophe in a comment made formatDate's body 1,863 lines long. 1 mutant.

35. **Two instrument lessons.**
    - A walk hung one MCP call for 30 minutes with the host at 0.36 GB free. Its waits on a handle, the identity read
      and the storage clear had no timeout. Every wait in the LB3 walk is now bounded.
    - A press's CPU window holds more than the page: the browser's own hit test before the input (about 11 ms at 4x),
      Playwright's hit-target listener inside the click (5-9 ms), and any collection that finishes there. The
      breakdown above is what separates them.

**Measuring.** The host has 7.8 GB, and with VS Code, the Docker VM and the MCP servers resident, Windows held 2.2 GB
compressed and 0.63 GB free. A traced run (the phone step under a Chrome trace) read an 838 ms task, and a 634 ms task
on desktop, on a page whose code had not changed: a trace run gives the composition of the slow tasks, never the budget
numbers. The next clean run of the same logbook code read 57 ms on desktop.

**Gates.** long-list-render R1-R21 (49 mutants; R17 now follows a row builder passed or called by name). prover-reads-whole-list (new, 9 mutants): every instrument that reads innerText on a long-list page draws every row or reads the skipped rows back. in-list-chunked (new): every `.in()` on the served pages and shared scripts is a fixed list, asked through whInChunks, sliced by hand, or bounded with its reason, and whInChunks holds its 18 cases (6 mutants: the helper unchunked, not de-duplicated or swallowing an error; pm-scheduler and project-manager put back; a reason removed).

**Where it stands.** 74 of the 76 rows are banked through the MCP browser on a returning visit; three are descoped
(their pages hold no list a thousand rows can reach). The walk books every task by its main-thread CPU time times the
throttle (the trace's `tdur` x 4 at phone speed), with its wall time beside it.

After findings 32-35, three of the five rows that were open banked on 2026-10-22, at 390 with the CPU 4x slower:

| Row | Page | Slowest interaction (CPU), before -> banked | Longest task after the rows arrived (CPU) |
|---|---|---|---|
| SL3125 | dayplanner | 219-256 -> 184 ms | 105 ms |
| SL3126 | hive | 230-245 -> 147 ms | 138 ms |
| SL3137 | project-manager | 210-265 -> 196 ms | 111 ms |

At 1280 all three are within budget (interactions 36-46 ms of CPU, longest tasks 15-16 ms).

**The other two - logbook (SL3130) and inventory (SL3129) - and the scroll-up layout shift are deferred to the end of
this roadmap** (Ian, 2026-10-22), in the section "Deferred to the end: LB3's two CPU-ms rows", with what each one
measures now and what would close it.

### §SL.20 Walk 20 — LB4 a bounded cadence: a page refreshes on its own schedule, and never for nobody (2026-10-22)

**The ask.** "The platform must refresh this page on a bounded cadence, never two refreshers feeding each other." 35
pages, each as its row's cast (signed out for the visitor's pages, the platform admin for oversight), walked through
the Playwright MCP in their own browser context with service workers blocked, so every request a page made was seen.
Each page was opened, settled until its network went quiet, and then left alone - no click, key or scroll - for 75 s
visible at 390 and at 1280 (longer than the slowest poll in the roster, 60 s), and for 75 s hidden at 390
(visibilityState hidden + visibilitychange, as a phone does when its screen goes off). Every request it made on its
own, every frame on its realtime socket and every repeating timer it started were recorded, with the page's rendered
words as proof it had loaded. The budget, per window:
- no request repeating faster than every 10 s, none more than 8 times, at most 40 requests;
- no two copies of one request landing together more than once, no realtime channel joining again, no write repeated
  while idle;
- at most 2 requests while hidden.

**What the walk found.**
1. platform-actions sent all 14 of its queue reads every minute to a tab nobody could see. Its only stop was
   `pagehide`, which fires on leaving the page, not on hiding it. The minute's refresh now runs through `whPoll`
   (utils.js), which skips a hidden tab, refreshes the moment the tab is shown again and never runs two at once.
   Re-walked: 14 requests on the minute while visible, 0 hidden.
2. Four more refreshers of the same shape, which an idle walk cannot reach, now skip a hidden tab:
   - marketplace's live-job map, every 10 s while a job is tracked;
   - founder-console's chosen auto-refresh;
   - connectivity-widget's 4 s status refresh, which online pings the backend, for a popover left open in a hidden tab;
   - voice-handler's presence heartbeat.
3. Three timers that must run hidden say why beside them (`refresh-hidden:`): the offline queue's drain (a queued
   write should reach the server from a background tab too), the told-notice retry (at most 20 tries, then it stops),
   and report-sender's reset countdown.
4. Everything else held. On the walk that banked them, 22 pages made no request at all while idle. 10 sent a single
   request: an analytics ping on 2 public pages, and on 8 an auth health check, which is the connectivity probe
   answering an event, throttled to once per 25 s. Three pages poll:
   - alert-hub refreshes once a minute (nine reads) and stands down hidden;
   - audit-log polls every 30 s through `whPoll` and stands down hidden;
   - platform-actions refreshes once a minute and stands down hidden, after the fix in finding 1.
   One health check landed in audit-log's hidden window on the second walk (0 on the first). No realtime channel
   re-joined and nothing was written while idle.

**What the instrument got wrong first.**
- Its request key held only the parameter names, so alert-hub's two briefing reads in one refresh (today's,
  `shift_date=eq.`, and the history, `shift_date=neq.`) read as one request sent twice. The key now carries each
  filter's operator.
- Its first walk did not record the page's rendered words. The recorder refused all 35 rows, rightly: a page that
  failed to load is quiet too. All 35 were walked again with them (342 to 7,692 characters a page).

**Gates.**
- refresh-stands-down-hidden (new, 7 mutants): every setInterval on a served page or shared script whose tick reaches
  the network (three calls down) stands down in a hidden tab, or says why it must not. Eight network refreshers, all
  held.
- validate_timers L2 ("a timer inside a loop") had been red since LB3. It looked back four lines for a loop opener,
  so a one-line `for (...)` above a single flagged setTimeout read as a timer per iteration. A timer now counts only
  inside the loop's body; `--self-test` covers 6 cases.
- idle-network, skew-heal and scripts-parse also hold.

**Where it stands.** All 35 rows are banked through the MCP browser at both widths (one more is descoped). The LB
layer reads LB1 33/33, LB2 34/34, LB3 71/76 and LB4 35/35.

**NEXT (LB).** LB3's five rows and the scroll-up layout shift (SL.19 NEXT). Then the RL sub-layers RL1, RL2 and RL3
(91 rows): their static survey, fixes, gates and walk instruments are being prepared in parallel, and their walks
follow through the MCP browser.

### §SL.21 Walk 21 — RL one person cannot flood the backend, and a limit says which and when (2026-10-22)

**The asks.**
- RL3: "the platform must debounce this page's typing and space its polling so one person cannot flood the backend."
- RL2: "the platform must tell a person, in a sentence, when this page has hit a limit and when to try again."
- RL1: "the platform must keep what this page spends on AI and functions inside its hive's budget, and say when it is
  spent."

Each row's page as its cast (signed out for the visitor's pages, the platform admin for oversight), at 390 and 1280,
through the Playwright MCP in its own browser context with service workers blocked, on the local stack, with every edge
call carrying x-wh-walk-no-model (no model is called).

#### RL3 — one press acts once (36 rows)

**The measurement.** Every search or filter box on screen (up to three) typed into as a person types ("pump motor", ten
keys 90 ms apart), with every request from the first key to 3 s after the last recorded by shape. Then the same box got
one Enter and nine repeats 33 ms apart (a key held down). Each key-command control (a card that opens or toggles) got the
same held Enter. A page with no LB4 idle reading was also left alone for 75 s at each width. The budget: no request
shape more than twice in a burst, at most two requests while the keys were still going, at most six for a held key, and
the LB4 idle rules.

**What was fixed (the RL sub-layer's static survey; the walk is what proves it).** A held key repeats about 30 times a
second, and on eleven surfaces every repeat acted again:
- achievements' cards flipped open and shut;
- asset-hub's assets and skillmatrix's disciplines re-opened, re-reading each time, and a held arrow spun asset-hub's
  tabs;
- founder-console's R ran the whole refresh per repeat, and logbook's cards re-opened per repeat;
- Enter went past the button locks on index.html's Sign In and Create Account (whose lock also came only after the
  breach check's first wait), and on hive.html's coach, join and create boxes.

Each acts once per press now. Walked: an achievements card under a held Enter made 1 request. Logbook's search sent 2
requests after the pause and none while typing. Marketplace's search sent 3, none while typing: the listings, plus one
count for each of the other two sections, asked only on a miss.

**What the instrument got wrong first.** Five pages write their search into their own address (history.replaceState, so
Back restores the view): community, inventory, logbook, marketplace and pm-scheduler. The banker read that as the page
leaving. Only a different PATH counts now, and it also checks the box held what was typed.

#### RL2 — a limit says which, and when (24 rows)

**The measurement.**
- healthy: the page as served.
- r429: every data read answered as a rate limit answers it (429, Retry-After 30).
- f429: every edge call answered with the platform's real 429 body, on a page that calls one at start-up.
- saves: the page's own save-sentence maker handed five database limits (a daily cap, a hive quota, the feedback limit,
  the listing limit and a gateway's 429).

A sentence counts when it names the limit and when to try again. A hive quota does not reopen with time, so its remedy
(archive older records, or a supervisor raises the limit) is its "when".

**What the walk found, fixed in this walk (11 surfaces).** Each one picked its failure sentence by the branch it was in,
not by the error that reached it:

### §ENH.S · The solar power-station planner, built once and carried by both surfaces (2026-10-22) - 17 of 17

**What was built.** `solar-planner.js` is the planner Ian named:
- list the appliances (from a list of common loads, or typed in) with their watts, how many and their hours a day;
- add them up to the daily energy, with the losses stated (inverter 93%, wiring 97%, battery round trip 95% for LiFePO4
  and 85% for lead-acid);
- size for the peak and the largest starting surge (a compressor or a pump about 3x, a fan motor 2x);
- take the days without sun and size the battery bank by its chemistry and depth of discharge (LiFePO4 80%, lead-acid
  50%);
- turn the energy into panels using the place's peak sun hours (the suite's own PAGASA values, or a custom value), a
  module derate and a rainy-season margin;
- size the inverter at 125% of the running load, its surge rating checked against the start;
- choose the battery voltage, size the MPPT charge controller, and estimate the cost in pesos with prices the person
  replaces;
- save it on the device, share it by a link that carries the whole plan, and print a spec sheet a supplier can quote
  from.

The method is IEEE 1562 / IEEE 1013 stand-alone sizing, installed to PEC 2017 Art. 6.90. It carries it to two places:
- **The public calculator.** `tools/solar-pv-calculator` gains a "Plan an off-grid solar power station" section. A
  visitor uses it with no account, and nothing they enter leaves the page. Its script loads right after its element, so
  it is drawn during the parse and nothing below it moves. The page's chip now says the planner calculates on the
  reader's device. The generator (`build_calc_pages.py`) carries the block, so a rebuild keeps it.
- **The Engineering Design suite.** Its Solar PV type gains "Not sure of the daily energy? Plan it from your
  appliances", which loads the script only when that type opens. "Use this plan in the calculation" carries the plan
  into the suite's own form: the daily energy, off-grid, the days and depth of discharge, the battery voltage, the panel
  size and the place. The suite's own calculation then runs, and it saves to the person's account. Its share link
  opens this calculator.

**What building it found.**
- **The battery voltage.** Choosing it from the inverter alone gave a small home 12 V and a 1.65 kWp array 172 A of
  charge current: two controllers and thick cable. The rule became the lowest of 12, 24 or 48 V that keeps both DC
  currents within 100 A (24 V, 86 A).
- **The empty plan.** The hand-worked test caught a planner with nothing listed still sizing a 300 W inverter and a
  10 A controller and pricing them at ₱5,520. An empty plan now sizes nothing.
- **The suite's printed sheet.** The suite prints its report with `body * { visibility: hidden }`, so the planner's
  sheet was laid out and printed blank. The walk read its text as empty. The sheet now asks for its own visibility.
- **The shared place.** Two places share a sun-hours value (Metro Manila and Tacloban at 4.5), so the plan carries its
  place by name.
- **The measurement.** `enhancement_inventory.py` looked for each capability in a surface's own text. A surface that
  loads `solar-planner.js` is now measured in the script it loads, and the S class reads nothing missing.

**How it was walked (Playwright MCP, phone-390 and desktop-1280, each width a fresh context, service workers
blocked).**
- **The public calculator, as a visitor (10 rows).**
  - Appliances were added from the list and typed in, then one removed.
  - 3,360 Wh a day became 3,725 Wh from the battery and 3,921 Wh from the panels.
  - 180 W running, 420 W at the fridge's start.
  - 4.7 kWh of battery at one day, 9.3 at two, and 14.9 on lead-acid.
  - Wp needed: 1,281 in Metro Manila, 1,373 in Baguio, 1,048 at a custom 5.5 h.
  - The controller: 1,650 Wp / 24 V x 1.25 = 85.9 A, so 100 A.
  - The plan was read back after a reload, then from its share link in a fresh browser with empty storage.
  - The print view held the sheet and the platform's print stamp alone.
- **The suite, as the solo owner junvanowner, signed in with no hive (7 rows).** The same figures, plus:
  - a panel price replaced and the total moving by exactly the array's change;
  - the share link opening the calculator itself in a new tab with the device copy removed;
  - the plan carried into the suite, whose calculation then ran ("Solar PV System: Off-Grid", kWp stated).

Every figure was checked against the hand-worked method, never read back from the planner.

**Gates.** `solar-planner` (new):
- S1, the sizing chain against hand-worked cases (`tools/test_solar_planner.mjs`, 39 checks);
- S2-S4, the page, its chip and its generator;
- S5, all 16 capability mechanisms;
- S6, the suite.

Its self-test runs 15 mutants, among them the page and the suite as they were before the build (2980a3c0). The other
gates are `scripts-parse` and `design-detector-ratchet` (no primary finding; the advisories left are the 16 px input
floor and the printed sheet's black ink).

**Where it stands.** ENH-S 17 of 17, closed. In the header's walk order, the F lane's product rows come next: ENH-C (41
open critic cells on signed-in pages) and OPC (99, the one operator console). The public ENH-P and ENH-L rows come after
every product lane.

### §ENH.L · A learn guide sends its reader to the tool: the measure was wrong, and four things around it were (2026-10-23) - 45 rows

**The measure was wrong.** Class L counted a guide as missing its tool when its source had no calculator link and no
"learn-link" token. No guide can carry that token: `learn-link.js` returns on every /learn/ page, because it links a
TOOL page to its guide, not the other way. So only a calculator link could pass, and every guide about an app tool was
counted. Read one by one, **all 45 end on a button to their tool** ("Open the Logbook", "Open the PM Scheduler", "Open
the AI Companion"), and 22 of them were already walked live by W4's "follow the tool this guide is about" rows. It is
the same miss `cta_gate.py` recorded on 2026-08-17: a gate's vocabulary narrower than the content it grades. The fix is
to teach the measure, not to bend 45 pages.

**What was really broken, found while checking it.**
- **Nine shipped guides were outside the catalog** that seven validators read (`wh_pages.LEARN_ARTICLES`). The pillar,
  problem and comparison generators wrote them, and so did one hand-made page. So tool-aligned-CTA, audience-block,
  em-dash, GA4, sitemap, llms and contact graded 45 of the 54 guides a reader can open.
- **`learn_links.json` said it was generated from the catalog, and nothing generated it.** It still filed the LOTO guide
  under Audit three and a half weeks after the catalog moved it to the Logbook. It was also missing the power-rates
  guide on Engineering Design and all nine uncatalogued guides.
- **The pillar builder was a loaded trap.** Run once to see what it emits, it wrote three shipped pillars back to its
  template, and its post-build sweeps put back none of what mattered. It removed 122 lines: the critic batch's contrast
  (text back to 0.78, 0.55 and 0.5 alpha), its readability rewrites, the CMMS `<abbr>`, `touch-action`, and the
  end-of-article button turned back into a bold inline link. The pages were restored from git.
- **Eight of the nine had no "Who this is for" block.** The catalog's audience gate had never read them.

**Built, and what holds it.**
- `wh_pages.py`: the nine are catalogued, each with the tool its own button opens. The three platform comparisons
  declare the landing page, as the overview does.
- **tool-aligned-cta**, now five layers:
  - **L0:** every guide on disk must be in the catalog.
  - **L1 and L4:** both read the article body, not the header or footer.
  - **Deep links count:** `/index.html?companion=1` reaches its declared target.
  - **Guides about WorkHive itself** must end on sign-up or the landing page.
  - **`--self-test`:** seven mutants, registered as `tool-aligned-cta-selftest`.
  - **Teeth:** on the catalog as it was, L0 names the nine; on the pages as they are, 54 of 54 pass.
- `tools/build_learn_links.py` generates the file and has a `--check` mode. `pull-help-coverage` now fails when the file
  is not what the catalog generates, and its self-test gained that mutant. On the file as it was it names three
  drifted pages; regenerated it passes. No page's first guide changed, so every tool page's chip is the same.
- `build_pillar_pages.py` writes new pillars only. A shipped pillar is kept unless `--force`. The problem and comparison
  data modules now say they are not rendered: their pages carry 147 to 177 lines that the data does not.
- The audience block went onto the eight pages as whole new lines only. It is the majority variant of the 46 guides
  that already carry one. Gates: audience-block 54/54, em-dash, jargon-glossed, design-detector-ratchet (0 primary),
  cta and public-surface all green. The header did not move: 16,573 of 16,871 before and after the edit.

### §ENH.P · The calculator features: two built in the calculator itself, two already there (2026-10-23) - 226 rows

**What the measure read.** Class P read each `tools/<slug>/index.html`, which is an SEO door: a worked example computed

four features, measured against that calculator:
- **Export / print (59):** already there. Download PDF is on every calculator's report, which carries the inputs and the
  standard. The rows are refuted by W4's walks. The Analytics pair is checked on its own page.

- **Scenario compare (59):** missing. **Built.**

  - a PASS or FAIL with its remedy, such as "FAIL. Minimum N bolts required. Add bolts or increase bolt size/grade" or
    "BEARING UNDERSIZED: select a bearing with…".

  is the static audit. The walk records each report's own recommendation line. Where none exists (harmonic distortion

**Built, once, for every calculator type** (`engineering-design.js` / `.html`, shell v565):
- **Share link** sits beside Download PDF and Save (the row wraps at 390).
  - **What travels:** the link names the calculator in `?calc=` and carries the inputs in the `#share=` fragment.
    Nothing in a fragment ever reaches a server, a log or a page view: `logPageView` records the page name only.
  - **How it is sent:** a phone uses its share sheet, a desktop copies the link, and a browser with neither shows the
    link in a field.
  - **Opening it** reduces the inputs to what that calculator's own form produces: the form's keys, each coerced to the
    form's type, text stripped of the characters markup needs, and lists capped and shaped by the form's first row.
    Some renderers still print an input raw, so a link must not carry markup.
  - **Then it runs** the same engine and the same `_renderComputed` a Run does. That is runCalculation's post-engine
    block, moved unchanged (184 lines, proved byte-identical) so a Run and a link cannot draw differently.
  - **Through sign-in:** the identity gate now carries the fragment, so a signed-out colleague signs in and lands on the
    calculation. The C27 deep-link poller stands aside for a link: its late `selectCalcType` would empty the report.
- **Compare** keeps a calculation as scenario A: its headline figures exactly as its report shows them (each
  `.res-label` beside its `.res-value`), and its inputs. The next run of the same calculator sets A beside it, figure
  by figure, with a changed figure in bold (and said, for a screen reader), plus the inputs that differ, named in words

- **Gates.** `calc-share-compare` holds the wiring (S1-S6) and names 17 failures on the page as it was. Its self-test

  `tools/test_calc_share_compare.mjs` runs the pure core: round trip, damaged links, sanitising, compare. Also green:

**MTBF and OEE: the calculator a stranger could not use (built 2026-10-23).** These two pages sent their reader to

## §LW · The LIVE-WALK wave and its MCP instruments (Ian, 2026-09-06)

Ian: *"live deepwalk each trajectory or group of categories, but do not repeat what you already done"*, then
*"utilize appropriate and applicable MCP that we have or do not have, connect it, according to the trajectories"*,
and for the header: **two buckets on live evidence**.

**Why the wave exists.** The registry said 99% GATED while only 537 of 1,377 in-scope rows had ever been exercised
against the running system. Reading each row's own `basis` for the KIND of evidence it holds separates a walk from a
claim: `live` (an instrument RAN), `board` (a page's score inherited), `gate` (a static gate), `prose` (an argument).
`tools/live_walk_manifest.py` is that classifier, the header's source, the gate `live-walk-manifest`, and the
**no-repeat ledger** — a row classified `live` is never walked again.

### §LW.1 The MCP doctrine (Ian, 2026-09-06)

> *"We have to maximize the usage of our MCPs, we have to use appropriately the MCPs depending on the type or kind of
> trajectories... but if there are needed other MCPs we don't have, we have to proactively connect another kind of MCP."*

Four rules, in force for every walk from here:

1. **The instrument is chosen by the KIND of trajectory, never by habit.** A journey is walked step by step; a contract
   is asked over HTTP; a number is checked against the database; a crash is read from the error tracker. Using one
   instrument for every kind is how a program ends up 99% gated and 39% walked.
2. **Prefer the OUTSIDE witness.** Where a claim can be checked from another system - Postgres for state, Sentry for
   crashes, Grafana for liveness, the mail connector for delivery - use it, because a page cannot be cross-examined
   with its own story. The strongest evidence in this wave came from exactly that: the DB said 4 pending while the
   tile said 4, and the audit table showed what the click actually wrote.
3. **A kind with no matching MCP is a QUEUE ITEM, not an excuse.** When a family has no suitable server, connecting one
   is the first slice of that family's walk. This is the same rule as "build the structure": we do not downgrade the
   lens to fit the tools we happen to have.
4. **Batch with the library, walk with the MCP.** A 40-surface sweep is one command through the Playwright library and
   400 tool calls through the MCP; a persona journey is the reverse, because each step's snapshot decides the next.
   Both drive the same Chromium - the choice is the shape of the walk, and it is written into the table below.

chrome-devtools (added in this wave) · the claude.ai connectors (Gmail, Drive, Supabase-cloud).

with its time rather than a new standing claim: a later listing, taken while a browser walk had the host, could
not answer at all. Re-read the container list before relying on either state.*

### §LW.2 · WALK THE TRAJECTORIES THROUGH THE MCPs — the default, so triage happens in REAL TIME (Ian, 2026-09-09)

> *"I prefer you drive the roadmap realtime so that you can triage realtime, so that we can move fast on
> completing the headline percentage to 100%"*, and then: *"I want you to put it in our roadmap that we have to
> do the trajectories using MCPs, so that we can proceed realtime."*

This **supersedes the free choice in rule 4 above**. Rule 4 said batch with the library, walk with the MCP, and
left the shape to judgement. The default is now the MCP: a trajectory is driven step by step through the
playwright and postgres servers, with the findings read AS THEY LAND. A headless batch script is the exception,
taken only when a sweep is genuinely uniform and nothing in it needs deciding mid-flight.

**Why, measured on 2026-09-09 rather than argued.** The Tier-A journey wave was run the old way — one
`prove_full_journeys.mjs --tier A` process, 130 stories, headless. What that cost:

- **~3 hours before a single finding could be acted on.** Everything the walk learned sat inside the process
  until it wrote its JSON at the end. Two seed gaps it had already proven — a fleet hive whose parts have never
  moved, four hives with nobody to send a report to — would have waited hours to be seen.
- **It took the machine down once.** 130 stories in one process reached 158MB free of 7.8GB with 33 chromium
  processes alive, and the Docker engine beside it began answering 500. The run had to be killed at story 20.
- **It manufactured findings.** Its own load pushed a sub-millisecond query past `community.html`'s 15s client
  bound, so the page honestly reported a connection problem that existed only because the walk was standing on
  the machine — and the walk recorded it as a defect. Loading that page by hand through the MCP, as the same
  person, showed a correct empty state. A batch cannot notice that about itself; an operator watching can.
- **What real-time triage found in the same window:** the missing `skill_profiles` across all three fleet hives,
  fixed generator-first mid-run, flipping journeys to passing on the next pass rather than the next session.

**The rules that follow:**

1. **Drive with the MCP by default.** playwright for the walk, postgres for the effect, the mail connector for a
   delivery — one step, one reading, decided before the next step. This is what makes a finding actionable at
   the moment it appears rather than at the end of a run.
2. **Triage as it lands, and fix what is fixable immediately.** A seed gap found at story 30 is filled before
   story 60 walks, so the rest of the wave measures the platform as repaired. Waiting banks the same failure
   dozens of times.
3. **Keep the batch prover as the RATCHET, not the discovery tool.** `prove_full_journeys.mjs` and its siblings
   stay, registered as gates, to re-prove in bulk what an MCP walk has already established — that is what a gate
   is for. Discovery moves to the MCP.
4. **Serial, always, on this host.** Whatever the shape, one browser at a time: every false finding this session
   produced was contention, and the DB answered a plain read in 180s while a walk had the machine.
5. **A kind with no MCP is still a queue item** (rule 3 above is unchanged) — the answer to a missing server is
   to connect one, never to fall back to a batch script and call the lens covered.

### The instruments, per family

| Family | Instrument | MCP / runtime | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| degradation & state | `tools/prove_db_pages_degradation.mjs` (both modes, 34 surfaces) | playwright library | `db-pages-degradation` |
| render & CSS | `tools/prove_render_contract.mjs` (4 lenses, 41 surfaces) | playwright library | `render-contract` |
| edge & API contracts | `tools/prove_edge_contract.mjs` (4 asks, 62 functions) | local edge stack over HTTP | `edge-contract` |
| data honesty | `tools/prove_data_honesty.mjs` (basis, windows, caps) | playwright library | `data-honesty` |
| **journeys + the 222 cross-cutting arcs** | **step-by-step walk** | **playwright MCP** (snapshot → act → snapshot) + **postgres MCP** (the state actually changed) | per-arc |
| **ops & observability** | health/cron liveness read from the outside | **grafana MCP** (container `workhive_grafana`, start it for the family) + **sentry MCP** | per-arc |
| mobile deep | `tools/prove_phone_fit.mjs` extended (768 landscape, install) | playwright library + **chrome-devtools MCP** | `phone-fit`, `phone-fit-360` |
| a11y deep | keyboard path / landmarks / announcements | **playwright MCP** (a real tab walk) | to build |
| public funnels | arrival as a crawler sees it | **crawl4ai MCP** + curl for headers | to build |

**Library vs MCP, decided once:** a 40-surface sweep is ONE command through the Playwright library and 400 tool calls
through the MCP, so batch lenses use the library. The MCP is the right instrument where the walk is a JOURNEY — a
persona doing a task step by step, where each step's snapshot decides the next — and where the evidence lives in
another system (Grafana, Sentry, Postgres). Both drive the same Chromium; the choice is about the shape of the walk.

## ★THE TARGET — all 500 trajectories at 100% each

**Ian, 2026-08-31: _"we have to finished all 200 trajectories to each 100%, put it to our roadmap"_ —
and later the same day, the exhaustive expansion: the program is now T1–T500, and the target spans all
of it.** `.momentum_drive` stays armed for this program.

That is the standing objective, written here rather than left in a session transcript so every future
session reads it before anything else.

**What 100% MEANS, stated so it cannot be reached by flattery.** The registry's pct is fixed per status
(`specced 5 · walked 25 · fixed 60 · locked 100`), so **100% is `locked`, and nothing else** — and
`tools/validate_trajectory_registry.py` holds `locked` to naming **at least one gate that is registered
in `run_platform_checks.py`**. A trajectory therefore cannot reach 100% by editing a number: it needs a
gate that actually runs on the board. "All 500 at 100%" is exactly **"all 500 locked, each with a
registered, running gate."**

**Where the program stands is ALWAYS the generated scoreboard above — never a count typed here** (a
hand-typed table drifted against the header within a week of being written; the generated block cannot).
Structurally the distance decomposes as:

- **locked** — done; nothing to re-earn while its gates stay green on the board.
- **locking** — gate built; finish the row's own `Remaining:` line, then lock. The cheapest closures.
- **fixing** — the genuine build queue of the original 200.
- **walked** — capstones sequenced last by design (T196, T200).
- **specced** — the T201–T500 expansion catalog: honest 5% until each is actually walked.

**The pct-weighted headline must not be read as progress toward this target.** The doctrine's own rule
applies to this very number: one metric at a comfortable value while the axis Ian named — *every*
trajectory at 100% — is measured only by the locked count. Adding the 300 expansion arcs correctly
DROPPED the headline; a header that cannot drop cannot be honest.

**The honest sequencing, from the 62 `locking` rows' own `Remaining:` lines:**
- **1** (`T179`) is waiting on the wave-close **re-earn only** — it closes when the restamp lands.
- **57** carry real, named remaining work — the cheapest distance to 100%, because each already has its
  gate built and sits at 72–99%.
- **4** carry no `Remaining:` line and need their state re-read before they can be claimed either way.

`WAVE_CLOSE_QUEUE.md` (generated) holds every one of those remainder lines; it is the work list for this
target, not a summary of it.

### Wave W — Security & adversarial personas (T361–T384, 24)
- **T361** · BOLA: guess another hive's asset id — _adversary enumerates /rest/v1/assets?id=<other-hive> hoping the ref, not RLS, is the only guard_
- **T362** · Broken function-level auth: worker hits admin RPC — _signed-in worker calls an owner-only RPC directly, betting the button was the only gate_
- **T363** · JWT-in-body trust — _attacker sends a claim in the request body hoping an edge function trusts it over the verified JWT_
- **T364** · Tenant boundary via forged hive_id — _attacker posts a write with someone else's hive_id to cross the tenant wall_
- **T365** · Mass assignment on profile update — _attacker adds role:owner to a profile PATCH hoping the column is unguarded_
- **T366** · IDOR on marketplace order — _buyer edits an order id in the URL to read a stranger's transaction and address_
- **T367** · Stored XSS in a logbook entry — _attacker plants <script> in free text hoping a consumer renders it unescaped_
- **T368** · SQL/PostgREST injection via filter param — _attacker crafts a filter operator to widen a query past its intended row set_
- **T369** · SSRF via a webhook/callback URL — _attacker points an outbound integration URL at an internal address_
- **T370** · Rate-limit / brute force on login — _attacker scripts the login edge function to credential-stuff_
- **T371** · Password-reset token reuse — _attacker replays a supervisor-reset-password token after it should have burned_
- **T372** · Enumerate users via signup error deltas — _attacker distinguishes 'exists' from 'created' by response timing/text_
- **T373** · Invite-code forgery / replay — _attacker crafts or reuses a hive invite code to self-join_
- **T374** · Privilege escalation via stale membership — _removed member's cached session still writes before the wall catches up_
- **T375** · File-upload content smuggling — _attacker uploads a mislabeled file to a storage bucket to bypass a MIME gate_
- **T376** · Signed-URL scope abuse — _attacker widens or reuses a storage signed URL past its object_
- **T377** · CSRF on a state-changing GET — _attacker tricks a session into a cross-site state change on a non-idempotent endpoint_
- **T378** · Webhook signature bypass (gcash-receipt-inbound) — _attacker posts a forged payment webhook without a valid signature to mark a txn paid_
- **T379** · Race to double-spend a marketplace credit — _attacker fires two concurrent redemptions of the same credit_
- **T380** · Exfil via export-hive-data as a low-role — _low-privilege member triggers a full-hive export they should not receive_
- **T381** · Prompt injection into an AI agent — _attacker plants instructions in user content that an AI orchestrator later executes_
- **T382** · Denial-of-wallet on a metered AI endpoint — _attacker loops an expensive AI call to exhaust the owner's budget_
- **T383** · Open redirect on return-url params — _attacker crafts ?return= to bounce a signed-in user to a phishing origin_
- **T384** · Audit-log tampering / gap — _attacker performs an action on a path that writes no audit row, hiding the trail_

### Wave X — Accessibility spectrum (T385–T402, 18)
- **T385** · Screen-reader: complete a work order end-to-end — _a blind supervisor drives logbook->assign with NVDA/VoiceOver, intent = finish without sight_
- **T386** · Keyboard-only: no mouse anywhere — _a motor-impaired user tabs through every interactive control, focus never trapped or lost_
- **T387** · Low-vision at 400% zoom — _a partially-sighted user zooms to 400%; no content clipped, no horizontal scroll trap_
- **T388** · Color-blind: status conveyed beyond hue — _a deuteranope reads asset health where red/green alone would be ambiguous_
- **T389** · Switch-access single-input navigation — _a quadriplegic user drives the app with one switch and scanning_
- **T390** · Voice-control (Dragon/Voice Access) — _a user speaks 'click Assign' — every control has a spoken-accessible name_
- **T391** · Screen-magnifier follow-focus — _a low-vision user's magnifier follows focus and new content into the viewport_
- **T392** · Deaf/HoH: captions & no audio-only cues — _a Deaf user needs every audio alert mirrored visually (voice-journal playback captioned)_
- **T393** · Cognitive load: plain-language + steps — _a user with a cognitive disability needs a long form chunked and jargon explained_
- **T394** · Reduced-motion respected — _a vestibular-disorder user with prefers-reduced-motion sees no parallax/auto-animation_
- **T395** · Reflow at 320 CSS px (WCAG 1.4.10) — _content reflows to a single column at 320px with no loss of function_
- **T396** · Focus-visible on every control — _a keyboard user always sees where focus is; no invisible focus ring_
- **T397** · Form errors announced to AT — _a validation error is programmatically associated and announced, not just colored_
- **T398** · Live-region for async updates — _a screen-reader user hears a toast/status change via an aria-live region_
- **T399** · Touch target >=44px on phone — _a user with a tremor can hit every phone control without mis-tapping a neighbor_
- **T400** · Skip-link & landmark navigation — _a screen-reader user jumps past nav to main via a skip link and landmarks_
- **T401** · High-contrast / forced-colors mode — _a Windows High Contrast user retains all borders, icons and state_
- **T402** · Timeout & session-extend accessible — _a slow user is warned before a session/auto-save timeout and can extend it_

### Wave Z — Data pathology deep (T421–T438, 18)
- **T421** · Partial write: order paid, fulfilment row missing — _a half-committed transaction leaves the UI asserting a state the data denies_
- **T422** · Orphaned child after parent delete — _an asset is deleted but its work orders survive, pointing at nothing_
- **T423** · Timezone-crossing shift at midnight — _a shift spanning midnight in Asia/Manila is counted in the wrong day_
- **T424** · Float precision in a cost/hours rollup — _accumulated rounding drifts a financial total the user can check by hand_
- **T425** · Migration half-state as UX — _a user hits a page mid-migration where old and new columns disagree_
- **T426** · Duplicate rows from a double-submit — _a retried POST creates two identical records the list now shows twice_
- **T427** · Null-vs-zero conflation in a metric — _a missing reading is averaged as 0, deflating an availability number_
- **T428** · Stale cache after a write — _a user saves, navigates, and sees the pre-save value from a warm cache_
- **T429** · Unicode/emoji in names breaks a render — _a worker named with non-Latin script or emoji breaks a downstream label_
- **T430** · Very long text overflows every container — _a 10k-character logbook note must not break layout or truncate silently_
- **T431** · Clock skew between client and server — _a client with a wrong clock stamps events out of order_
- **T432** · Soft-deleted row leaks into an aggregate — _a soft-deleted asset still counts in a hive's totals_
- **T433** · Enum drift: a status value no code handles — _a legacy status value renders as a blank chip nobody planned for_
- **T434** · Cross-hive id collision in a shared table — _two hives' sequences collide in a table keyed without the hive_
- **T435** · Large dataset pagination correctness — _a hive with 50k assets pages without dropping or repeating rows_
- **T436** · Currency/precision at scale (centavos) — _GCash amounts in centavos survive rollup without a rounding leak_
- **T437** · Backfill leaves created_at in the future — _an import sets timestamps ahead of now, breaking 'recent' ordering_
- **T438** · Referential repair crosses the tenant boundary — _an automated fix touches a sibling hive's row — the boundary must hold_

### Wave AE — Compound systemic failures (T493–T500, 8)
- **T493** · DB failover mid-write storm — _the primary fails over while many hives are writing; no lost or dup rows_
- **T494** · Edge-function cold-start cascade under load — _a traffic spike cold-starts many functions at once; the queue holds_
- **T495** · Auth outage with cached sessions active — _the auth service is down but signed-in users must degrade safely_
- **T496** · Storage unavailable during an upload wave — _object storage blips while uploads are in flight; they retry, none corrupt_
- **T497** · Realtime + REST disagree during a partition — _a network partition splits realtime from REST; the UI reconciles on heal_
- **T498** · Third-party (GCash) outage mid-checkout — _the payment provider is down during checkouts; orders park, none half-pay_
- **T499** · Cron/scheduled-agents backlog after downtime — _scheduled jobs pile up during an outage and drain without double-firing_
- **T500** · Region-wide degradation, graceful global — _one region degrades; the platform stays coherent for everyone else_

## Second program catalog — P1–P500 (specced 2026-09-05)

The second comprehensive program: **issue-driven, matrix-guided** across the entire sitemap (156 real pages) + the edge-function layer, spanning all 13 full-stack layers and the 102-dim UFAI rubric. Every row is generated as *(a real surface on disk)* × *(a named probe lens)* by `tools/seed_p_program_catalog.py`, which asserts each referenced page/function exists — no phantom surfaces. All 500 enter at the honest `specced` (5%). The deepwalk (Phase 2) FILLS the specifics; this catalog is the structure.

| Wave | Arcs | Range | Layers | Probe lenses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **P-A** · Frontend render & CSS integrity | 72 | P1–P72 | F | CSS contract · empty vs failed · render resolves · escHtml coverage |
| **P-B** · Auth, RLS & tenant depth | 40 | P73–P112 | AU/S/LM | cross-hive read refusal · write-authz depth |
| **P-C** · Data correctness & KPI truth | 48 | P113–P160 | D/F/LM | tile == DB canonical · cap is not a total · window & label agree |
| **P-D** · Realtime & subscriptions | 28 | P161–P188 | A/D/LB | channel filter is tenant-scoped · listener lifecycle · reconnect & backfill · repaint keeps focus & draft |

| **P-F** · LLM / AI-chain grounding | 44 | P221–P264 | C/A/RL/LM | grounding containment · provider fallback chain · rate-limit bucket · refusal & error shape |

### P-M · Phone fit: wrap, overflow & menus (added 2026-09-06, Ian's direction)

Ian (2026-09-06): *"extend some trajectories for my entire platform, I've seen some text are become wrapped on their
container in inventory, then also in the hive board, when you tap the more, it overflows and extended on left when using
phone, just refine my thoughts and be proactive to hunt and fix other kinds of issues aside from what I raised."*

**The lens, refined.** The two sightings are one class: the page was laid out for a wide screen and a phone squeezes it
until something gives — a control label breaks onto a second line, a long token spills past its card, a right-anchored
menu runs past the left edge. Four measurable shapes, one prover — `tools/prove_phone_fit.mjs` (390×844 touch context,
signed-in supervisor, every page in the P-H pool; `--page` for one, `--width 360` for a narrower phone):

| Lens | What is measured (live boxes, never classes) | The seed sighting |
|---|---|---|
| no horizontal overflow | `scrollWidth` vs viewport; any visible element PARTIALLY outside either edge (fully-parked closed sheets and decorative off-canvas art excluded) | — |
| labels stay on one line | button / tab / pill / badge / KPI label whose text occupies ≥2 LINE BOXES (a `Range`'s client rects — the padded height read "Save" as 2 lines) | inventory's control labels |
| text stays in its card | a text node whose box ends past its parent's box, the parent not a scroller | inventory's wayfinding crumb: `Spare-Parts Inventory: WorkHive` (nowrap) past a 300px nav |
| menus stay in the viewport | every more/kebab/menu trigger tapped; the revealed menu's box inside `[0, vw]` | hive's More menu: right-anchored 210px at the button; header wraps → button sits left → menu off-screen |

**Fixed at the root, first (2026-09-06):** hive's `wireHiveMenu` clamps the menu after opening (measure → re-anchor left
or right so it stays ≥8px inside the viewport); wayfinding strips `: WorkHive` from the crumb (only `·|—-` were stripped)
and the current-page span ellipsizes itself (text-overflow on an inline-flex box never reaches a child span). Both are
shared: every page's crumb, every page that hosts a right-anchored menu inherits the rule.

**Lock plan.** Rows enter `specced` (the honest drop in the header %). A page's four rows move together: the prover's
pass over the page = the walk (findings receipted per row), the fix cluster lands, the page reads `ok` at 390 and 360 →
`locking` on the registered gate **`phone-fit`** (`run_platform_checks`), `locked` by the full board (Ian's gate).

## Pain registers (landed) — per-trajectory findings with receipts

### P-program · 2026-09-05 · first authed deepwalk (full 90-dim rubric board, 32 pages, mean 99)

_Instrument: `tools/family_rubric_sweep.mjs` (now browser-recycling — Phase 0) on the 8 GB host without a
crash; anon breadth `post_deploy_smoke.mjs` vs PROD 119/119 clean. Every finding below was DISPOSITIONED

**Synthesis — rounds 1-5 of 2026-09-05, clustered by the job each finding does (the design judgment, not the list):**

1. **The instrument was wrong more often than the page (rows 6, 9, 10, 14, 28, 30, 41, 42, 43).** Nine "silent" pages were showing the platform's own fixed-position notice; two provers walked the seller profile without its query key; the SW prover navigated signed out; the rubric graded catalog cells as marketese. Verdict: FUSE the visibility, session and query-key preambles into ONE shared prover harness that every `prove_*.mjs` imports - today each prover carries its own copy and each copy grew a different blind spot. `tools/prover_harness.mjs` AUTHORED 2026-09-05 (SEEDER/HIVE/WORKER, signIn(ctx), PAGE_QUERY keyed by the page's own parameter, VIS_JS = checkVisibility, psql/psqlAs, SETTLE_MS); all nine provers wired and re-proved on it in chains 4-5 (degradation, hand-off, founder backfill, notice probe, SW identity, focus, backfill, fourth-state; claims in flight), its self-test registered as the fast gate `prover-harness-selftest` - DONE 2026-09-05. Blast radius: 9 prover files, no page. Owner: QA.
2. **Missing data was recorded as a ceiling (rows 45, 21, 27).** Sixteen "no second hive" rows were one seeder away. Verdict: the generators' n/a line now names its own fix ("missing DATA, not a ceiling: run tools/seed_second_hive_rows.py" - DONE 2026-09-05); the seeder stays in `tools/` beside the generators it serves - an n/a that names its own fix is a queue item, not a verdict.
3. **One central fix, several timing holes (rows 29, 44, 39, 23).** The transport settle ran too early; realtime pages never backfilled; the founder inbox class repeated on hive and community. Verdict: the backfill handler belongs in utils.js - DONE 2026-09-05: `whRealtimeBackfill(refetch, { tag })` (one instance per page, debounced across channels, refetches on 'online', exposes window._whRt); hive wired (community follows once the running chain releases it); the settle passes stay in utils. Keep distinct: the poll pages (alert-hub, platform-actions) - a 60 s poll IS the backfill and needs no handler.
4. **A cap that feeds a count (rows 8, 16, 26, 40).** Four founder tiles, the GCash badge, two 50-row badges. Verdict: the `reference-pages-uncapped` gate ALSO flags a count/badge painted from `.length` within the window after a capped read unless the read asks `count: 'exact'` or the line carries a `+` disclosure (DONE 2026-09-05, self-test bites on the GCash shape; 19 pages green) - the cap-ok annotation must name the consumer, and a badge is never rows-only.
5. **Rebuilding via innerHTML destroys the person's place (rows 46, 3, 13).** alert-hub and hive feeds, the marketplace svc pane before them. Verdict: one shared pair in utils.js - DONE 2026-09-05: `whFocusCapture(container)` before the first destructive step (a skeleton or a rebuild) and `whFocusRestore(container, cap)` after the last synchronous render (signature, then position, then first focusable; never steals focus the person moved); hive and alert-hub wired, the page-local IIFEs removed; the focus prover holds focus across the REAL tick for every polled feed in its roster.
6. **Lenses that do not apply were carried as debt (32 descoped today).** Platform-scoped surfaces, read-only pages, static posters, functions without an LLM call. Verdict: descope with the recorded reason is the honest state; the percentage is of in-scope rows and the reasons are auditable in the registry.
7. **A byte no diff can show (rows 44, 47, 48, 49, 51).** Four rewrites of the transport settle chased timing, isolation, repaint races and visibility; the cause was two backspace bytes where `\b` should have been, written through a heredoc, and the same byte sat in the rubric survey, a gate and the checks runner. Verdict: the class is PREVENTED by one fast gate (`no-control-bytes`, PASS over 2,933 code files, registered) and DIAGNOSED by one move - print the predicate's source from inside the runtime before theorising (`probe_hive_settle_trace.mjs`). Keep distinct: ANSI and unit-separator bytes in reporters and vendored code are program data, not mangled escapes - the gate targets only U+0008/0007/000B/0000.
8. **A critic wave closes per finding, never per row (rows 55-58).** The 339 'owed' critic rows were the rubric's own residual dimensions on the pages already fixed today; the honest close is `close_critic_findings.py` (a finding is clean when the page's CURRENT sweep no longer fails its dim; a row closes only when every finding is clean; partial rows print their remaining dims) driven by page-set sweeps, and the residuals fall in CLUSTERS that cross pages: sentences (B3), off-scale radii (S1), i18n keys and mechanism (N1), a filled primary action (A1), layout shifts (I1: the scrollbar gutter, reserves), silhouettes (R3), plus kind calibrations recorded in the rubric with their reason. Verdict: keep the closer strict (no bulk), sweep in sets of 8-14 pages, fix by cluster, re-sweep - the same loop the P-program used, one lens deeper. The 14 live-calculator rows are honestly blocked on promotion.

### Board triage (2026-08-28) — one real defect, three lying instruments

Run against the standing FAIL list. The theme: most reds were the INSTRUMENT, and the one real
defect was invisible to every gate because the two copies of the truth agreed with each other.

| # | Finding (receipt) | Fix | Lock |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **T11, found AFTER its lock.** One ledger row `restock +4` recorded `qty_after 6` on a shelf holding 6 — 4 units invisible (shelf 10, system 6). `trg_inventory_sync_balance` mirrors `qty_after` onto `qty_on_hand`, so it guarantees the copies AGREE, never that either is RIGHT; the wrong total was canonised as the balance. Producer = inventory.html's fallback lane, chosen by `if (HIVE_ID && navigator.onLine)` — a false-negative `onLine` takes the client read-modify-write branch while the INSERT still succeeds, bypassing `inventory_restock`'s atomic `FOR UPDATE`. T11's four recorded fixes all walk the DEDUCT direction; restock was never walked | row repaired (6→10, balance mirrored); migration `20260828000006` derives `qty_after` for relative movements (`use`/`restock`/`add`), leaves absolute `adjustment` authoritative, and SKIPS backdated inserts so a seeder replaying history is not rewritten. One DB fix covers both client lanes (1774 use + 1889 restock) | `inventory-ledger-reconciled` green; **4 behaviours proven, cleanup exact**: a wrong relative total is corrected (999→15) · a CORRECT one is a no-op (10+3=13 stored verbatim, so `inventory_restock`'s atomic path is untouched) · a backdated insert keeps its own number (777) so a seeder replaying history is never rewritten · an absolute `adjustment` stays authoritative (42). **A defect in the FIX itself, caught by reading the gate's own ordering:** the gate chains with `lag(qty_after) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id)`, while my predecessor took the greatest key among `created_at <= NEW.created_at` — so on a same-transaction timestamp TIE (the MR4 shape, now() is fixed) it could chain a row off a sibling the gate sorts AFTER it. Now compares the full `(created_at, id)` key, matching the gate exactly; the residual bulk-tie case is documented in the migration as deliberately out of scope (a BEFORE trigger cannot see rows that do not exist yet, and it is still strictly better: the tail row is corrected where previously both kept the bad value) |
| 2 | `marketplace-state-inducers` accused the page for 25s: `page.route()` **cannot intercept requests that pass through a service worker**, so the abort matched NOTHING (0 interceptions), the grid filled with 9 real cards, and the gate blamed the product. **And the lever WORKS where the property is real: one row converted, permanently.**
`one_brief_per_day` ("an AMC briefing is one per hive per shift_date") is pure DB truth, enforced by
`uq_amc_briefings_hive_shift`. Built `tools/psql_probes/alert-hub__one_brief_per_day.sql` in the house style
and it PASSES all six assertions: the unique index exists · **68 groups checked** (non-vacuity printed, so an
empty table cannot masquerade as agreement) · 0 duplicate days · a second brief for a taken hive+date is
REFUSED with 23505 · a control insert for the SAME hive on a free date is ACCEPTED (teeth the other way -
what separates a working uniqueness rule from a table that rejects everything) · and the count is restored
after rollback, so no residue. Two bugs of my own on the way, both caught by running it rather than reasoning
about it: `brief` is a JSON column and I passed a bare string, so the "duplicate refused" teeth silently never
fired - the fix reuses the live row's own brief, which is self-grounding anyway. **That row never needs a
browser again.** The 87 remaining CD-invariant rows are now a known, sized conversion queue rather than an
**A second row converted the same way:** `asset-hub__hierarchy_acyclic` ("a node cannot become its own ancestor") - 96 nodes walked by recursive CTE, 0 cyclic paths. Nothing in the schema REFUSES a cycle (a parent_id cycle is not expressible as a CHECK), so there the guard is the DETECTOR, not the database - its teeth mint a real cycle from a live parent/child pair inside BEGIN/ROLLBACK and require it to be SEEN. Both probes verified to leave zero residue (96 nodes / 0 cycles, 68 briefings / 0 probe rows).
**A third:** `asset-hub__rpn_recomputed` ("RPN equals S x O x D exactly, recomputed rather than trusted from a stored column that can drift") - 300 modes, 0 disagreements, and the strongest answer was already in the schema: `rpn` is GENERATED ALWAYS, so the drift this oracle exists to catch is structurally impossible rather than merely absent. Asserted anyway, because a later migration could drop the generation and leave a plain column that silently accepts anything while every row still read correct on the day it changed - so its teeth require Postgres to REFUSE a hand-written RPN ("can only be updated to DEFAULT ... is a generated column"; my first regex guessed the INSERT wording and the teeth silently never fired until I read the real error). 300 modes intact afterwards.
**A fourth:** `asset-hub__delete_orphans_nothing` - an orphan here is invisible (the node leaves the tree while its FMEA modes and sensor readings sit in the tables forever, counted by every aggregate that does not join back to a node). It asserts TWO separate claims on purpose: **13 FKs reference asset_nodes and 0 lack an explicit delete rule** (so a new child table cannot quietly arrive with NO ACTION and start orphaning), AND that the rules actually FIRE - a live node with 4 FMEA children is deleted inside BEGIN/ROLLBACK and the children must be gone in the same transaction. Rule-declared and rule-works are different claims; both are checked. **A fifth:** `community__xp_once_and_reverses`. Reading `trg_community_post_xp` first showed WHY it is worth pinning: the trigger does not defend the once-only rule in application logic - it writes `community_post_xp_awards (post_id, reason)` with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and increments XP only when that insert actually CLAIMED a row (`GET DIAGNOSTICS claimed = ROW_COUNT`). So the guarantee IS the unique key: if it goes, a replayed trigger silently pays twice and nothing else notices. 20 awards, 0 duplicate pairs, a replayed claim REFUSED with 23505, a free (post, reason) pair ACCEPTED.

**A sixth, and it taught the day's recurring lesson a THIRD time:** `engineering-design__delete_respects_links`. Projects link to calcs through `project_links (link_type, link_id)` - POLYMORPHIC, so no foreign key and no delete rule - and my first read of that concluded "unenforced, holds by luck" and I wrote a probe whose teeth asserted a delete WOULD dangle. It didn't: the link vanished with the calc. `trg_cleanup_project_links` does the work, and **a foreign key cannot express a polymorphic reference**, so a trigger is the RIGHT mechanism here, not a missing one. Same shape as whSignInWall and the headers const: a guard I had not looked for, read as a guard that was not there. The probe now asserts the trigger AND keeps `enforced_by_foreign_key | f` deliberately, so the day someone adds a real FK that line changes and gets noticed.

**A seventh, and it closes the loop on this morning's inventory defect:** `inventory__no_negative_stock`. There is NO CHECK constraint on `qty_on_hand` - the guarantee lives entirely in `inventory_deduct`, which computes `GREATEST(0, v_qty - p_qty)`. So the probe CALLS it rather than grepping for GREATEST (a comment or a renamed helper would read identically), and it calls it **as a real member** assumed from a live `hive_members` row, because the RPC is SECURITY DEFINER and re-checks membership - running as postgres would bypass the very path under test. Asking for 9,999 more than the shelf holds leaves the balance at 0, never negative, and - the assertion that matters - **the ledger records what ACTUALLY left, not what was asked**. That is the same class as the restock row repaired this morning: a movement the shelf could not make must never appear as one it did. Two wrong assumptions of mine on the way, both caught by running it: the RPC returns the NEW quantity rather than the moved amount, and `stock_conserved` was dropped as redundant once I checked - the `inventory-ledger-reconciled` gate already asserts it.

**An eighth:** `pm-scheduler__one_completion_one_mirror` - the "not two" half is a DATABASE guarantee: `pm_completions_dedup_uidx` is a PARTIAL unique index on (scope_item_id, worker_name, (completed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date) WHERE scope_item_id IS NOT NULL, so a double-tap, a refresh-mid-submit or a replayed request cannot pay twice for the same scope item on the same day. The probe HONOURS that partial predicate in its duplicate count rather than ignoring it - counting rows the index does not cover would report duplicates the guarantee never claimed to prevent, which is the oracle-vocabulary error this bank keeps designing against. 1,597 completions, 0 same-day duplicates, a replay REFUSED, the same pair on another day ACCEPTED.

**A ninth:** `project-manager__no_orphans_on_archive` - 6 FKs reference projects, none without an explicit delete rule, and a live project with **19 children** deleted inside BEGIN/ROLLBACK leaves zero behind. Its child count is taken from the CATALOG rather than a list written into the probe, so a seventh child table added tomorrow is covered without editing it - the same reason the FK-presence claim is asserted separately from the FK-fires claim: a schema can pass the first and fail the second after a table is rebuilt.

**A tenth:** `pm-scheduler__scope_bound` - a completion carries its own `asset_id` AND a `scope_item_id`, and if those disagree the tick was filed against a machine the scope item does not belong to, so every compliance figure that groups by asset counts it under the wrong one, silently and forever. The FK forces the scope item to EXIST; a cross-table agreement between two asset_ids is not expressible as a CHECK, so the guard is the DETECTOR and the teeth mint a real mismatch and require it seen. `hive_id` agreement is checked alongside `asset_id`, because a completion filed under the wrong HIVE is the tenancy version of the same defect. 1,597 completions, 0 mismatches on both axes.

**An eleventh:** `project-manager__links_tenant_bound` - `project_links` is polymorphic, so NO foreign key can carry tenancy and the link table is exactly where it is easiest to lose: one wrong link_id renders another hive's asset, logbook entry or completion on a project page with no error anywhere. The probe resolves EACH link_type against its OWN table and compares to the project's hive, rather than trusting `project_links.hive_id` - the link row's own column agreeing proves the ROW is filed correctly, not that the thing it POINTS AT belongs here, and only the second is the oracle. 54 links across 5 domains, 0 cross-hive; teeth mint a real cross-hive link and require it seen.

**ELEVEN converted, all passing together, zero residue** (txns 454 / pm 1,597 / projects 12 / calcs 30 / nodes 96 all at baseline afterwards). Queue SIZED rather than guessed: of 84 distinct CD-invariant oracles, **59 are DB-only shaped and 25 are mixed** - the mixed ones name a UI fact as well (a chart's rendered series, a page break, "the surface says which"), which is exactly WHY they are live-walk and why they should stay that way. So the convertible queue is ~47, not 84. And even that is an upper bound: `xp_is_ledger_sum` is DB-only in SHAPE yet provably unprovable (the fire-and-forget ledger above), so each candidate still needs the property verified before a probe is written. `aggregate_tenant_bound` was skipped for the opposite reason - a `hive-isolation` gate already backs 132 rows, and converting it without a no-redundancy check would duplicate coverage rather than add it.

**The conversion exercise is AUDITING the oracles, and two have already failed that audit.** Writing a probe forces the property to be stated in SQL, and that is where a claim nobody could check gets checked. (1) `xp_is_ledger_sum` asserts conservation the code explicitly declines to provide (`EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL` around the ledger write). (2) `reaction_count_distinct` asserts *"one person cannot react twice to one post"* while the unique index is on **(post_id, worker_name, emoji)** - the same person reacting twice with different emojis is permitted BY CONSTRUCTION; and with **1 row in the whole table** a probe would pass vacuously anyway, the exact failure the non-vacuity rail exists to stop. Neither was silently re-specced: a row whose ORACLE is wrong needs the claim fixed, and that is Ian's call, not a quiet edit buried in a probe.

**Three distinct reasons a candidate is NOT convertible, all met in practice - which is why the queue must be walked, not batch-converted.** (1) The oracle asserts what the code declines to provide (`xp_is_ledger_sum`). (2) The population is too small for the assertion to mean anything - `reaction_count_distinct` has 1 reaction row, and `plan_links_not_duplicates` has **228 schedule items of which 0 carry a `logbook_ref`**, so a probe would pass over an empty set, the exact vacuity the non-vacuity rail exists to stop. (3) An existing gate already covers it (`aggregate_tenant_bound` vs the `hive-isolation` gate's 132 rows). Each of these is only visible by MEASURING first; none is visible from the oracle text.
undifferentiated walk - and the xp_is_ledger_sum result above is the discipline that goes with it: convert
only where the property is actually true.

**Trying to convert ONE of those CD-invariant rows found an oracle that cannot be true.**
`PB-achievements-055-CD-invariant-xp_is_ledger_sum` asserts *"the XP total equals the sum of
achievement_xp_log"* - textbook ledger-conservation, and exactly the shape a psql recipe should own. Measured
first: **45 of 58 (worker, achievement) pairs disagree**, with totals like 349,455 against a ledger of 95 from
a single entry. My first query was wrong and I caught it (`worker_achievements` is one row PER ACHIEVEMENT,
72 rows / 20 workers, so a per-worker join was a category error) - but the correct grain still disagreed.
**The reason is in `award_achievement_xp` itself:** it upserts `xp_total = xp_total + p_xp`, then writes the
ledger row inside `BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL; END`, commented *"fire-and-forget: failure is
acceptable, never block the action"*. So the balance moves while the ledger entry may silently never exist -
by design. **The oracle asserts a property the implementation explicitly declines to provide**, which is why
it can only ever be hand-walked: no probe can prove it, and any probe written to would be permanently red.
Same shape as the inventory mirror earlier today - a total that no ledger can audit - and the same class as
[[feedback_a_trust_claim_no_query_enforces]]. Two honest repairs, both Ian-scoped because they change what is
CLAIMED: restate the oracle to the delta that IS provable (one award writes one entry and moves the total by
exactly that amount, in a rolled-back transaction), or make the ledger write non-optional so conservation
becomes real. Not silently re-specced here - the row stays live-walk with the reason now recorded.
