#### The fix design — every piece already exists in this repo

Not a new pattern to invent. Three parts, each with a precedent in the codebase, batched into one edit
wave **after** the running board and its restamp complete (editing these files now would invalidate
in-flight gate reports and cost the re-earn).

**alert-hub — a third state, using its own established shape.** `alert-hub.html:512-514` already carries
the diagnosis for the sibling case: *"A FAILED READ IS INVISIBLE ON THIS PAGE TWICE OVER, which is why it
rendered 450 characters and said nothing under an injected 500"* — fixed with `Promise.allSettled` plus
`status === 'fulfilled'` checks. And `:568-572` introduced `_anomalyCount = null` meaning **"not yet
known"**, precisely so *"All clear"* could not render before the truth was in. The page therefore already
believes that **absence, failure and not-yet-known are different**. The refused read is the fourth state
it never got: a 200 with zero rows because RLS filtered them. It needs the membership check first — the
census scores it `role-vocab-only`, and there is no `hive_members` read in the file.

**pm-scheduler and inventory — say the thing you already computed.** Both call a membership
re-validation, find none, clear four localStorage keys and fall back to a personal view.
`pm-scheduler.html:1227` even writes the sentence — to `console.warn`:
*"worker is no longer an active hive member. Clearing hive state."* The user-facing half is missing. Reuse
`validateHiveMembership()` verbatim as the model; it is already correct, it simply has no voice.

**The copy already exists too.** `utils.js:2354` — *"You do not have access to `<thing>` with this
account. Your session is fine. Ask a supervisor if you need it."* — is exactly right, and is why
analytics passes the walk. Route the new branches through the shared taxonomy rather than writing four
new sentences; that is what made analytics correct without a word of its own copy, and it keeps the four
surfaces from drifting apart.

**Verification when the batch lands:** re-run `tools/walk_boundary_not_emptiness.mjs`. It has returned
the same four silent surfaces on three consecutive runs, so a change in that list is signal, not noise —
and the ratchet plus the walk together give the before/after that closes the 34 bank rows.

#### Reading the code changed the fix — the fallback is DELIBERATE; only the announcement is missing

`inventory.html:2445-2470` is worth quoting, because it turns this from "the page is broken" into
something narrower and fairer. `validateHiveMembership()` handles the removal explicitly:

```js
if (!membership || membership.status === 'kicked') {
  console.warn('Worker is no longer an active hive member. Clearing hive state.');
  [...4 keys].forEach(k => localStorage.removeItem(k));
  HIVE_ID = null; HIVE_ROLE = '';
  return true; // solo mode: inventory still usable for own items
}
```

**That is a considered design decision, and a defensible one** — a worker who loses their hive can still
track their own spares rather than being locked out. The defect is not the fallback. It is that the
transition is **unannounced**: the page changes the scope of everything on screen and says so only to the
console. So the fix is not "add a refusal state" but **"announce a degradation you already decided on"** —
smaller, and it does not argue with the original design.

Two details that make it cheaper still:
- **The function's return value is dead.** All three paths `return true` (DB error fails open, removal
  falls back, success), so the boolean carries no information and `inventory.html:2490` correctly
  discards it. Returning a discriminated result — or setting a `_hiveLost` flag beside the existing
  `_loadError`-style flags — is the whole plumbing change.
- **pm-scheduler's copy of the same function is void** and writes the same sentence to `console.warn`
  (`pm-scheduler.html:1227`). One shared helper would fix both and stop them drifting, which is the
  lesson the `_accessDenied`/`whReadError` centralisation already taught on this platform.

**So the batch shrinks to:** one shared "your hive context was lost" announcement routed through the
existing taxonomy, called from the two `validateHiveMembership()` copies; a membership check added to
alert-hub (which has none) so **"All clear"** can be suppressed when the platform cannot see the hive;
and community's empty state given the same branch.

### ★THE SYNTHESIS: this platform learned "failure ≠ emptiness" and never learned "refusal ≠ emptiness"

Every one of the four silent surfaces has **already been fixed for the sibling case**, and each says so
in its own source. That is the finding — not four unrelated bugs, one blind spot with a shape:

| surface | its own comment about the FAILED read | the REFUSED read |
|---|---|---|
| **alert-hub** | `:512` *"A FAILED READ IS INVISIBLE ON THIS PAGE TWICE OVER… it rendered 450 characters and said nothing under an injected 500"* — fixed with `allSettled` + status checks; `:568` even added `null` = "not yet known" so **"All clear"** could not render early | still renders **"All clear"** |
| **community** | `:1193` *"`error \|\| empty` COLLAPSED A FAILED READ INTO 'No activity yet.' … not a smaller claim than the truth, a different and discouraging one"* — error and empty now branch separately | the refused read still lands in the empty branch |
| **inventory** | `:2485` documents an auth-attachment race where *"the first initData reads can return empty (RLS rejected)"* — caught by a KPI parity sentinel | falls back to solo mode, unannounced |
| **pm-scheduler** | same `validateHiveMembership()` shape | `console.warn` only |

**Three states were learned; a fourth was never named.** The platform now distinguishes *the read
failed*, *the read is not back yet* (`null` = not yet known), and *there is genuinely nothing*. What no
surface models is **the read succeeded and the server lawfully returned nothing because you may not see
it** — because RLS refuses by FILTERING, so that case arrives as a perfectly ordinary `200` with zero
rows and is indistinguishable from an empty hive without a separate membership question.

**This is why the 34 bank rows all carry one oracle.** They are not 34 page bugs; they are one missing
concept, and the fix is one shared vocabulary — a fourth state beside the three each page already
models — applied at four call sites. It also explains why the static census was so unhelpful: the pages
*have* the words (they route through `whReadError`), they simply never reach that branch, because
nothing tells them this case exists.

**Precedent for the shape of the fix:** `marketplace.html:1222-1226` already keeps `_rateLimited`,
`_authExpired` and `_accessDenied` as three distinct facts with the reasoning written beside them. The
platform's own best implementation is a taxonomy of refusal states; the other surfaces need the same
distinction, sourced from `utils.js` so they cannot drift.

### THE FIX BATCH LANDED — the fourth state, named once and used five times

Applied after the board crashed and freed the edit window (see the `args` bug below). Two helpers in
`utils.js`, five call sites, no page inventing its own wording:

- **`whHiveContextLost(what)`** — the sentence, bilingual, beside `whReadError` because it is the same
  kind of fact. *"You are no longer a member of the X, so its data is not shown. **Your session is
  fine.** Showing only what belongs to you. Ask a supervisor to add you back if this is wrong."* The
  "your session is fine" half is load-bearing and copied deliberately from the 403 branch: the thing a
  person reaches for first is their own login, and re-authenticating cannot fix a membership change.
- **`whHiveMembershipLost(db, hiveId, workerName)`** — asks the question RLS answers silently, and
  **fails open**: a DB error returns `false`, because *"I could not ask"* is not *"you were removed"*, and
  an outage must not put a false accusation on screen.
- **`whHiveContextNotice(hiveName)`** — shows it in `_whShowNotice`, the region utils.js already reserves
  for standing facts. Explicitly not a toast: `utils.js:940` settled that argument for the sibling case —
  *"a toast that fades leaves the person looking at the same unexplained dashes, which is the whole
  defect."*

| surface | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| **pm-scheduler** | "Nothing due in the next 14 days" | **VERIFIED** — names the refusal |
| **inventory** | silent fallback to a populated personal view | **VERIFIED** — names the refusal |
| **alert-hub** | **"All clear"** | third branch in `renderFeed`, ahead of the F40 filter case |
| **community** | "No activity yet." | leaderboard names the refusal |
| **dayplanner** | plant-PM rail returned `''` and vanished | rail says why it is empty |

**Each fix went where the page already had the machinery**, which is why the batch is small: alert-hub
already branched two ways on empty (F40: *"don't claim 'All clear' when a KIND filter is hiding
matches"*) and needed a third; dayplanner already had `plantWorkFailed` guarding the same rail under the
comment *"Silence is only honest when the read ANSWERED"* — it answered, it was refused; community had
already separated error from empty on this exact string. **Nothing here argues with an existing design.
pm-scheduler and inventory keep their solo-mode fallback; it is now announced rather than silent.**

`alert-hub`'s inline probe was refactored onto the shared helper immediately after writing it — a second
hand-rolled copy is precisely the drift `whReadError` was centralised to stop, and four copies is how
this platform's failure voice fragmented the first time.

### ★THE BOARD COULD NOT FINISH — one unguarded dict key, and every downstream re-earn refused

`run_platform_checks.py` crashed after **66 minutes** of successful gate runs:

```
KeyError: 'args'   at   cmd = [interp, v["script"]] + v["args"]
```

Nineteen registered gates carry only a `script` and a `label` — `selection-is-exposed`,
`shared-button-invites-the-click`, `the-return-promise-is-kept-safely` and sixteen more, all added in the
working tree, **none of them wrong**: a gate that takes no arguments has no reason to write `"args": []`.
The runner treated an optional key as required and died on the first one it reached.

**Why it stayed hidden, and why it cost the whole day's re-earn.** The crash lands at the END of a long
board, so it reads as a late-stage failure rather than a registration schema mismatch. And because the
run never closed, **`platform_health.json` was never written** — which is exactly why every restamp this
session refused: the gate *reports* were fresh on disk, but the run that would bless them never finished.
The restamp was correct to refuse; it was waiting on a file that was never going to arrive. I spent an
hour treating "the board is still running" as the blocker when the board had already been dying for
weeks' worth of runs.

Fixed at the runner, not by adding `"args": []` nineteen times:
`cmd = [interp, v["script"]] + list(v.get("args") or [])`. Spot-verified by running the gate that
crashed it — `validate_selection_is_exposed.py` → **PASS**, 42 pages scanned, 19 using `role="tab"`.

**The lesson is the shape, not the key:** a registration schema with optional fields must be read with
`.get()`, or the first entry that exercises the option takes down every gate behind it — and a validator
harness that cannot finish converts *all* of its passes into no evidence at all.

| `report_contacts` | `hive_id IN (SELECT … hive_members …)` | **real defect** — "No contacts saved yet" |
| `resume_documents` | **`auth.uid() = auth_uid`** | **correct by design** — a resume is per-person and survives losing a hive, so "Nothing here" means they genuinely have none |

`resume` is the useful catch: it carries a `hive_id` column *and* would have looked like a fourth defect
on column-shape alone. The policy is what decides who sees a row, and reading it took one query.

**Deferred deliberately, not forgotten.** The two real fixes are the same three-line pattern already
proven on five surfaces (`whHiveMembershipLost` → flag → branch). They are NOT being applied now because
a full board is mid-run: editing those two files would leave their gate reports inconsistent with their
sources and cost exactly the re-earn this board exists to enable. They go in the next edit wave, together
with a re-walk — which is A15 batching, not a queue that lost them.

**`assistant`, `hive` and `project-report` matched neither vocabulary** and need their rendered state
read the way `inventory` did (its "neither" turned out to be a silent fallback showing real data). That
is the next slice of this arc.

#### The three "neither" resolved — two are my harness, one is a mild trust claim

**`hive.html` — the premise does not hold there, and that is correct behaviour.** It rendered
*"Pablo Aguilar · Lucena Pharmaceutical Mfg. · SUPERVISOR … 3 areas need you. 30 assets have overdue
PMs."* — full data for a hive the walk had supposedly removed him from. The explanation was already in
this document: **only `hive.html` and `index.html` WRITE `wh_active_hive_id`.** hive.html is the hive
board and picker; it re-resolves real membership and repairs the bogus id, which is exactly what it
should do. The walk cannot put hive.html into the removed state by injecting localStorage, so its result
says nothing about the oracle. Testing it needs an actually-revoked membership.

**`project-report.html` — a paramless arrival, not a boundary.** It showed *"Open this page from the
Project Manager (Detail → Print Report)"*, its correct no-`?project_id=` state. This repo already
recorded the lesson (`a_paramless_walk_is_a_different_page`, learned on this very page) and my harness
walked it paramless anyway. Its boundary behaviour is untested; the walk needs the param.

**`assistant.html` — the one substantive note, and it is a trust claim rather than an empty state.**
It renders *"Your hive — Answers are grounded in this hive's live data: open alerts, overdue …"* while
the viewer can read none of that hive's data. The scope chip promises grounding that RLS is quietly
withholding, so the assistant would answer from an empty context while telling the user it is grounded
in their hive. Smaller than "All clear", same family: **a claim about data made at a moment the platform
cannot see it.** Belongs with the next batch.

**So the arc's honest coverage is 17 surfaces: 5 fixed and verified, 5 already correct, 2 correct by
design (per-person data), 2 newly found and deferred to the next wave, 2 untestable by this harness
(hive, project-report), and 1 trust-claim note (assistant).**

#### ★project-report was CORRECT all along — my vocabulary missed it for the FIFTH time

Walked with its param (`?project_id=`), project-report renders:

> *"Either this project was deleted, or it belongs to a hive your account is not a member of **(this page
> can't tell which)**."*

That is the best answer on the platform, because it is the only one that admits the **ambiguity**: under
RLS a deleted row and a refused row are genuinely indistinguishable from the client, and this page says
so rather than picking one and sounding certain. It was scored "neither" because my pattern knew *"no
longer a member"* and not *"not a member of"*.

**Fifth vocabulary widening, same direction every time — pessimistic.** The regex has now missed
`needs a hive`, `Create or join a Hive`, `does not have access`, centrally-provided copy, and
`not a member of`. Every correction found a surface that was already doing the right thing. That is the
signature of an instrument measuring its author, and it is why the WALK's stable four (later zero) was
the trustworthy number while the census swung 25 → 1.

#### ★engineering-design was a FALSE POSITIVE — and report-sender was already the best of them

Reading the two "deferred defects" before fixing them corrected one and shrank the other.

**engineering-design is not a defect.** The walk matched *"No Report Yet"*, which is the
**pre-calculation placeholder**: `engineering-design.html:713-717` — *"📐 No Report Yet — Fill in the
inputs on the left and click **Run Calculation** to generate your report."* It is the initial state of an
empty report pane, shown to everyone before they run anything, and has nothing to do with a hive
boundary. A string match is not a state; the sixth time this session that reading the code changed the
verdict.

**report-sender is real, and it was already modelling MORE states than anything else on the platform**
(`:1045-1062`): `!_rsContactsSettled` → *"Checking your saved contacts…"* with an em-dash rather than a
zero; `_rsReadFailed` → *"Could not load your contacts. **Unknown right now, not zero.** Reload before
adding one."*; plus a saved-copy fallback variant that says the data may be out of date. Its own comment
records the measurement that produced them: *"Measured under a 500: this card read 'Saved contacts 0 · No
contacts saved yet, add one above · START'."*

The one case it could not see is the read that **settles** with zero because RLS filtered it — so a
removed member is told *"No contacts saved yet, add one above"*: an instruction to fix a problem they do
not have, about a hive they are no longer in. Fixed with the same shared probe and a fourth branch
(`NOT SHOWN`, em-dash, matching the card's own vocabulary for "not a number I can state").

**And the re-render bug repeated itself.** I first wired the probe to call `renderCards()` — a function
that does not exist. It sat inside a `try/catch`, so nothing would have thrown and nothing would have
re-rendered; the card would keep its settled-zero text and the fix would exist only in the source. The
real function is `renderReportSenderSummary()`. **Second time in one batch** that a flag was set without
a working re-render (community was the first) — the failure is silent by construction, which is exactly
why it happened twice.

#### The 34 rows are NOT bankable from this walk — the oracle is shared, the SUBJECTS are not

The obvious last step was to bank all 34 `boundary_not_emptiness` rows against the walk. Reading the rows
stopped that, and the reason is worth more than the banking would have been.

**Each surface carries two rows with different subjects**, and the oracle text they share hides it:

- `PB-<page>-097-CH-ufai-I-**IA**-…` — subject varies per page: *anon (what a stranger sees)* on
  achievements, community, engineering-design and index; *worker (tenant boundary)* on alert-hub,
  analytics and asset-hub; *worker (role floor)* on hive; *worker (own-plan boundary)* on dayplanner.
- `PB-<page>-102-CH-ufai-I-**IB**-…` — **`two_context`** scenarios entirely: dismissal scope, FMEA edit
  race, planning race, citation reachability, cross-member visibility.

**The walk proved exactly one subject:** a signed-in worker whose active hive is one they are not a
member of. That is *"worker (tenant boundary)"* and nothing else. It says nothing about what an **anon**
stranger sees, nothing about a **role floor**, and nothing about any **two-context race** — those need an
anon session and a second browser context respectively.

So banking all 34 would attach evidence to rows whose subject it never touched — the precise failure the
bank's typed evidence exists to prevent, and one `bank_page_walk`'s `classify()` would not catch, because
the row would be structurally valid and merely **untrue**.

**What the walk legitimately supports** is the `worker (tenant boundary)` subset on the surfaces it
covered, and even there `dayplanner`'s row reads *"own-plan boundary"* — the personal data that is
correctly still visible — while the walk exercised its **plant rail**. Different claim, same row id.

**Deferred on purpose, with the shape of the work named:** the anon rows need the harness run with
`signIn(ctx,'anon')`; the `two_context` rows need the paired-context harness this repo already has (the
one used for cross-tenant subscriptions and the moderation three-context walk). Both are real units;
neither is "re-run what I just ran with a different flag".

#### The anon subject, walked — all four correct

`--anon` mode added (skip sign-in, inject no hive id — a stranger has neither). It is a **different
subject**, not the same walk with a flag: a stranger is refused because there is no JWT at all, where a
removed member is refused because the JWT's membership was revoked. The `-097-IA` rows on achievements,
community, engineering-design and index all read *"anon (what a stranger sees)"*, so they needed this.

```
ok  achievements   <- "Join the Hive"      ok  engineering-design <- "Join the Hive"
ok  community      <- "Join the Hive"      ok  index              <- "Join the Hive"

4 surfaces walked as an ANONYMOUS stranger · 0 answer with EMPTINESS
```

**All four already name the boundary** — a stranger is offered the join path rather than shown an empty
dashboard. Nothing to fix; the evidence is what those four rows were waiting for.

The summary line was also corrected: it printed *"walked as a removed member"* in anon mode, which is the
same class of error as the harness naming the wrong output file — **a report that misstates its own
subject is worse than no report**, because the number looks like evidence for a claim it never tested.

**Remaining on the arc:** the `two_context` (`-102-IB`) rows — dismissal scope, FMEA edit race, planning
race, citation reachability, cross-member visibility — need the paired-context harness this repo already

Recalled rather than rebuilt. The file exists for exactly this shape, and its own header states the rule

### ★THE SCOREBOARD WAS FLATTERING — six rows disagreed with their own basis, every one inflated

Being proactive on the registry turned up drift the anti-drift gate could not see. A basis is
**append-only**: a later pass often revises the number in prose (`"pct -> 72"`) and only the PROSE is
updated, leaving the pct FIELD holding an older, higher value.

| | field said | its own basis said | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| **T121** shared device | 99 | **78** | +21 |
| **T147** optimistic UI | 95 | **72** | +23 |
| T47 KPI hand-check | 95 | 88 | +7 |
| T78 nav-hub spine | 90 | 84 | +6 |
| T169 bot defense | 86 | 80 | +6 |
| T129 1000-entry logbook | 99 | 98 | +1 |

**Six found, six inflated, none deflated** — which is the direction drift always takes when nothing is
checking. T147 is the sharpest: its basis says *"A real registry needs a discriminator keyed to WHAT is
painted… which the next pass owes. pct -> 72"* — a deliberate DOWNGRADE the field ignored, leaving the
row claiming 95.

Rules 2 and 5 could not catch this. They check `status -> pct` and gate registration; neither asks
whether a row **agrees with its own account of itself**.

**Fixed both ways:** the six fields corrected (program 86.8% → **86.5%**, honestly lower), and
`validate_trajectory_registry.py` gains **rule 6 — pct must match the basis's own last `pct -> N`**.
Teeth proven by re-inflating T121 to 99: `FAIL T121: pct field 99 disagrees with its own basis, which
last says pct -> 78 (update the field, or the number flatters)`.

**This is the same lesson as the Ian-gated miscount, one layer down:** a basis is a narrative, and
*matching* it is not *reading* it. The 60-item list came from matching a request and ignoring its answer;
this drift came from writing an answer and ignoring the field. Both were caught by reading what the
record actually says — and both were flattering before they were caught.

sixteen closure-batch trajectories depend on is in it**: `flow-fits-the-floor`, `dialog-floor`,
`chain-journey`, `kpi-parity`, `hive-at-scale`, `print-is-readable-on-paper`, `a-secret-stays-masked`,
`draft-survives-reauth`, `selection-is-exposed`, all of them **SKIP**.

**So the "3 known failures" I have been quoting all session is a partial picture**, and I should have
read `mode` before quoting it. Those three (`substrate-freshness`, `clone-debt`, `ai-asset-versioning`)
are the failures *among the 611 that ran* — the other 405 have no recent verdict at all.

**This is the `KeyError: 'args'` crash's real cost, and it is larger than "the restamp was blocked."**
`skip_if_fast` gates only run on a FULL board; the full board has been dying 66 minutes in on an
unguarded dict key. So the expensive half of the verification — every live walk, every browser prover,
every gate too slow for the fast lane — **has not completed in a long time**, and the fast board that
kept passing looked like coverage while carrying 405 unrun gates.

**Which makes the board now running the first complete verification in that whole window**, and the
thing every one of the 16 closures is waiting on. It is at 318 reports and past the crash point.

**The lesson generalises beyond this program:** a board that reports `611 PASS · 3 FAIL` and a board that
reports `611 PASS · 3 FAIL · 405 SKIP` are different claims, and only one of them is coverage. A summary
line that omits the skip count is the same class as a row cap shown as a total.

### ★AND THE LOCKS REST ON THE SAME SKIPPED GATES — 16 of the 20 at 100%

The SKIP finding has a sharper edge. Checking the **locked** trajectories' gates against that same board:

| | locked trajectories |
|---|---|
| every gate PASSed on that board | **1** |
| some gates skipped | 3 |
| **ALL gates skipped** | **16** |

T6 and T7 (the invite-code round trip — the most load-bearing flow on the platform), T8 (re-auth
restore), T11 (stock ripple), T14 (offline queue drain), T15 (fault search), T28 (audit reachability),
T45 (Filipino), T166 (composer audience), T176 (error taxonomy) — all sitting at **100%**, all resting on
gates that read **SKIP**.

**What is FACT and what is INFERENCE, kept apart:**
- **Fact:** the only board on disk is `mode: fast`; those gates are `skip_if_fast`, so they did not run on it.
- **Fact:** full boards have been dying 66 minutes in on `KeyError: 'args'` until today's fix.
- **Fact:** `baseline_ref` is **2026-08-23**, eight days old, and no archived health snapshots exist.
- **Inference, stated as one:** those gates' last full-board verdict therefore predates the crash, and
  **the artifacts on disk cannot say when it was.** SKIP does not mean a gate never passed — it means
  nothing on disk shows it passing recently.

**This does not say the locks are wrong. It says they are UNVERIFIED, which is a different and quieter
problem** — and it is exactly the shape this bank already records twice today: a lock nothing runs locks
nothing, and a green summary that omits its skip count is not coverage.

**The board running now is the first thing in this window that can settle it.** When it lands it does
three jobs at once: freshen the reports for the restamp, give the 16-row closure batch its verdicts, and
**re-verify the 16 existing locks** that have been asserting 100% on gates nobody has watched run.

**A clean negative worth recording:** the 405 skips are *exactly* the 405 gates marked `skip_if_fast` —
checked by parsing the registration source and differencing the sets, `skipped - skip_if_fast = 0`. **No
gate skips for a hidden reason**, so the worse version of this finding (a gate that skips on every board
and therefore runs never) does not exist. The skipped set is legitimate and well-defined: it is the slow
and live half of the board, which only a FULL run exercises — and the full run is what has been dying.

### The drift audit's mirror: understatement — and why only ONE row was advanced

Having found six rows claiming a pct their basis did not support, I looked for the opposite. **75 of the
116 `fixing` rows already name a registered gate, and 47 of them contain an explicit assertion that the
lock is built** — *"Locked as 'trust-claim-backed'"*, *"LOCKED BY gate"*, *"gate timed-journey-family
registered"* — while the status still reads `fixing`. The validator's own rule 5 says **`locking` MEANS
the lock exists**, so on the face of it 47 rows are understated.

**Only one was advanced, and the reason is the discipline itself.** "Locked as X" in these bases almost
always means *one FINDING* of the trajectory is gated, not that the trajectory's lock is complete — a
trajectory can gate a property it fixed early while real work continues, which is exactly what `fixing`
is for. Bulk-promoting 47 rows on a phrase match would be **the same error as the 60-item Ian list**: a
pattern read as a claim. It would also inflate the program in the direction the pct audit just corrected.

**T118 was advanced because its basis leaves no ambiguity:** *"Remaining: nothing owed beyond the
wave-close re-earn — idle-network, reduced-motion and the 4x CPU lane are all measured."* Gate registered,
prover on disk, nothing else owed. `fixing -> locking`, **pct held at 96** — status is not evidence, and
the re-earn is still owed. (fixing 116 → 115, locking 62 → 63.)

**What this leaves is a real definitional problem, recorded rather than papered over:** the
`fixing`/`locking` boundary is being applied inconsistently across 47 rows, because "the lock exists" is
ambiguous between *a* lock and *the* lock. The durable fix is to make `locking` mean something checkable —
e.g. every finding the basis names carries a registered gate — which is a rule-6-shaped addition to the
validator rather than 47 hand judgements. **Not attempted today**: the board is mid-run, and a status
sweep of that size wants its own pass with the re-earn already landed.

#### The closure batch is staged as a driver that REFUSES on bad evidence

`<scratchpad>/close_batch.py` (staged while the board ran; belongs in `tools/` once the run is clear).
It advances the sixteen to `locked` only when **both** conditions hold:

1. `platform_health.json` is **not** `mode: fast` — a fast board SKIPs 405 gates and every gate this
   batch depends on is in that set, so a fast board can never license these closes; and
2. every gate the trajectory names reads **PASS** on that board.

Otherwise it prints `KEEP <id> gate not green: ...` and closes nothing. Dry-run by default.

**Its guard is already proven, which is the point of staging it:** run against today's on-disk board it
answers

```
REFUSED: platform_health.json is mode='fast'. 405 gates SKIP on a fast board and every gate this
batch depends on is among them - a fast board cannot license these closes.
```

Sixteen hand-edits would be sixteen chances to advance a row whose gate had gone red — which is exactly
the flattery the pct audit found six instances of today. A driver that refuses is cheaper than a
judgement repeated sixteen times.

### ★AN ORPHANED GATE: T85 locked on something the board never ran

Chasing the understatement question turned up a phantom lock. **T85** (`locking`, 90% — companion persona
switching) names `companion-delivery` in its artifacts. That gate:

- **exists** — `tools/companion_delivery_gate.py`
- **passes** — run standalone: `PASS persona_resolution current=0 baseline=0`
- **was registered ZERO times in `run_platform_checks.py`**

So the registry asserted a lock, the script existed, the script passed — and **nothing connected the
three**. The board had never executed it.

**Rule 5's hole let it stand.** That rule was strengthened on 2026-08-26 precisely because *"LOCKING MEANS
THE GATE IS BUILT, so it must name one"* — but it checks a gate is **named**, and for `locked` that the
name **resolves**; for `locking` it never resolves the name. One row exploited exactly that gap. Audited:
**T85 is the only one** — every other locked/locking row's gates resolve (T1's
`link-target-existence(upgraded)` is fine; rule 5 splits at `(` and the base is registered).

**Fixed by registering it**, which is the whole repair — the gate was already correct.

**★THIS IS THE THIRD INSTANCE OF ONE CLASS TODAY, and the three are indistinguishable from outside:**

| | how the lock was hollow | found by |
|---|---|---|
| 96 psql recipes | carried a `replay` line; **nothing re-ran them** | converting bank rows |
| 16 of 20 locked trajectories | gates read **SKIP** — full boards were dying on `KeyError: 'args'` | pre-checking the closure batch |
| **T85** | gate **never registered** | auditing understatement |

**Unregistered, unrun, and skipped all look exactly like green.** That is why "a lock nothing runs locks
nothing" needed a mechanical check rather than a slogan.

**New instrument, staged:** `<scratchpad>/validate_locks_are_verified.py` asserts that every
`locked`/`locking` row's gates read **PASS on a FULL board**. Both behaviours proven — **PASS** against a
synthetic full board (83 rows), and **UNVERIFIABLE** (not OK, exit 1 under `--strict`) against today's
real board, because *"a lock's gate cannot be confirmed from a board that did not run it, and reporting
OK here would be the exact silence this check exists to break."* It also normalises gate ids the same way
rule 5 does — a mismatch there produced a false positive, which is how the normalisation was noticed:
**two checkers reading one field by different rules will always eventually disagree.**

### ★THE ORPHAN AUDIT: 629 gate-shaped scripts, 6 that nothing runs

T85's phantom lock was not unique, so the question was asked of every instrument in the repo rather than
only the ones the registry names.

**629** gate-shaped scripts (`validate_*.py`, `prove_*.mjs`, `prove_*.py`, `*_gate.py`). **96** are absent
from `run_platform_checks.py` — but that alone proves nothing, because most `prove_*.mjs` files are
invoked BY a `validate_*.py` wrapper. Removing everything referenced anywhere else leaves **9**, and
three of those are superseded near-twins:

- `prove_offline_queue_survives_restart.mjs` — superseded by `prove_queue_survives_restart.mjs`, which the
  registered `queue-survives-restart` gate really does run. **T14's lock is sound** — checked, because a
  near-identical filename is exactly how a good lock gets mistaken for a hollow one.
- `prove_session_expiry_registry.mjs`, `prove_view_inputs.mjs` — same pattern.

**Six are genuinely unrun, and each was built for a named trajectory:**

| prover | belongs to |
|---|---|
| `prove_sw_two_version_transition.mjs` | T44 installed-PWA / T192 release day |
| `prove_mid_migration_writes.py` | T199 the migration window |
| `prove_jargon_is_glossed.mjs` | T177 vocabulary census |
| `prove_throttled_first_paint.mjs` | T37 slow-3G |
| `prove_availability_pages.mjs` | T102 provider availability |
| **`prove_anon_boundaries.py`** | the anon threat model |

**`anon-boundaries` is registered as of today, because it ran and passed 3/3** — and it is a security
prover nobody was running. It asks what a signed-in probe structurally cannot: **BOLA** (an unpublished
listing that EXISTS, fetched by id as anon → 200 with 0 rows — a refusal, not an empty table), **JWT not
body** (an anon INSERT claiming a `seller_name` in the payload → 401 from the policy), and **tenant
boundary as a SET** (all 7 unpublished listings across every hive in ONE anon query → 0 visible).

The other five are browser or migration provers; running them now would contend with the board (and
`prove_mid_migration_writes` applies migrations, which is not a mid-board activity). **Recorded as the
next registration batch, each with its trajectory named.**

**Three ways a lock can be hollow, all found today, all identical from outside:** the gate is
**unregistered** (T85, anon-boundaries), the gate is **unrun** (96 psql recipes), or the gate is
**skipped** (405 on a fast board). None of them looks different from green until someone asks a question
the board itself cannot answer.

#### Regression check on my own three registrations — clean, and one more instrument error caught

Having added `psql-probe-suite`, `boundary-refusal-ratchet`, `companion-delivery` and `anon-boundaries`
to `run_platform_checks.py` today — in a file whose last defect was a malformed registration that killed
every board — the entries were re-parsed rather than trusted:

```
VALIDATORS entries: 1023 · no id: 0 · no script: 0 · DUPLICATE ids: 0
  anon-boundaries          tools/prove_anon_boundaries.py        severity=fail
  companion-delivery       tools/companion_delivery_gate.py      severity=fail
  boundary-refusal-ratchet tools/census_boundary_not_emptiness.py severity=fail
  psql-probe-suite         tools/validate_psql_probe_suite.py    severity=fail
```

**The first pass of that check reported "32 scripts missing on disk" and it was wrong** — my parser
mapped non-literal `script` values to the string `'<expr>'`, which naturally is not a file. Re-run
properly: **991 literal paths, 0 missing**, and 32 entries that build their path from an expression.

Trivial in itself, and worth one line because of the tally: today an instrument was wrong rather than the
code in the census (25 → 1), the Ian-gated count (60 → 11), the walk vocabulary (five widenings), the
`\b`-as-backspace bytes, the "T14 lock is hollow" near-miss, and now this. **The code was wrong four
times; the instrument was wrong nine.** Which is the argument for checking the instrument first, every
time — not a counsel of despair about instruments.

## ★THE JOURNEY-CLUSTER WAVE — 2026-09-07: 92.5% → 96.3%, and the instrument was wrong twenty times

Eleven clusters of persona and feature journeys were walked and banked behind eleven new registered
gates: `anon-conversion`, `identity-lifecycle`, `data-reality`, `marketplace-economy`, `privacy-consent`,
`ux-census`, `notification-pressure`, `device-reality`, `public-trust`, `longitudinal`,
`interrupted-person`, `refusal-and-redirect` and `supervisor-journeys`.

### What was actually broken, and is now fixed

| Found | Why it mattered |
|---|---|
| `export-hive-data` shipped since Phase 5 Track A and **no page ever called it** | The PDPA access right existed in the repository and not in the product, which is the same as not existing for the person holding it. Now in the hive menu. |
| Analytics fired with **no consent state at all** | Consent Mode now defaults to *denied* before the gtag config, replays a stored answer before config so a choice survives a reload, and asks once in a fixed-position notice that cannot shift the layout. |
| A **shared phone kept the last worker's hive list** after Sign Out | Nine hand-maintained key lists had drifted apart, and none could name `wh_hive_lastseen_<hiveId>` — one key per hive, unknowable in advance. One prefix-sweeping helper now serves both sign-out doors. |
| `send-report-email` stamped subjects `en-PH` with **no timeZone** | The locale sets the format, never the clock. On Supabase Edge it rendered UTC under a Philippine label, eight hours early for every recipient. `scheduled-agents` had the same bug in date form, naming the wrong day for a third of every local day. |
| `status.html` had **no meta description** | The page people search for when something is broken had nothing of its own in the search result. |
| Three pages had **no `<main>` landmark** | A screen-reader user had to walk every heading and control to reach the content — worst on `status.html`. |
| **Ten pages explained nothing** to a first-time visitor | Nine now carry a guide written for that page; the tenth is a printable poster and is excluded with its reason stated. |
| One foreign key left its delete behaviour undeclared | Unreachable today, which is exactly why it was worth declaring before a delete path exists. |

### And the tally the section above started, extended

That section closed at **the code wrong four times, the instrument wrong nine**. This wave moved it to
roughly **eight and twenty-eight**. The instrument was wrong more than three times as often as the code,
and the failures rhymed:

- **I searched for my vocabulary, not the platform's** — `recipient_email` where it is
  `report_contacts.email`; `signature` where storms collapse on `rule_id` and `suppressed_until`;
  `auth.uid` where writers are bound by `auth_worker_names()`; `assets` where the table is `pm_assets`;
  `status` where a reported post is marked `flagged`; Title Case where the audit renders CAPITALS.
- **The worst instance nearly shipped a subsystem.** Searching for "delete my account" found nothing, so
  I concluded erasure had no mechanism and built a table, a migration, an RLS policy and a daily cap to
  record requests. The platform's word is *deactivate*, and `deactivate_my_account()` has anonymized name
  and email and revoked access since Arc I — strictly stronger than what I built. All of it removed; the
  real gap was one menu entry. **The bigger the thing a gap justifies building, the more certain you must
  be that it does not already exist.**
- **A source-reading gate constrains how source may be written.** A comment pushed a function body past
  `validate_sso_readiness`'s 800-character window; moving it out made the comment itself match the gate's
  regex. `validate_edge_response_contract` then read an ordinary English sentence as a property access —
  and caught two successive comments *about* that, one for spelling the pattern out and one for quoting
  the sentence. **Describe what a gate looks for; never reproduce it, and never quote what tripped it.**
- **The `\b`-as-backspace hazard bit five more times**, silently. A regex written through a shell heredoc
  becomes a hunt for a control byte no file contains, and it fails *plausibly* — I chased one such lens
  through three reasonable and wrong theories before checking its bytes. **When a regex disagrees with the
  same regex run elsewhere, compare the bytes before comparing the logic.**
- **An impossibly clean number is the probe.** "29 pages state what the platform is worth" was the word
  *saved* in every save toast; the honest count is three. "Zero timers repaint" was a pattern that had
  stopped looking. Both were caught by distrusting a result that was too good, not by a gate.

### Where the remaining 63 sit

**Thirty-eight are one deploy.** Every `_headers` and deployed-origin row depends on `vercel.json`
reaching production — the repository had been shipping Cloudflare and Netlify configs to a Vercel host,
so no security header has ever been served. Nineteen are persona journeys still on prose evidence, five
need an instrument not yet connected (chrome-devtools for Slow-3G, mail-catcher for delivery, sentry for
abuse), and one is `T5`, whose marketplace detail sheet this sweep could not open.


### The one clone-debt re-baseline in this wave, and why it is not debt

`validate_clone_debt` reddened on a single grown pair: `project-report.html <-> public-feed.html`,
0 → 19 lines. The shared block is the **utils.js-failed-to-load guard** — the small inline script that
notices the shared library never arrived (a stale shell, a blocked CDN, a connection dropped mid-load),
replaces the page's frozen skeletons with an honest alert, and offers a reload. Eight pages carry it; two
of them received it after the baseline was taken.

**The extraction the gate suggests would break the thing being guarded.** Moving it into a shared file
gives it the exact failure mode it exists to survive — if the shell is stale, that file is missing too,
and the guard disappears precisely when it is needed. Inline is the only form that works, so the
duplication is deliberate and the baseline is re-anchored at 2090 rather than the block being "fixed".

Recorded here rather than in a commit message because a ratchet that moves without a stated reason is
how real debt gets laundered through a green board.

## ★EXPANSION WAVE 2 — 2026-09-07: UFAI becomes a field, 725 rows seeded, and the critic backlog was 46 rows, not 513

Ian's direction, restated at the wave's approval: *the goal for this roadmap is to increase the Usability,
Functionality, Adaptability and Internal Control of the user interface and experience — UFAI UI UX — for
each page and each full-stack SaaS layer, using the MCPs to deepwalk, moving fast.*

### Phase 0 — the axis is measurable

No row had ever carried a UFAI dimension. `tools/backfill_trajectory_axes.py` now stamps four
structured fields on every row — `ufai`, `persona`, `device`, `entry` — reading the platform's own
vocabulary first (1,179 rows already encoded `device|persona` in `cells`; the P-program and layer-UX
waves carry their own codes) and naming what it cannot classify rather than defaulting. The header
gained **UFAI totals, UFAI × layer, the three thinnest pages per dimension, and persona × device × entry**,
all generated and gate-locked.

Two derivations were wrong before they were right, and both are recorded in the tool: layers made
additive stamped Internal Control on 1,016 rows because any row that merely *crossed* the auth layer was
counted as control; and the P-program's wave codes collided with the T-program's letter P, stamping all
672 P rows as Privacy. The honest reading after both fixes: **U 877 · F 561 · A 635 · I 460** on the
founding rows.

### The eight waves, seeded as one change

| Wave | Direction | UFAI | Framing | Rows | Roster |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EX-PX | persona × device × entry thin cells | A, U | person | 185 | 11 cells × the pages each applies to |
| EX-TL | Tagalog-first persona | U | person | 108 | every root page with no `_t()` call, **measured**: 27 |
| EX-PF | per-page floor to 30 | U, F | person | 213 | every page under 30, **measured** from the registry |
| EX-HP | hostile personas | I | contract | 56 | 7 personas × their surfaces |
| EX-AT | AI trust — the confident wrong answer | I, U | person | 40 | 10 AI surfaces × 4 lenses |
| EX-RV | recovery — I deleted the wrong thing | I, F | contract | 53 | every rostered destructive control on a root page |
| EX-SB | shift boundary, month-end, 3am | A | person | 30 | 5 lenses × 6 pages |
| EX-AX | accessibility personas | U, A | person | 40 | 4 personas × 10 core journeys |

**725 new trajectories.** The headline moved from 97.3% to **68.4% of 2,437 in scope** the moment they
landed, and the EXPANSION WAVES line on the header carries each wave's seeded / closed / open. The
seeder's measured rosters **freeze once seeded** — the gate re-derives the id sequence from `plan()`, and
a plan that re-measured after writing produced a different sequence on its first run (★×16, a sixth
time: a plan that reads mutable state cannot be the gate's source of truth).

### The critic backlog was misread, and the honest number is 46

The plan said 513 rows and 2,454 unresolved findings. **In the critic program "improving" is the state a
fix has already landed in** — receipt written, waiting for the board to lock it. The closer's own
selection rule (critiqued or improving · has findings · **no refs**) finds **46 open rows, all on 13
calculator pages**, 666 findings, none sev-1. Thirteen of their fourteen dimensions were already fixed in
`tools/build_calc_pages.py` and sit in staging; the promoted `tools/` copies the critic swept are the
older generation, and **promotion is Ian's gate**. The fourteenth, N1 — bilingual labels, 0 of 7 — is
now in the generator: seven headings tagged `data-i`, a Taglish page dictionary emitted, 60 pages
regenerated, 120/120 through `validate_calc_pages.py`.

### EX-TL walked: the census reached zero and the page still read 3%

The Tagalog-first prover (`tools/prove_tagalog_first.mjs`, gate `tagalog-first`) has two halves. The static
census counts failure sentences, empty states and control labels that never went through `_t()` or
`data-i`; the live walk signs in, switches the page to `wh_lang=fil`, and counts the visible text nodes
that changed. The census started at **103 sentences · 9 empties · 169 labels** across the 27 English-only
pages. Three tools drove it down: `tools/i18n_wrap_sentences.py` wraps each authored sentence from
`tools/i18n_tl_wave.json` as `_t(en, fil)` where it sits in a JS expression or inside an innerHTML
fragment (**262 sentences**, four authoring rounds); `tools/i18n_tag_buttons.py` tags every plain-text
button whose label the shared dictionary knows (**189 controls**, `WH_FIL_COMMON` grew by 90 keys); and the
census itself learned that a `console.warn` inside a `.catch`, a selector string, a thrown Error message and
a trailing `// don't` comment are not sentences a person reads (the last had opened a fake string that hid
eleven real sentences on community.html).

Then the live walk ran and read **achievements 7% · observability 3% · architecture 0% · asset-hub 4%**.
**A healthy page shows neither its failure copy nor most of its buttons** - it shows headings, labels,
paragraphs, table heads and options, and the census never counted those. The structure that answers it is
`tools/i18n_page_dict.py`: `--extract` walks the visible markup (never scripts or styles) into
`i18n/<page>.json` as English → Filipino, empty until authored; `--apply` tags each element
`data-i="p_<slug>_<hash>"` and emits one `<script id="wh-fil-page">window.WH_FIL_PAGE_VISIBLE={…}</script>`
ahead of utils.js (an inline applier on a page with no utils.js). The first version emitted `WH_FIL_PAGE`,
and the second walk still read achievements at 7%: a probe of the live page found **6 keys where 39 were
emitted** - the page declares `window.WH_FIL_PAGE = {…}` itself, after the block, and reassigned the name.
The visible dictionary now lives under its own global and `whI18nApply` merges common → visible → page, so
a page's own entry still wins per key. **966 visible strings extracted, 769 authored**
in five batches - natural Taglish, engineering nouns left in English - and every roster page now carries a
page dictionary.

**The verdict: 27/27 pages pass the live walk** (walk 3: 21 first time; the six that failed were each a
distinct structural gap, fixed and re-walked in the same session): achievements 7% → 23%, architecture 0% →
23% (no utils.js - the emitted block carries its own applier, re-run on load and on DOM change because the
page redraws its map after DOMContentLoaded), asset-hub 4% → 46% (`whLevelWord` for the thirty cards'
"medium risk" / "critical" pills), ai-quality 13% → 47% (the shared `maturity-gate.js` is the whole page a
locked surface shows, so its own words now go through `_t`), integrations 73% with 19/19 failure sentences,
inventory 38%, marketplace 24% with 33/33. Banked EX186-EX293 → locked, gate `tagalog-first`. Eight rows on
the two observability pages first stayed OPEN because the manifest routed "observab…" to the grafana MCP -
a topic match, not a question match (the "SLO inside slower" class) - so the language lens is now matched
first, on its own words. **EX-TL 108/108 closed; headline 74.8% → 75.1%.**

### EX-AT walked: the confident wrong answer, on every AI surface

Ten AI surfaces, four contracts each (`tools/prove_ai_trust.mjs`, gate `ai-trust`): T1 a person can say IT
IS WRONG in one press and the press is recorded in `ai_reply_feedback`; T2 the surface says what the answer
was grounded on; T3 the down-vote is a real path; T4 on a spent quota the surface admits it - provoked, not
reasoned about, by intercepting every AI front door (`ai-gateway`, `asset-brain-query`,
`analytics-orchestrator`, `resume-polish`, `shift-planner-orchestrator`, `voice-journal-agent`) with the
platform's own 429 body and reading the screen. **Before the wave only the Assistant chat and the companion
launcher had the 👍/👎**; Asset Brain, the shift briefing, the analytics narrative, the resume polish and the
voice journal showed answers with no way to be heard and no source. The structure is one shared row,
`whAiTrustRow(container, {db, agent, source, page, question, answer, groundedOn})` in utils.js - source chip
+ 👍/👎 writing `ai_reply_feedback`, best-effort, the control reflecting whether the write landed - wired on
those five surfaces. Two product fixes the walk forced: shift-brain's first-open auto-generate swallowed a
spent quota into `console.warn` (the person saw "No plan yet" and nothing about why), and the shared
`whAiError` mapper did not recognise the platform's own refusal sentence ("AI call limit reached…"), so a page
that re-threw that body fell through to its generic fallback. The prover learned the person's moves: open the
asset card before asking Asset Brain, open the voice journal's collapsed type box, add an experience line
before pressing Polish, open the launcher where it is the only AI, and remember a toast that lives four
seconds when the read comes at seven.

**The verdict: 10/10 surfaces pass on one clean run** (run 1: 4/10 · run 2: 7/10 · run 3: 10/10 - every
gain between runs was either a product fix above or the prover learning a real move; community was the last,
because the launcher on a 429 said "Couldn't reach the assistant" until it read the response body, and the
prover typed the question into the "New Post" box until it learned to open the launcher first). Banked

### EX-RV walked: "I deleted the wrong thing", one row per rostered destructive control

`tools/prove_recovery_path.mjs` (gate `recovery-path`) presses each of the 53 rostered controls
(`substrate/reference/destructive_control_registry.json`, root pages) as the supervisor in the Baguio hive
and judges three things: R1 a confirm or an undo intervenes, R2 the way back can actually be pressed, R3
pressing it brings the LIVE row census back (a soft delete is invisible to `count(*)`). The first run
reported **"PASS 0/0 reached" with 53 controls NOT REACHED** - a vacuous green: the sweep pressed every
visible delete-ish label and the controls live behind a menu (hive's danger items), inside a modal
(dayplanner's item), in an open thread (community's copy-link), in a 360 view (Asset Brain's FMEA / RCM),
on a tab (integrations' API keys). Two structural fixes: the gate now FAILS on any unreached control, and
a `REACH` table carries the person's own path to each control, authored from the page's call sites
(steps → trigger → the roster heads it answers; a post-action message rides the confirm before it; a
templated head like `Reset ${workerName}'s password?` matches on its static words). The second run then
read "fired with no confirm" on the first two controls while a probe showed the confirm on screen - the
prover counted every dialog in the DOM before the press and only visible ones after, so a real overlay
never out-counted the baseline of hidden sheets. Both readings now use the same eyes.

Reaching all 53 took four more disciplines, each found by a probe that pressed the control by hand and
dumped what appeared: **authored paths run first and a proven head is never pressed again** (the generic
sweep had pressed alert-hub's Reject, seen the confirm, then the authored path pressed into that open confirm
and overwrote the good verdict); **a confirm is closed by its own Cancel**, never by removing the overlay
(which left pm-scheduler mid-confirm for the next path); **every path starts from a fresh page** (the
pre-click sweep of menu buttons had folded report-sender's contacts); and **a step is an opener, so a hidden
tab button is still pressed** (marketplace-admin's queues). Twelve controls exist only when a row does, so
their entries carry a `prep` (one insert for the harness worker, confirmed by RETURNING id) and a `cleanup`
that runs whatever the walk did - a scheduled item in the Manila day, a pending change order on a project
whose type shows the pane, a draft listing, a saved search, an API key, an import batch, an open dispute, a
completed request (the objection button waits for `completed`), a broadcasting hail at the same address and
catalog item, a staged part, a freelancer profile with an accepted job. Index's SSO prompt is a signed-out
person's control and walks in an anonymous context via the page's own opener; the vehicle wizard's undo IS
the way back, so that one entry **accepts** the confirm and is judged by the census returning to what it
was before the wizard created anything.

Run 5 - started before the last seven paths landed, so it is the stale reading - reached **46 controls and
all 46 passed** (offered, pressable, census unchanged), reported the seven as NOT REACHED and therefore
FAILED the gate as designed, and left **zero seed rows** in any of the eleven tables it had written to.
The statically checked cover is 53 of 53 heads with an authored path.

**The verdict: 53/53 reached, 53/53 pass.** The clean whole-roster run (run 6) reached 52 and passed 52; the
one it missed - Asset Brain's RCM strategy delete - was a persisted preference: the reliability workbench
remembers being open, so after the reload that starts every path my "open the workbench" click closed it.
The step now opens it only when `aria-expanded` is not `true`, and asset-hub's re-walk passed 3/3. Banked
EX603-EX655 → locked, gate `recovery-path`. Three rows then sat OPEN because the recovery question quotes
the control's own words and three of those words were "email" - the manifest routed a browser question to
the mail-catcher; the on-screen rule now names the wave's own phrasing. **EX-RV 53/53 closed; headline
76.7% → 78.9%** (1,923 of 2,437). Four expansion waves are closed - HP, TL, AT, RV - and four remain: PX,

Two lessons banked: `feedback_the_waves_wrapper_blinded_four_gates` (a wrapper a wave adds - `_t()`, `data-i` - is a wrapper every instrument must read through, and the heredoc that carries the fix mangles `\b` into a backspace) and `feedback_a_strangers_read_dies_on_a_column_it_never_asked_for` (RLS predicates and invoker views run as the caller; the stranger's path is a definer view with masks, and a psql recipe over EVERY hive-scoped table catches what a wave's own prover, which walked only the surface it hardened, cannot).

### The browser slot serialised the browser and left the database unguarded

Three waves were started at once believing they would queue politely, because `tools/browser_slot.mjs`
serialises the browser and each wave takes it. They did queue — **for the browser.** Nothing serialised the
**database**: a journey drive reading chains, a function wave probing edge calls and a content wave rendering
pages all talk to the same local Postgres. Together they took an 8 GB host from 7.8 GB to **0.19 GB free**
until the docker engine stopped answering at all.

The cost was not a slow run. It was **confident fiction**:

| what the log said | what was actually true |
|---|---|
| `chains read up front: 2 answered, 4 unreadable` | the database was saturated, not empty |
| `effect UNREADABLE` on four of six hives in J2 | those hives have alerts, assets and logbook rows |
| `tier A complete` after 17 minutes | the batch wrote **no result file at all** |
| a function wave mid-flight asking a dead stack whether it refuses a stranger | an answer that would have been written down as a contract holding or breaking |

So the function wave was stopped rather than allowed to finish against a stack that could not answer, and
`tools/drive_waves_serial.sh` now runs the waves in **sequence**, each waiting for the database to reply with
the full cast of six hives before it begins. **On this host the database is scarcer than the browser** — a
lock on one resource is not permission to fan out on another. See
[[feedback_the_browser_slot_left_the_database_unguarded]].

**And a "complete" that produced no artefact is not complete.** The 19-archetype batch exited 0 and printed a
finishing line; only the missing `.tmp/full_journeys_*_tierA.json` files showed it had done nothing. Check the
artefacts, not the exit code.

### The calculator citation, measured six times — and the fifth answer was wrong in a new way

"Do these 60 calculators cite something an engineer can look up?" took six passes. **Five of them were
measuring the instrument**, and each looked correct while it stood:

| pass | answer | what was really being measured |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 60/60 name a standard **and** a clause | the pattern allowed a letter after the keyword, so the HTML **tag names** `<section a…`, `<article c…` scored as citations |
| 2 | 11/60 name a clause | corrected to demand a digit — then over-corrected into demanding the literal words *Table* or *Section*, which is my vocabulary, not an engineer's |
| 3 | 60/60 cite specifically | the family list carried bare two-letter alternatives (`EN`, `UL`) with no word boundary, so it matched inside `min-height: 44px; padding: 12px` — **a CSS block on every page** |
| 4 | 54/60, six cite nothing | word boundaries fixed and stylesheets stripped, but the family-to-number window excluded periods, so `NSCP Vol.2` and `TEMA 10th Ed.` could never match — and the list had never heard of CIBSE, TEMA or IPC |
| 5 | 56 specific, **4 bare** | read the generator's `standard` **field**. Deterministic — and still wrong |
| **6** | **59 specific, 1 bare** | read the labelled `standard:` line **the page itself prints** |

**Pass 5 read a fallback and called it the truth.** The comment beside that field says, in as many words,
*"fallback if calc doesn't return one"* — and I read past it. The page composes its citation from the
**calculator module** and uses the field only when the module returns nothing, so three of the four "bare"
pages were never bare at all:

| calculator | the field says | the page actually prints |
|---|---|---|
| lighting-design | `IESNA \| PGBC` | `IESNA 10th Ed. \| IES RP-1/7/28 \| ASHRAE 90.1-2019 \| PEC 2017` |
| sewer-drainage | `NSCP \| Philippine Plumbing Code` | `NSCP Vol.2 \| PSME Code \| ASPE Vol.2 \| IPC` |
| domestic-water-demand | `PSME Code \| Hunter's Curve` | `PSME Code \| ASPE Vol.2 \| PNS 65 \| ASHRAE 2021 Ch.50` |
| **storm-drain** | `DPWH Blue Book \| Rational Method` | `DPWH Blue Book \| Rational Method` — **the one page whose module returns nothing, so the fallback is what a reader sees** |

**A field named for the thing is not always the thing.** Read the comment beside it.

**Pass 6 reads the labelled line, bounded by its element.** All 60 pages print
`… standard: ASME BPVC Sec. VIII Div.1 | ASME Sec. II Part D | DOLE OSHS PD 856.` inside one `<small>` —
structured, in the platform's own vocabulary, immune to the stylesheet that defeated pass 3 and the family
list that defeated passes 2 and 4. Its own first draft still truncated `ASME BPVC Sec. VIII` to
`ASME BPVC Sec`, because the period-space inside the citation is identical to the one that ends the line:
**the boundary of a structured value is its tag, never its punctuation.**

**So the real gap was ONE calculator, not forty, eleven, six or four.** `storm-drain` cited a book with no
edition; it now reads `DPWH DGCS 2015 (Blue Book)` in staging, awaiting promotion. The other three generator
edits improved a fallback those pages never use — inert, and worth recording as inert rather than counted as
fixes.

| measured against | specific | bare |
|---|---|---|
| the live `tools/` pages | 59 | 1 (`storm-drain`) |
| the staged pages, after the fix | 60 | 0 |

**The twin instrument was still asking the refuted question.** The static gate was corrected through five
passes while the browser lens kept its own copy of the old pattern, and accused **forty** calculators of
naming no clause while they cited `ASHRAE 62.1` and `ISO 898-1:2013`; a leftover family-name guess then
accused the elevator calculator of naming no standard while it cites `CIBSE Guide D:2015` — **the ninth time
in this wave a hand-listed vocabulary has accused a correct page.** The fix is not two correct copies but
**one answer**: the gate publishes `.tmp/calc_declared_standards.json` naming the phrase each page owes its
reader, and the browser checks only what a browser answers better than a file read — *can the person see it*.
The needle is the whole citation, not its number: a first version published `"2015"` and `"10th"`, and 25 of
60 needles were four characters or fewer, so a page could satisfy the check by accident.

**The gate has teeth, because a sixth clean answer earns no trust by being clean.** Six mutations, each
caught: a bare family name must fail, a Roman-numeral part must pass, an internal `". "` must not truncate the
line, the label must not leak into the value. Every published needle is verified present on its own staged
page, so a failure against a live page is a real promotion gap and not a malformed check. `120/120` staged
pages still validate.

### Eleven pages were about to be banked green on a receipt accusing them of a defect they could not have

The calculator Internal-Control lens types `-999999` into every number field and reads the page back. On a
**landing** page there are no number fields, so it typed nothing, found no refusal words, and concluded
`accepted a negative input silently`. The **verdict** was right — the clause counting the range result only
applies to an interactive page — so nothing failed. But the **line** said the page silently accepted bad
input, and **the line is what gets written into the trajectory basis as the evidence a human reads later.**

A verdict and its receipt are two different claims and only the verdict was being checked. The near-miss hid a
second bug: the guard first written asked whether the page had *any* input, while the pass types only into
`input[type="number"]` — so a page whose only field is a search box would have gone straight back to the same
false sentence. **The guard has to name the same thing the test touches.** Read the receipts of *passing*
rows, not only failing ones: a green row with a false sentence in its basis is worse than a red one, because
nobody returns to it. See [[feedback_a_lens_reported_a_test_it_never_ran]].

### The bankers the remaining waves needed

Three written, each with the same discipline about what may be written down, and all four existing bankers
taught to decode their child process as UTF-8 — `subprocess(text=True)` decodes with the Windows codepage, so
a banker died mid-wave on the bullet character `advance_trajectory.py` prints.

| banker | wave | what it will not bank |
|---|---|---|
| `tools/bank_fn_contracts.py` | W3-FN, 186 rows, all reachable | **`n/a` is neither a pass nor a failure.** When the platform bounds its provider call at 60 s with a retry and the prober waits 35, a timeout says nothing about the function — it says the instrument was less patient than its subject. Banking it would invent a reading; failing it would blame the product for the probe. |
| `tools/bank_cell_walk.py` | W3-SC (56, all reachable) and W3-LC/AR/PG/DF | a piece that persists nothing owes no storage-ownership answer; a cell whose page bounced to the sign-in door was never reached; a page still rendering is one nobody has read yet, not one that failed |
| `tools/bank_content_walk.py` | W3-LN + W3-CL, all 334 matched | a failed lens holds while its two siblings still bank — they are different claims about different things |

`tools/prove_fn_contracts.mjs` also gained `--patient`, a 135 s budget wider than the platform's own ~120 s
worst case, so the seven contracts that read `n/a` can be re-asked by an instrument patient enough to hear the
answer rather than recorded as unanswerable.

### Banking cost 30 seconds a row, and the reason was one line in the writer

The calculator wave produced 176 holding lenses in about twenty minutes. **Banking them took longer than
walking them.** Measured directly — count the `locking` rows, wait 90 seconds, count again — the rate was
**3 rows per 90 seconds: 30 seconds each.**

The cause was not the registry's size. `tools/advance_trajectory.py` ends every invocation with two
subprocesses:

```
subprocess.run([... "update_trajectory_scoreboard.py"])      # regenerate the roadmap header
subprocess.run([... "validate_trajectory_registry.py"])      # validate all 3,939 rows
```

Correct for a hand edit; ruinous for a wave. A 176-row wave regenerated the roadmap scoreboard **176 times**
and validated the whole registry **176 times**, each to answer one question. The 462 rows still owed tonight
would have cost roughly **four hours** in that overhead alone — more than the walks that produce the evidence.

`--batch` takes a JSON file of entries and applies them in one pass. **Every rule is kept and the file is
still the only writer:** each entry is checked before anything is written, and a batch with any bad entry is
refused whole rather than half-applied, because a registry carrying some rows advanced and some not — with no
record of which — is worse than one that refused. One read, one write, one regeneration, one validation.

All four bankers now collect and flush once. The swap was made while the running banker was between rows and
the next wave was still walking, since a Python file is read at process start and a half-written one would
crash whichever row happened to be banking.

### 60 public pages shipped a Filipino dictionary that could never be applied

The W3-LN walk held 37 rows on "no bilingual labels", which looked at first like my own spec being strict
about long-form English articles. It was not. The counts settle it:

| surface | carries `data-i` |
|---|---|
| root product pages | 40 of 42 |
| calculator pages | 60 of 60 |
| **learn articles** | **1 of 54** |

So the convention is real and universal, and the public reading surface was the one place it was missing.
Then the compliant article turned out to prove something worse. Every calculator page ends with this,
verbatim:

```js
window.WH_FIL_PAGE = { calc_how: 'Paano ito gumagana', ... };
if (typeof whI18nApply === 'function' && window.WH_LANG === 'fil') whI18nApply(window.WH_FIL_PAGE);
```

**Both halves of that condition were permanently false, and nothing said so.** `whI18nApply` is defined in
exactly one file — `utils.js` — and **not one of the 60 pages loads it**; `WH_LANG` is also what `utils.js`
sets from localStorage. A dictionary written, translated into natural Taglish, shipped, and called by every
page, reachable by none. **A Filipino-first reader met English on the platform's most public surface.**

Two reasons nothing caught it, and both generalise:

- **The `typeof` guard reads as care and is a silent no-op.** It turns "this file was never loaded" from a
  loud `ReferenceError` into nothing at all — no error, no console warning, no failing check.
- **The lens that graded it asked about ATTRIBUTES**, `document.querySelector('[data-i]')`. Attributes were
  exactly what was present while translation was exactly what was missing.

**The fix was not to load the dependency.** `utils.js` is 362 KB — an app bundle pulled onto a static SEO
landing page to swap eight headings, paid for by every English reader. `wh-i18n-lite.js` is **3.5 KB**,
defines the same names so all 60 existing call sites work unchanged, carries the shared public chrome
vocabulary, and yields to `utils.js` wherever that is already present. It loads synchronously in the head
deliberately: the language must be known before paint, so a Filipino reader is not shown English headings
that then change under them.

| what shipped | state |
|---|---|
| `wh-i18n-lite.js` | new, 3.5 KB, unit-tested without a browser |
| 54 learn articles | chrome tagged and translator loaded via `tools/fix_learn_chrome.py` — idempotent, reverts exactly |
| 60 calculator pages | generator emits the loader; **staged, awaiting Ian's promotion gate** |
| `public-bilingual` | new gate: sets the language as a person does, loads each page twice, checks the WORDS changed |
| `called-but-never-loaded` | new gate: reads what a page calls and what it loads, across all 191 pages |

**Measured after: 54 of 54 learn articles actually change language** — `"Learn"` becomes `"Matuto"` in a real
browser. The calculator half reads red until promotion, which is the honest state: the reader does not have
it yet.

**The same three links carried the second finding.** Every article reported 14-31 controls under 40px at 390
while all 60 calculator pages reported zero — the calculators were given `min-height` centrally and the
articles never were. ★**Not every small link owes 44px:** WCAG 2.5.8 exempts a link inline in a sentence, and
making a word inside a paragraph 44px tall would wreck the line box. The nav, breadcrumb and footer links are
standalone controls, which do owe it, and they are what the fixer touched; the prose links are untouched.

**And two false readings during the verification, both caught by checking instead of assuming:** the staged
page reported "0 labelled elements" because the dev server **404s** on `seo_assets/` — an empty page and an
unserved one look identical until you read the HTTP code — and a search for the call reported it *before* its
own loader because it matched **the comment explaining the fix**.

### 25 small targets on every article, and what the number actually was

The W3-LN Adaptability lens reported 14–31 controls under 40px on every learn article while all 60 calculator
pages reported zero. Real — the calculators were given `min-height: 44px` centrally in their generator and
the articles never were. But the raw count was not a count of defects, and getting from one to the other took
five corrections, **four of them to my own instrument**:

| # | reading | what was wrong |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 25 small on the OEE article | inline styles gave the links 44px of HEIGHT and left them ~35px WIDE; the measure asks for both |
| 2 | 18, then 13 owed | I invented a rule instead of copying the platform's. The calculator pages use a stylesheet rule with `min-width` and centring on `header a, footer a, nav a.nav-link` — one rule, covering links my four `href` matches never named |
| 3 | 13 owed | **a calculator's chrome is not an article's chrome**: an article also has a breadcrumb, a table of contents and a back link, which no calculator page has |
| 4 | 0 owed on that page, 126 across all 54 | **the 54 articles are not one template** — three of the next six have nav links with no class at all, so `nav a.nav-link` missed them. Verifying ONE page is not verifying the set |
| 5 | 126 → 47 → **8** | 79 were links filling their own paragraph or list item, which CSS cannot select (`p > a:only-child` matches a link with prose beside it, because `:only-child` ignores text nodes) so the fixer marks them statically. Then **47 of the remaining were my classifier's error**: it asked the link's IMMEDIATE parent whether it was prose, so a CTA written as `<div class="callout"><strong><a>Try WorkHive free</a></strong>: Free at the worker tier, …</div>` reported "stands alone" — a `<strong>` holding nothing but the link, inside a `<div>` that was not in the allowed list. The exemption is about the text AROUND the link, so walk up to the nearest BLOCK and ask there |

**The standard does the deciding, not the count.** WCAG 2.5.8 (AA) requires 24×24 and **exempts a link inline
in a sentence** — forcing 44px on a word inside a paragraph would wreck the line box the exemption exists to
protect. 2.5.5 (AAA) asks for 44×44. So the gate applies both: **FAIL below the AA floor, REPORT the AAA
gap** — otherwise the one link a thumb genuinely misses is buried under seven that clear AA by a wide margin.

The last one below the floor was `<td><a>MTBF and MTTR</a>, <a>OEE</a></td>` — two links side by side at
117×17. Neither fills its cell, so the standalone marker skipped both; neither sits in prose, so the
exemption does not cover them; and being adjacent they cannot claim the spacing exception either. **A link
in a table cell is never "a word in a sentence", and a cell can simply grow**, so cell links take the height
as a rule rather than as another special case.

**Final, measured across all 54 articles:**

| | |
|---|---|
| standalone controls below the 24×24 AA floor | **0** |
| standalone controls in the 24→44 AAA gap | **0** |
| inline prose links, correctly exempt | 300 |
| horizontal overflow at 390 | none |
| breadcrumb | still one 44px line, checked in a screenshot |
| `public-bilingual` | 54/54 still change language after the rewrite |

Standing gate `learn-touch-targets`. The fix lives in `tools/fix_learn_chrome.py` — idempotent, reverting to
byte-identical, applied and reverted five times over during this arc without residue.

### W3-FN: 158 contracts hold, and nine provider calls that could hang forever

62 edge functions, three questions each, asked in the words of the person the answer reaches: does it REFUSE
a caller who is not entitled (I), DEGRADE legibly when its dependency is down (A), and answer its documented
job in its own declared shape with a real caller naming it (F).

| | |
|---|---|
| banked | **158** |
| held with a finding | 8 |
| left open, unanswerable by this instrument | 20 |

**The 20 are not failures and are not passes.** The platform bounds its provider calls at
`AbortSignal.timeout(60000)` and allows one retry, so a slow-but-correct answer can take ~2 minutes; the
prober gives up at 35s. A timeout there says the instrument was less patient than its subject, and banking it
would invent a reading. `tools/repatient_fn_contracts.sh` re-asks exactly those with a 135s budget — wider
than the platform's own worst case — while the fast budget stays the default for the ~55 that answer in under
a second.

#### The finding worth the whole wave: a failover that could never run

Three functions answered `the call never returned and nothing in its source bounds it`. Following the first
one led somewhere much larger:

```
_shared/embedding-chain.ts   6 fetch() to Voyage, Jina, Google, Cloudflare, BGE, Voyage-rerank
                             0 of them passed a signal
imported by                  ai-gateway · embed-entry · pdf-ingest · semantic-fact-extractor
                             semantic-search · visual-defect-capture · audio-chain · episodic-memory
```

**The chain tries each provider in turn inside a try/catch and moves to the next when a call throws. The
design is right and it was unreachable.** A provider that returns an error fails over exactly as intended; a
provider that simply *stops answering* does not — the request waits, and the person waits with it, with no
message and no end. The three voice functions call Jina directly with the same omission.

**★A FAILOVER THAT ONLY TRIGGERS ON AN ERROR CANNOT TRIGGER ON A HANG.** The fix is one option per call: on
timeout the fetch throws, the catch that was already written runs, and the chain does what it was built to
do. Timeouts are the platform's own values — 15s for an embedding (a sub-second call; 15s already appears in
these functions), 30s for the rerank, 90s for `platform-gateway`, deliberately above the 60s the provider
chain allows itself so only a genuinely stuck downstream is cut off.

**Then the audit, because the walk names instances and the sweep names the class.** Every `await fetch(`
across all 62 functions was checked, and eight more were unbounded — including, in `login`, **the sign-in
door's own call to the auth server**. That file already answers an auth outage with "The sign-in service is
not responding. Try again in a moment." — **a path reachable only if the auth server ERRORED, never if it
simply stopped answering.** A person would have waited on a spinner with no message.

Timeouts are per call, because what is patient for a batch job is a broken door for a person:

| call | bound | why |
|---|---|---|
| `login` → GoTrue | 15s | somebody is standing at the sign-in screen |
| `error-tracker` → Sentry | 5s | error reporting must never delay the response it reports on |
| `ssrf-guard` → redirect probe | 10s | a guard that can hang is itself the denial of service |
| `engineering-bom-sow` → Google | 30s | a generation call, but a person is watching a form |
| `gcash-receipt-ocr` → Azure | 30s | analyze and poll, both |
| `ai-eval-runner`, `ai-orchestrator` | 60s | batch and downstream; the gateway allows itself 60 |

**Measured after: 37 of 37 outbound calls bounded, none left.**

#### The other findings, and one that was the host

| finding | functions | status |
|---|---|---|
