| an unbounded provider call | `voice-semantic-rag`, `platform-gateway` | **fixed** |
| "the call never returned" | `platform-scraper` | **the host, not the function** — it has no outbound `fetch` at all; its awaits are database calls, and the database was saturated when the probe ran. To be re-asked on a quiet host |
| a code where a sentence belongs | `login` → `missing_credentials`, `supervisor-reset-password` → `missing_hive_or_target` | real: these reach a person at the sign-in door |
| answered with none of the keys its source builds | `marketplace-listing-assist`, `notify-push`, `resume-polish` | to check: the lens may be comparing a 4xx response against the success shape |

Deploying any of this is Ian's gate; the edits are local, and the local edge runtime needs its deno cache
cleared and a restart before it serves them.

### 37 rows retracted: every shared-component reading was of the sign-in door

`prove_shared_components.mjs` walks each shared piece on three host pages — a phone, a desktop and a wall
display — and asks whether it says the same thing everywhere, does its job, holds up, and never shows one
person another person's state. It banked 37 rows. **All 57 of its readings were of a page that is not the
subject.**

Without an identity, `/inventory.html` redirects to `/index.html?signin=1&return=inventory.html`. **The door
answers 200 and renders happily**, so nothing in the reading itself says which page it came from. The prover
walked the door three times for every piece and reported what it found there:

| the finding | what it was actually about |
|---|---|
| `0/3 define whAutosave()` | the door does not load `form-autosave.js`; the file defines `window.whAutosave` on its own first lines |
| `its element appeared on 0 of 3 host(s)` | the door has no such element |
| `2 of its element(s) are under 40px on a phone` | the door's elements |
| 30 × "no lens could answer this" | the door has neither the element nor the storage the lens asks about |

**The trail that found it** is worth keeping, because every step looked like a product defect: a component
reports its global is undefined → the file plainly defines it → maybe the host pages do not load it →
`grep -l` says three pages do → the browser says there is no such script tag in the DOM → maybe the file
404s → it serves 200 in 6,046 bytes → **so what page is this?** — `/index.html?signin=1`.

**Retracted, not left standing.** All 37 rows are back to `specced`, each carrying the withdrawal in its
basis: *"the walk that banked this never reached its page … the verdicts described the door, not this shared
piece."* The basis is append-only, so the false claim and its retraction both stay visible, which is the
point. **A green row whose basis describes a different page is worse than an open one, because nobody goes
back to it.** The headline moved 71.0% → 70.0%, which is the honest number.

**The guard, in the two provers that bank rows:** the landed URL is compared to the requested page and a walk
that arrived somewhere else grades nothing. `prove_lifecycle_cells.mjs` and `prove_full_journeys.mjs` already
had this; `prove_shared_components.mjs` and `prove_content_ufai.mjs` now do too. The content pages are public
and do not bounce today — the guard costs one `evaluate` and outlives the assumption that they always will be.

**Re-walking needs an identity, so it waits for the stack.** Nothing about these 76 rows can be measured while
the pages redirect.

### With the database down, 50 rows were still answerable — and one of them found a credential pointer

The stack had been returning 500 on every call for an hour, and the remaining waves all needed it. That is
not the same as the queue being empty, and the difference was worth about fifty rows: **a question is
blocked only if the EVIDENCE it needs is blocked.** Four of the open question-types turned out to need
neither a database nor an identity.

| question | rows | where the evidence lives |
|---|---|---|
| does anything catch this page's regressions? | 18 | the gate registry, the provers it runs, the test suites — files |
| which clock and which period do these figures belong to? | 11 | the page's own text |
| does this page record who did what, in a readable trail? | 9 | the page and the scripts it loads |
| you opened this from a pasted link, with no history | 12 | a fresh browser context, no data needed |
| first run, and 768 in both orientations | 24 | the page as it renders with nothing in it |

**The deep-link question has two honest answers and the wave had been treating it as one.** A private page
SHOULD refuse a stranger; the failure is refusing without saying where they were going. So a public page must
open, and a private page must reach the door **with the destination kept** — `?signin=1&return=<page>` — so
signing in finishes the trip. Nine of twelve answer honestly, three were still resolving and were left open.

**Two instrument corrections, both the same mistake this wave keeps making.** A page still showing skeletons
was passing a length check: `platform-actions` renders "Checking access… Loading…" over four shimmer blocks
and never resolves while its data is unreachable — 547 characters of placeholder that clears any threshold
while describing nothing. It is now `n/a`, because nobody has read that page yet. And the "what do I do next"
vocabulary missed `status.html`, which offers a **Refresh** control and a **How this page works** section:
orienting a reader is the next move on a page whose job is to be read. **The tenth hand-listed vocabulary in
this wave to accuse a page of lacking something it has.**

#### The finding under the finding: a credential pointer on three pages nobody was gating

Reading why one page had been flagged turned up this, rendered in page copy:

```
Grafana login: admin · password in infra/mcp/.env.mcp
```

It was removed from `marketplace-admin.html` on **2026-08-25**, with the reason written into the file: *"this
overlay renders for ANY signed-in visitor to the URL, not only the founder, and a credentials location baked
into page copy is a screen-share/shoulder hazard."* **Three sibling pages carried the identical paragraph and
were never touched — and they were worse than the page that was fixed, because none of them is auth-gated at
all.** It rendered for anyone who opened the URL.

It leaks no password. It names the account and points at the file that holds one, on a page anybody can read,
which is most of the work. Removed from all three, not reworded: the pointer is the part worth removing.

**The class recurs by COPY** — a paragraph written once, pasted onto siblings, and a fix applied to whichever
page somebody was looking at. Only a sweep of every page can see that, so `credential-pointers` now reads all
216 of them. It was proved to bite by putting the line back and watching it fire.

**Five gates added, each with its own teeth:** `regression-cover`, `clock-and-trail`, `deep-link-arrival`,
`firstrun-tablet`, `credential-pointers`.

### A gate that skips clean is a gate that can be green while measuring nothing

A memory hit while writing the shared identity helper pointed at an old finding: `tools/axe_scan.js` seeds a
FAKE identity on a static server, so every auth-gated write page bounced to the sign-in gate and was skipped
— the baseline covered eleven read-mostly pages while **the forms, modals and destructive surfaces had zero
accessibility coverage behind a green gate.** `tools/axe_scan_live.js` was written on 2026-07-07 to close it.

**I then got two things wrong about it, and both are worth recording.**

**Wrong once:** I searched `run_platform_checks.py` for `axe_scan_live` and found nothing, and concluded the
scanner had never been registered. It is registered — through a Python wrapper called
`tools/validate_axe_live.py`, which shells out to it. *Searching for the implementation's name misses a gate
registered by its wrapper's name.* I briefly added a duplicate registration and removed it.

**Right once, and it matters more.** The scanner **skips cleanly, exit 0**, whenever the password grant
fails. It failed twice in an hour while the identical request succeeded from curl and from node moments
later: GoTrue answers intermittently while the stack settles. So a flaky dependency turns this into a gate
that reports nothing while staying green — the "skipped" variety of a hollow lock, beside "unregistered" and
"unrun". It now retries five times before giving up.

**Wrong twice:** the retry I added assigned to a `const`, so it threw `Assignment to constant variable` — a
retry that works until the moment it is actually needed. Caught by running the gate through its wrapper
rather than the script directly.

**And running it found a real defect within the hour.** `marketplace.html` carried a serious
`aria-prohibited-attr`: `<div class="listing-grid" aria-label="Marketplace listings">`. A plain `<div>` has
role `generic`, which **may not carry an accessible name** — so the label was announced to nobody and the
attribute was invalid. Two divs fixed with `role="region"`, the least invasive role that permits a name:
unlike `role="list"` it imposes no contract on children that are rendered later, and the sibling area already
does the same thing implicitly as `<section aria-label>`.

**Measured after: 12 authed write surfaces, 0 violations, through the registered wrapper.**

### The identity, and what it was worth

Three provers were walking the sign-in door. The shared-component one graded it and 37 rows were banked on
that; the lifecycle one detected it and refused **105 of 202 rows**; the first-run one still had four. The
fix is the same forty lines each time, so it became `tools/wh_identity.mjs` — sign in once through the page's
own client, hand every context the same `storageState`. **Copying it a fourth time would have been the same
shape as the credential-pointer defect found the same night: a paragraph pasted onto siblings, corrected
wherever somebody happened to be looking.**

| prover | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| shared components | 33/76 lenses, every reading of the door | **75/76**, zero bounced, 44 rows banked |
| lifecycle cells | 105 of 202 refused as "reaches the door, not the page" | **zero bounced** |
| function contracts | 158 banked, 8 held | **182 banked**, 1 held |

**The function wave's three shape findings were the envelope bug.** `marketplace-listing-assist`,
`notify-push` and `resume-polish` now read *"in its own declared shape (ok, error, data)"* — the lens had
been reading each function's own file for a shape that lives in `_shared/envelope.ts`, which **59 of the 62**
use. `platform-scraper`'s "the call never returned" was the saturated host: on a healthy one it answers
legibly on all three lenses.

**And the lens was punishing the fix.** `login` was corrected to answer
`{"error":"missing_credentials","message":"Enter your username and password to sign in."}` — a code AND a
sentence, which is what a good answer looks like — and was still reported as "a code, not a sentence",
because the reader checked `error` before `message`. A lens asking whether output speaks to a person must
prefer the field that does. `platform-gateway`'s own "Missing fn" was a genuine one and now reads
*"That request did not say which platform action to run. Reload the page and try again."*

### Two more questions a file can answer, and one that a file cannot

**`consumption-bound`** asks whether a page that caps what it loads SAYS so. Eleven pages carry the row, and
the first run passed all eleven — on identifiers. Searching for the telling inside the concatenated
JavaScript matched `viewall` and `loadMore`, which no reader will ever read. **The bound is a fact about the
code; the telling is a fact about what a person sees, so the two halves are searched in two different places
on purpose.** Scoped properly: **4 hold, 7 findings** — pages that cap at 500 and say nothing anywhere, in
markup or in script. The defect is structural rather than about today's row count: the day the data passes
the cap, the page shows a wrong total and nobody is told.

**`empty-state`** asks whether a page with nothing to show says why and what to do first. An empty hive is
the expensive way to see an empty page; a filter that matches nothing is the cheap one. Two corrections were
needed to read it honestly: **the first search box on a page is often the shared nav hub's**, so filtering it
filtered the MENU and left the page's own text unchanged; and `"0 "` was accepted as a statement, which any
count or price satisfies. `report-sender` then read as a genuinely good empty state —
*"REPORTS SELECTED 0 · Pick 1+ from the 4 available"* — saying both halves.

### Banked is not closed, and the program's own classifier says so

About fifty rows were answered from files during the outage, and the headline barely moved. That is correct.
**CLOSED means walked LIVE against the running system, held by a registered gate, AND walked with the
instrument that row's lens demands.** A consumption-bound row whose lens asks for the database is banked when
a file answers it, and still not closed — the evidence is real but it is not the evidence that row asked for.
The classifier enforces the difference so the header cannot flatter the work. Both numbers are honest and
they are not the same number.

### What the lifecycle walk found once it could reach the pages

With an identity it banked **147 rows** (from 66) with **zero bounced readings**, and held 39 findings that
group into five real shapes:

| finding | rows |
|---|---|
| offers no export to read back | 8 |
| shows figures with no period named | 9 |
| nothing tells a returner what they are looking at or how old it is | 4 |
| nothing here can be taken away (no delete, no undo) | 3 |
| shows work with nobody named against it | 3 |

**The period findings agree with a second, independent instrument.** `clock-and-trail`, reading the pages'
own text from disk, found the same class on nine pages. Two lenses built at different times, reading
different sources, naming the same gap — which is the kind of agreement that makes a finding worth acting on,
and the opposite of the disagreements that ran this wave all night.

### The handover test that nearly called a working team a data leak

Sixteen shared-component rows ask whether a piece shows one person another person's state. The walk kept
answering *"this piece persists nothing of its own"* — true, and not an answer: **a piece with no storage can
still leave one person's draft on the screen for the next.** So the question was rebuilt as the thing a plant
actually does — a HANDOVER on one device: A signs in and works, A signs out, B signs in on the same browser.

**The first version checked whether A's NAME survived, and reported all sixteen pieces as leaking.** Pablo
and Hector are members of the same hive: Hector is *supposed* to see Pablo's name against Pablo's logbook
entries. **A test that cannot tell shared content from private state will call a working team a data leak** —
and it would have shipped sixteen false findings with a serious-sounding word attached.

Rebuilt around a SENTINEL only A could have typed, plus a refusal to conclude anything if the sentinel never
landed (a page with no writable field gives a clean "after" for reasons that have nothing to do with the
pieces). Measured: the sentinel landed in a field, and after the handover it is **gone from the screen, from
every field and from storage — 16/16.**

Standing gate `shared-handover`.

### "3 hops have no way onward" — the finding that would have marked most of 724 rows wrongly

The first archetype of the tier-A drive, J4 (audit season), failed in all six hives with the same line:
**3 hop(s) have no way onward at all.** Chasing it was worth more than the row.

Its declared path is `logbook → audit-log → analytics-report → report-sender → project-report`. Reading the
pages confirmed the prover: three of those four transitions have **no anchor and no mention** of their next
step. But the nav hub is not a way onward either — its links are built when it opens, and even opened, as a
supervisor, there is no link to the audit log.

**Then `nav-hub.js` explained itself, in a comment beside the entry:**

```js
// Phase H.2: hidden, surfaced via the "Audit Log" button on hive.html.
{ label: 'Audit Log', href: 'audit-log.html', hidden: true, roles: ['supervisor'], … }
```

**Five entries carry `hidden: true`, and a sixth — `analytics-report.html` — is not a hub entry at all.**
The platform deliberately parents these: the audit log is reached from the hive page, the project report from
the project manager, the analytics report from the analytics dashboard. **The archetype's path skips the
route the platform intends. The product is behaving as designed, and the spec is what is wrong.**

**24 of the 32 archetypes touch one of these destinations.** The running drive was walking with the old
wording, so it was on course to put a false navigation defect on most of the 724 journey rows. It was stopped
and restarted against a corrected prover, which now reports the difference:

> 1 hop(s) have no way onward at all; 2 hop(s) go straight to a destination the platform parents elsewhere
> (audit-log.html is reached from hive.html; project-report.html is reached from project-manager.html) —
> this archetype's path skips the intended route, it is not a navigation gap

**The map is DERIVED, not typed**, because a hand-typed list of five was already wrong — it missed
`analytics-report.html`, so J4's third hop was still being called a gap. The prover reads the hub's own hrefs
and, for any destination the hub does not offer, names the page that links to it. Three refinements were
needed and each one is the same lesson in a different coat:

| the first answer | why it was wrong |
|---|---|
| re-read every page for every other | ~190 × 190 file reads, slower than the walk it prepared for — read each page once, 125 ms |
| `project-report.html is reached from index.html` | **the landing page links to everything**, so it wins every tie and names nothing useful; rank a page sharing the destination's stem first and the landing page last |
| `audit-log.html is reached from community.html` | a link-graph guess, when the hub's own comment says `hive.html` — **reading the sentence beats ranking the candidates**, every time this wave has tried both |

### The class became a one-second check

`journey-paths` reads every archetype's declared path and asks, for each consecutive pair, whether the
earlier page LINKS to the later one or the nav hub OFFERS it. It answers from files in about a second, so
this class never needs to cost a walk again.

**55 hops across 39 archetypes skip a route the platform offers**, and every one names the page to route
through. Getting there needed four corrections, each the same lesson this wave has taught all night in a new
coat:

| the first answer | why it was wrong |
|---|---|
| every hop into a calculator or an article is unreachable | the link graph read only root `*.html`, and the platform links to a **directory** (`/tools/oee-calculator/`), not to `index.html` |
| a calculator with eight real routes reported as having none | the landing page was detected by FILENAME, and every article and calculator is `<slug>/index.html` too — **the landing page is the ROOT one only** |
| "route `ph-intelligence` through `learn/ph-industrial-benchmarks-intelligence`" | a page sharing three letters beat `analytics.html`, the surface a person would actually use — **a journey routes through product surfaces, not through articles** |
| "no page offers `learn/index.html` at all" | the hub's own link is `/learn/`, which normalises to the bare word and was dropped |

**Nothing now reports a destination as unreachable.** All 55 carry a named route, which is the difference
between a finding somebody can act on and a list somebody has to re-investigate.

The pattern across every one of these corrections is worth stating plainly, because it is the shape of the
whole night: **each first answer was confident, precise, and produced by an instrument measuring itself.**
The product was right far more often than the thing looking at it.

### The instrument graded its own mistake, three lenses at once

`prove_fn_contracts.mjs` asks each of the 62 edge functions three questions. All three graded the FIRST
reply the function sent, and for most functions that reply is a complaint about the request:

| lens | what it banked | what that reply actually was |
|---|---|---|
| **I** refuses an outsider | `refused a foreign-hive request with 400 and said so: "Missing or invalid op"` | the function telling me I had left a field out, before anything looked at whose hive I named |
| **A** degrades legibly | `degraded legibly: 400 "Missing required field: question"` | a request that died on its shape and never reached the dependency this row is about |
| **F** completes its job | `answered 400 in its own declared shape` | the house envelope carrying the complaint. A 400 completes nothing |

**128 of 186 rows stood on that.** Only 14 of the 62 refusal readings were real (11 × 403, 3 × 401).

Two repairs. The function now **teaches the probe its own shape** — the missing fields are read out of the
complaint, filled in, and the question asked again — and the verdict rests on a **differential**: the same
well-formed request sent twice, changing one thing only, whose hive it names. Asked properly,
`agent-memory-store` answers *"Caller is not an active member of this hive."* — which is the sentence the
row was always asking for.

Four corrections were needed inside the repair itself, and each is the same shape as the bug it fixed:

- a 4xx that is a **shape complaint** is not a refusal, and neither is a 405 (my method) or a 429 (my rate)
- **"Unknown agent 'status'. Available: asset, …"** is a function handing over its vocabulary; the first
  reader knew only *missing* and *invalid*, so it abandoned the exchange one step from an answer
- a complaint names **several** fields. Against *"Missing required fields: question, asset_id, hive_id"* the
  reader matched the word `field` inside `fields` and captured the leftover **`s`** — one regex accounting
  for 98 of the 108 contracts the corrected run still could not answer
- a field wanting a **real row** cannot be satisfied with a placeholder: `asset_id` gets a real asset, from
  `asset_nodes` — not `assets`, which does not exist and would have failed silently

A probe that asks for an option must **never pick the one that writes**: offered `"recall"` or `"store"`, it
takes `recall`. It was one careless line from storing rows in a stranger's hive to find out whether it was
allowed to read one.

### 55 hops, 4 retired pages, and a link graph that never opened its own index

The journey grid's paths were written as *the surfaces a story touches*, not as *a route a person can walk*.
`check_journey_paths.py` found **55 hops across 39 archetypes** stepping to a page the previous one does not
link to and the hub does not offer. Walking them would have recorded a navigation defect on most of 724 rows.

Repairing them took four corrections to the reading itself:

| the first answer | why it was wrong |
|---|---|
| route the founder's month-end **through `founder-console.html`** | that page is under a fixed, full-screen *"moved to Grafana"* card. **Four surfaces are retired this way**, three of them in J32's own declared path |
| route `project-report` **through `project-report`** | the page links to itself, and "prefer a page this journey already visits" handed it its own detour |
| route a calculator **through a sibling calculator** | the two link to each other; the section's own index is how this platform hands somebody a calculator |
| `learn/index.html` links to nothing | the glob `learn/*/index.html` needs a directory in between, so **the page carrying 56 internal links was never opened as a source**. It had already been taught to be a destination; being a destination and being a source are different memberships |

Inserting one page also makes a NEW hop nobody asked about — J30 ping-ponged between a calculator and the
article listing it, growing two pages a pass and never converging. A route is a **walk**, not a hop: the
answer is now the shortest path across "everything this page links to, plus everything the hub offers from
anywhere", found once and inserted whole. **55 → 0**, across 26 archetypes and 438 rows.

Each retired page's own banner says where its work went, and the two answers are different repairs: marketplace
moderation **moved to `platform-actions.html`** (re-point), while the LLM and agentic-RAG observability
**left the product for Grafana** (drop — that step cannot be walked here at all). No live page links to any
of the four, and the hub offers none of them, so the retirement itself is clean.

One finding survives the repair and is kept deliberately: **`public-feed.html` is linked from the landing
page and nowhere else**, so seven hops reach it only by going home first.

### Two chains blamed the product for the join they were written with

The journey drive held J17 and J18 in all three plant hives, each with a confident sentence:

- **J17** — *"the chain is empty in this hive (readings, and the alerts they raised)"*. It counted
  `anomaly_alerts`, which holds zero rows in every hive. The alert surface reads `v_alert_truth`, and its
  signals are computed **on demand** by `compute_anomaly_signals` when a member opens the hub. Run as a real
  supervisor of Lucena, that call returned **53** and wrote 42 signal rows from readings that were there all
  along (reverted after; the audit reads 0). The chain J2 sits on already carried this exact correction, one
  line above the one that repeated it.
- **J18** — *"risk scores naming assets this hive actually owns: 0"*, of all three plants. It joined
  `asset_risk_scores.asset_name` to `asset_nodes.name`, the human name (*"APC Symmetra PX 250"*). The column
  holds the asset **tag** (*"AC-001"*). On `name` the match is **0 of 3,315**; on `tag` it is **3,315 of
  3,315**. The chain accused the platform of naming assets it does not own, and the opposite was true of
  every single row.

Both are the night's one lesson again: **the instrument was wrong far more often than the product**, and each
time it was wrong it was confident, specific, and about to be banked.

### A day plan that mixed two plants, found by rebuilding the lens that had been passing it

Eight pages carry *"the platform must keep a person's two hives apart on this page, in both directions."*
The lens holding them graded it as **`chars > 400`** — "renders inside one hive scope" — which every page
that renders at all satisfies. Four of the eight had been banked on it. The live-walk ledger was right to
keep all eight open and to name `postgres-mcp` as the instrument they actually need.

Answered properly — as **Christine Dizon, a supervisor who really is in two hives**, through PostgREST with
her own token, never the owner connection — the claim has two halves, and the second is the one that stops
it being theatre:

- **SCOPED** — every read against a hive-owned table carries the active hive.
- **LOAD-BEARING** — that same read, made as her *without* the scope, really does return both hives. If it
  does not, the green is vacuous: the page passes because she has no second hive worth separating.

**Seven pages scope correctly. `dayplanner.html` did not.** Its PM rail reads `v_pm_scope_items_truth` with
no hive filter, and its comment states the assumption that made it look safe: *"RLS scopes the view to the
worker's hive"* — **singular**. RLS scopes it to the worker's hives, **plural**. Read live as her, that view
returns **293 rows: 150 from one plant and 143 from the other.** Her day plan listed both plants' overdue
PMs together, and because the rail uses `count: 'exact'` to state a number beside itself, that number was a
**two-hive total** — the same class of wrongness the code's own comment had already fixed once, for a
different reason, three lines above.

The page had no notion of the active hive at all: `HIVE_ID` appeared **zero** times. It was written as a
personal planner keyed by `auth_uid`, and the PM rail was added later without the hive coming with it. Fixed
with the platform's own accessor and pm-scheduler's own idiom, including the hive-less half so a personal
asset's PM still reaches its owner's day — and re-read at init, because the page's own note says these
accessors are empty when its script first runs, and a `HIVE_ID` that is empty at query time would have
shipped a fix that does nothing.

**The lens needed five corrections before it could be believed, and every one had turned a working page red:**

| it reported | what was actually there |
|---|---|
| all 8 pages mix hives | `utils.js` — 362 KB of platform-wide reads — was folded into every page. **8 of 8 is an impossibly bad number, and that is the probe, exactly as an impossibly clean one is** |
| alert-hub leaks `anomaly_signals` | that call is an `.update()` naming one row. **A write is not a read** |
| hive.html leaks `v_worker_truth` | those calls are `recoverHiveMembership` and `reconcileHiveList` — **the hive switcher must span hives; that is its job** |
| asset-hub leaks marketplace listings | **a marketplace that showed only your own hive would not be a marketplace** |
| asset-hub and pm-scheduler read unscoped | both scope through forms the reading could not see: a helper the page defines itself (`scopeNodes = q => q.or(...)`), and a filter applied to a variable a thousand characters later, **inside a PostgREST filter string** rather than as a method call |

All five are now mutations in its self-test, so a lens this easy to be wrong with carries its own history.
Gate `hive-separation`; 8 of 8 hold.

### Three navigation gaps the repair could not route around, and did not hide

Repairing a path means finding the route the platform really offers. Where the shortest route it found was
strange, the strangeness was the product's, and each one is verified from the link graph rather than inferred
from a journey reading oddly.

**1. No page inside the app links to a calculator.** 69 pages link to at least one of the 60 engineering
calculators, and **every one of them is a learn article**. Zero root application pages do. So a technician
standing in the logbook, the asset hub or the PM scheduler has no route to the OEE calculator at all — the
tools are reachable only from the public content that markets them. It is why J11's repaired path leaves the
app, goes back to the landing page, and enters through an article: that is the only walk there is.

**2. `platform-actions.html` has one live inbound link, and it is the marketplace.** Three pages link to it;
two of them — `founder-console.html` and `marketplace-admin.html` — are retired behind the overlay. The
Operator-Console → Grafana arc moved marketplace moderation *into* platform-actions and retired both of the
pages that pointed at it, so the surface that inherited the work kept one incidental parent. That is why the
founder's month-end now routes through the marketplace to reach the platform's own actions page.

**3. `public-feed.html` is linked from the landing page and nowhere else** — seven journey hops reach it only
by going home first.

None of the three is a broken link, and none would fail a walk. They are shapes in the graph that only became
visible when something tried to walk from one page to another and had to ask how.

### What the corrected function lenses settled: 71 re-earned, 103 retracted

Re-asked with the request repaired at each function's own asking, and decided on a differential:

| | rows |
|---|---|
| **re-earned honestly** — a real 401/403 in the caller's own words, a legible degradation, a documented job done | **71** |
| **retracted** — the row stood on a reading the corrected lens refutes, and today's ask does not replace it | **103** |
| held open — the probe itself ran out of patience or was rate-limited; that is a fact about the prober | 12 |

The retraction is written into each row's own basis, naming what the old reading claimed and why it could
not support it, and the rows go back to `specced`: **unproven, not disproven.** The three genuine findings
that survived are small and specific — one function whose source has no catch that returns a response, and
two whose 200 carries none of the keys their own source builds.

**Two ledger bugs surfaced in the same pass, and both were mine, not the platform's:**

1. **An instrument with no marker can never be shown to have been used.** The wave declared it needed
   *"invoke + PostgREST as the caller"*, and `live_walk_manifest.py` had no marker for that tag — so all 186
   rows sat in the re-walk queue no matter how honestly they were walked, and 71 freshly re-earned readings
   closed nothing. **A new wave that adds a required instrument must add the marker that recognises it in the
   same change**, or the ledger is asking for evidence it has no way to accept. Kin of the rule that a
   guard's bind must grow when the target does.
2. **A withdrawal must state its own number.** The registry gate holds every row's `pct` field to the last
   `pct -> N` its basis states. A retraction that only narrates leaves the basis still saying 60 while the
   field reads 5, and the whole batch is refused for dishonesty — by a rule that exists to catch exactly
   that. A percentage without a basis is a vibe; a basis whose number contradicts the field is worse.

**At the close of this arc the headline read 77.5%** (3,067 of 3,959), up from 74.9%, with 103 rows
deliberately given back on the way. The live figure is the generated one in the header above, which
has moved since; this line records what THIS arc did, not where the programme stands.

### The right to leave, exercised rather than looked for

Eight pages carry *"the platform must let a person take their record and go, and must be honest to those who
remain."* The lens holding them checked whether the words **export / download / csv / pdf** appear on the
page. That answers "can you take it" by looking for a noun, and never touches the second half at all.

Asked properly (`prove_leaving_honesty.mjs`, gate `leaving-honesty`), the claim is a **right and a duty**:

- **The right, exercised** — the PDPA Article 16 export runs for real, as Hector Salvador, a supervisor who
  is not a platform admin: **200**, carrying the hive's own tables.
- **The bound on it** — Jericho Bonifacio, a plain worker of the same hive, asks and is **refused 403**. A
  right anyone can exercise on anyone's behalf is not a right, it is a leak.
- **The duty** — every surface still names its author durably, so a departure shows up as a departure and
  not as work that suddenly belongs to nobody.

**8 of 8 hold.** Getting there took five corrections to the prover, and each is a shape this session has now
seen repeatedly:

| it reported | what was true |
|---|---|
| all 8 broken: "the supervisor could not take the record" | the edge runtime had been OOM-killed and every function answered `503 name resolution failed`. **A dead container is not a platform that cannot export**, and 8 of 8 is the shape of a probe |
| "the audit trail records no author" | it records `actor`. The list of author columns knew only `worker_name` — a finding about the prover's vocabulary, stated as a finding about the schema |
| "Oscar Ramos is a platform admin" | the admin count came back **empty from a query that never ran**, and `''` is not `'0'`. A failed ask read as a fact, in the probe's own setup |
| achievements has no hive column, so it fails | it reads four tables and none is hive-scoped — it is a **person-scoped page**, and demanding a hive of it would report a correct design as broken |
| the worker who must be refused is Pablo Aguilar | he is a platform admin. Had the export let him through, that would be the product working, and the refusal half would have proved nothing while looking like it had |

The page-to-table map itself was written from the page NAMES first and got three of eight wrong. Checking a
page's honesty against a table it never opens is a green about nothing, so the self-test now refuses a map
entry whose page does not read anything resembling it.

### "The day the data passes the cap" is a date — and every page that had passed it was my arithmetic

Twenty pages carry *"the platform must bound what this page can consume, and say so."* The file-only reading
could see the cap and the silence; it could not see whether any hive had already grown past it. Asking the
database turns a forecast into a measurement — and the first measurement was wrong in four different
directions, each of which I had to find before any finding could be trusted.

**It first reported five pages whose cap a real hive had already outgrown. After the corrections, none had.**

| the claim | what was true |
|---|---|
| `plant-connections` caps at 50 and a hive holds **164** | it filters to the **last 7 days**, where the largest hive holds **zero**. A cap on a windowed read cannot be judged by a whole-table count — and the page had said so in its own comment, `cap-ok` |
| `report-sender` "renders a count from what it fetched, so that number is wrong TODAY" | every count on that page is about the current operation — *"3 reports saved"*, *"2 recipients"*. The capped read feeds a separate history list. **The claim was louder than the evidence** |
| `count: 'exact'` proves a page shows a capped number | it proves the opposite. That option asks PostgREST for the **true total** independently of the row limit; counting it would have flagged the pages doing the right thing for doing it |
| `analytics-report` and `status` silently cap their lists | neither contains a single `.limit()`. The cap belonged to the shared `utils.js` — **the third prover in one session to attribute a shared script's code to each of its host pages** |

**Two pages did owe the reader a word, and both now say it.** `report-sender` listed the five newest reports
under the heading "Recent Reports" while a hive held **54**; its label is now composed from the exact count —
*"showing the 5 most recent of 54"* — with a static fallback in the markup so the note exists before the
script runs. `ph-intelligence` compared a plant against the network on the first **five** of its equipment
categories while a hive carried **ten**, so half a plant was silently absent from its own comparison; that
cap was arbitrary rather than protective, and is now an insurance bound that covers them all.

**Read the codebase's vocabulary before imposing your own.** This platform annotates a generous ceiling as an
*insurance cap*, *cap-ok* or *bounded-by-nature*. A 500-row cap on a table whose biggest hive holds 15 hides
nothing, and "showing the first 500" beside fifteen rows is noise. The annotation alone is not enough — a
comment cannot make a cap harmless — so it counts only while the measurement agrees, and the gate fires
again the day any hive reaches 60% of the ceiling.

**20 of 20 now hold**, seven of them as honestly unanswerable: a bound that resolves to no table cannot be
judged, and calling that a defect would assert the half that was never measured.
### Two silent overwrites, found by reading what each update WRITES

Eight pages carry *"the platform must not let two tabs or two people overwrite each other silently."* Five
were already covered by the concurrency census — their edit re-sends the row's last-seen `updated_at`, so a
second writer with a stale stamp matches no row and is told. **Counting** the other three pages' updates
would have grouped them together; **reading what each update writes** pulled them apart:

- **`dayplanner.html` — nothing to guard.** Its single update sets `logbook.status = 'Closed'` by id and
  already returns `.select('id')` so a zero-row refusal is detected rather than assumed successful. Two tabs
  closing the same entry reach the same place.
- **`hive.html` — three idempotent transitions and one free-text edit.** Promote, kick and a one-shot
  backfill are safe. The hive **rename** was filtered only on the hive id, so two supervisors on two devices
  ended with the second save discarding the first, and neither screen said anything.
- **`marketplace-seller.html` — the costliest and least visible.** The listing edit rewrites **nine fields at
  once, including the PRICE**, filtered only on id and seller name. A seller editing in two tabs, or on a
  phone and a laptop, lost whichever save landed first.

**Both are fixed, and the fix is proved by racing it.** `marketplace_listings` had `updated_at` but no
trigger — its stamp moved only because the page remembered to send it — and `hives` had no such column at
all. Both now carry the canonical `touch_updated_at()` trigger, so the stamp is server-authoritative; the
hive read gained the column through `v_hives_truth` **with `security_invoker` re-asserted in the same
migration**, because a replace strips it and that is how a previous change here opened anonymous access.
Verified after: anonymous reads **0 rows**, a two-hive member reads her **2**.

Raced live in a rolled-back transaction, twice:

| | writer A | writer B (same, now-stale stamp) | survived |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hives` rename | 1 row | **0 rows** | A's name |
| `marketplace_listings` price | 1 row | **0 rows** | A's price |

Two details worth keeping. The listing guard was **added to the existing chain rather than delegated to the
shared `ocUpdate` helper**, which filters on id and stamp only — using it would have dropped the
`.eq('seller_name', …)` check, and a concurrency fix that quietly widened who may edit a listing is a poor
trade. And **zero rows has more than one cause**: it means somebody saved first, *or* the row stopped being
yours to edit, *or* the read was refused. Both pages now ask the row which it was before naming one, because
telling a seller "someone else edited this" when they have actually lost access is a confident sentence
about the wrong thing.

The gate's table map grew from 9 to 11 in the same change, so the lock covers the claim rather than sitting
beside it: `the-concurrency-guard-can-fire` PASS across 11 tables, `oc-guard-speaks` PASS across 12 guards,
every one of which tells the person.

### Three hives could not live most of the stories, and the seeder that was meant to fix that had never run properly

The tier-A journey drive banked its first archetypes and failed in a pattern: J1 in Tan Delivery Vans, J2 in
all three FLEET hives, *"the chain is empty in this hive"*. Read against the data, the walk was right and the
product was not at fault:

| hive | logbook | assets | alerts | members |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Manila Electronics Assembly | 1,700 | 30 | 61 | 8 |
| Lucena Pharmaceutical Mfg. | 1,170 | 36 | 40 | 6 |
| Baguio Textile Mills | 944 | 30 | 27 | 3 |
| Dela Cruz Delivery Fleet | 16 | 3 | 0 | 3 |
| Ramos Jeepney Line | 8 | 2 | 0 | 1 |
| **Tan Delivery Vans** | 8 | **0** | 0 | 1 |

A seeder for exactly this already existed — `tools/seed_fleet_history.py`, written when an earlier wave hit
the same wall. **It had already been applied, and two of the three things it promised had never happened:**

- **It never wrote a PM record.** Its only `pm_assets` statement was a DELETE on revert, filtered on a
  `notes` column that table does not have. The delete could only ever fail, and it failed **silently** —
  every revert printed *"None PM record(s)"*, which reads like a count.
- **Its "never invent assets" rule broke from the other end.** The rule is right; the
  `["Unit 1", "Unit 2"]` fallback beside it meant that for a fleet owning nothing, eight jobs were written
  about two vans the product does not have. **A delivery-van hive with no vans is not a fleet.**

And psql's own command tag was being read as data: `insert … returning name` comes back as the rows **plus**
the literal `INSERT 0 2`, so a van called "INSERT 0 2" was registered and every count this seeder had ever
printed was one too generous — *"wrote 9 logbook row(s)"* from a list of eight.

Fixed and re-seeded: Tan owns two vans cloned from the shape the other fleets carry, all three fleets hold a
coherent history with PM schedules, and `--revert` now removes vehicles and PM rows too — reporting `0`
where it used to report `None`.

### The journey walk itself needed four corrections before any of its failures could be believed

With the paths repaired, the tier-A drive still failed — and every early failure turned out to be the
instrument, the seed, or my own contention. In order:

| it reported | what was true |
|---|---|
| J19, all six hives: *"1 hop goes straight to a destination the platform parents elsewhere"* | `hive.html` reaches the audit log through a real `<a href="audit-log.html">` inside its own menu, carrying `class="hidden"`. The prover already knew the shared nav hub is a **closed drawer** and counted its links whether open or not — and stopped there. A page's own menu is a closed drawer too. **0/6 → 6/6** |
| J17 and J18, all three plants: *"the chain is empty in this hive"* | both chains asked the wrong table. J17 counted `anomaly_alerts`, which holds zero rows everywhere — the alert surface reads `v_alert_truth`, computed on demand. J18 joined `asset_risk_scores.asset_name` to `asset_nodes.name`, the human name, when the column holds the **tag**: **0 of 3,315 matched on `name`, 3,315 of 3,315 on `tag`.** Both now **3/3** |
| J1 and J2 in the fleet hives | a genuinely incoherent seed, fixed and re-seeded (above) |
| J11 and J12: *"the chain could not be READ (the database did not answer)"* | **my own contention.** I was running psql-heavy provers against the same 8 GB host while the browser walked it. That is a statement about this machine, not the platform, and both archetypes are queued for a clean re-walk |

**And one correction to the correction.** Teaching the prover that arriving *from* a parent page is not
skipping it must not swallow the harder finding: if we are standing on the parent and it still shows no way
onward, that is a navigation gap, not a mis-written path. It is re-filed under what it actually is rather
than dropped.

**One chain will stay empty, deliberately.** J13 asks whether what the AI wrote is attributable, against
`ai_audit_log` — zero rows platform-wide. The first reading of that looked like a missing writer; it is not.
`voice-handler.js` inserts a row on every confirmed voice-driven write, by design. No voice action has ever
been taken in a seeded hive, so the trail is empty. **Every other empty chain here is a seeding job — this
one is the exception.** An audit log's whole worth is that it records what actually happened, and writing
plausible AI decisions nobody made would put a lie in the most sensitive table on the platform to make a
walk go green. It stays empty until a real voice turn writes to it, and the chain now says so in its own
words.

### Audit: which lifecycle lenses can answer their own claim

Two lenses were replaced today after each turned out to be graded by *"did this page render 400
characters"*. That is a class, not two accidents, so every lens in `prove_lifecycle_cells.mjs` was read
against the claim its rows carry. Sorted by what the lens can actually establish:

**Cannot answer it — replaced or named as unanswered**

| claim | how it was graded | what it needs |
|---|---|---|
| keep a person's two hives apart | `chars > 400` | a person really in two hives, read through PostgREST — **built today**, gate `hive-separation` |
| let them take their record and go | does the word *export* appear | exercise the PDPA right and check the bound on it — **built today**, gate `leaving-honesty` |
| two tabs must not overwrite silently | does the page print the word *saved* | race two writers on one stale stamp — **the concurrency gates already do this**; the lens now defers to them |
| identity honest when a session ends | `chars > 400` | a prover that actually ends a session. **No rows carry this lens**, so it is annotated rather than built |

**Answers something narrower than it claimed — label corrected, evidence kept**

`responsive as its data grows` was banked on 12 rows for *"renders its list without hanging"*. The reading
is real, against the largest seeded hive, but it is about **today's volume**, not growth. The sentence now
says exactly that, and names what growth would need: the same page against a hive an order of magnitude
larger. **A label is a claim; narrowing it is cheaper and more honest than retracting a real reading.**

**Answers its claim honestly, by deferring to the gate that owns it** — the release leg to the
service-worker gate, the header contract to `deploy-headers-local`, the refusal itself to PostgREST. Those
were already written as deferrals, and they are the pattern the four above have now been moved onto.

The general rule this leaves: **a lens that would pass for any page that renders is not a lens.** When the
claim is about a relationship (two hives, two writers, two sessions, two volumes), only an instrument that
can produce BOTH sides can answer it, and a single page-load can produce one at most.

### Caught before it banked: 254 Filipino rows that never checked for Filipino

Tier B is 381 rows and exists to say one thing — that a journey holds up **on another device and in another
language**. Reading the prover before queueing that tier: it sets the viewport per device, sets
`localStorage.wh_lang = 'fil'`, sets the browser locale — **and never looks again.** No verdict, anywhere,
mentions the language.

So a page that ignored the setting entirely would have walked, passed and banked exactly like its English
twin. **254 of the 381 tier-B rows are Filipino cells**, and every one of them would have been evidence
about a `localStorage` write rather than about a person reading their own language.

The check reads **the platform's own dictionary** — `WH_FIL_COMMON` in `utils.js`, 195 usable strings — so
it tests the translation the product actually ships rather than a word list of mine, and it asks two things
a set-and-forget cannot:

- **Did any page answer in Filipino?** If every arrived step shows zero dictionary strings, the walk asked
  for Filipino and got English throughout, and it says so with the counts.
- **Did the language survive the walk?** `wh_lang` is read at every step, so a journey that drops a Filipino
  reader back into English mid-story is a finding rather than a pass — the same rail the identity check
  already rides.

It is judged only on steps that ARRIVED, and only where the dictionary itself could be read: an empty
dictionary would otherwise convict every page of ignoring a translation that was never there to apply.

**This one cost nothing, because it was found by reading the instrument before trusting it rather than after
banking 254 rows on it.** That is the day's lesson arriving early for once.

### The same fault one tier further: 40 rows named a condition the walk never applied

Having found that tier B set a language and never checked it, tier C got the same reading before it was
queued. The registry asks for four conditions across the journey wave:

| condition | rows | what the walk actually did |
|---|---|---|
| `normal` | 664 | — |
| `offline-3g` | 20 | delayed every request by 120 ms. Its own comment said *"slow, and it drops"*; it never dropped anything |
| **`dependency-down`** | **20** | **nothing at all** |
| **`release-mid-way`** | **20** | **nothing at all** |

Forty rows would have walked in perfect conditions and banked as evidence about a failure that never
happened — a normal journey filed under "the dependency was down". All three are now real:

- **offline-3g** drops roughly one request in twelve as well as delaying, which is what makes a page's retry
  and its empty-versus-failed distinction worth anything.
- **dependency-down** fails every `functions/v1` call with a 503 carrying a readable sentence, while the
  page, its assets and its direct database reads keep working. That is the shape a provider outage actually
  has here, and it is precisely what "degrades legibly" is supposed to be true about.
- **release-mid-way** drops the service-worker registration and its caches, so the person crosses a version
  boundary mid-journey instead of walking around it.

And a degraded condition is now allowed a wider settle budget, because a page falling back from a 503 or
re-fetching after its worker vanished is doing work a normal walk never does — a cap that ignored that would
report **the condition** as the page hanging.

**Two tiers, two set-and-never-check faults, both caught by reading the instrument before trusting it.**
Together they were 294 rows of evidence about settings rather than about people.

### A hop can be linked and still unreachable: the role the cast is wearing

J26 — the multi-hive worker's day — failed live in both hives with *"1 hop has no way onward at all"*, and
the hop was `pm-scheduler → alert-hub`. Nothing was broken: the nav hub **does** offer the alert hub, but
tagged `roles: ['supervisor']`, and J26 is walked by a worker. **A destination the cast's own hub mode is
not offered is a destination that cast cannot reach**, and `check_journey_paths` had only ever asked whether
a link or a hub entry exists — never who was looking.

**Finding it took three vocabulary corrections, and each one cut the number roughly in half:**

| reading | why it was wrong | count |
|---|---|---|
| compare the registry's `persona: 'worker'` against the hub's `roles` | — | **28** |
| the hub's word for a worker is **`field`**, not `worker` | comparing the two vocabularies made the **LOGBOOK** look forbidden to the people who live in it | **14** |
| a row whose persona reads "worker" is walked by the **SUPERVISOR** when its `pair` names one | the prover casts on exactly that rule; the registry's `persona` is not who walks | **6** |

That is the day's lesson in miniature, three times inside one investigation: **the instrument was wrong more
often than the product, and each time it was wrong it was confident.** The gate now uses the prover's own
casting rule rather than a field that looks like it means the same thing.

**The six that survive split cleanly in two**, and the gate says which is which:

- **Three have a real route** — `alert-hub → asset-hub` and `pm-scheduler → alert-hub` both pass through
  `hive.html`, which this cast can reach and which links them.
- **Three do not.** For a field worker the only page linking `analytics.html` is the landing page, and
  *"route a signed-in worker through the marketing home page"* is not a route. Those three archetypes send
  a worker to a surface the product reserves for supervisors and engineers, so the **cast or the path** is
  what needs changing — not the platform.

### The six role-gated hops, repaired — and what "re-cast or re-route" meant in practice

The six split as the gate said, and both halves are now closed:

**Three had a real route.** `alert-hub → asset-hub` (J16, J17) and `pm-scheduler → alert-hub` (J26) all pass
through `hive.html`, which a field worker is offered and which links both. Inserted, 32 rows rewritten.

**Three did not, and the honest repair was to stop the journey where the product stops the person.** For a
field worker the only page linking `analytics.html` is the landing page, and routing somebody already signed
in through the marketing home page is not a route. Those three journeys were making a claim about a surface
their own person is never shown:

| archetype | was | is |
|---|---|---|
| J13 the AI-assisted day | … audit-log → **analytics** | ends at audit-log (5 pages) |
| J16 the same journey, degraded | … pm-scheduler → **analytics** | ends at pm-scheduler (6 pages) |
| J28 GCash top-up to receipt | marketplace-seller → **analytics** → hive | marketplace-seller → hive (4 pages) |

Each still spans the four pages a journey row promises, and each now ends somewhere its cast can actually
stand. 66 rows rewritten.

**All three classes are ratcheted.** `journey-paths` now fails on a hop with no route, on a path that names a
retired page, and on a hop the cast's own hub mode cannot reach — so the next wave cannot seed a story that
sends somebody where the product does not show them. Three of J17's rows were already banked on the old
path and are queued to re-earn on the repaired one, because evidence for a route that no longer exists is
not evidence.

### A cell is a person, and the walk had only one

The role-gated finding raised the same question one wave over: `prove_lifecycle_cells` answers 198 rows of
**persona × device × entry** cells. It honours the device per row (four viewports) and the entry per row
(`?ref=chat`, `?src=email`, `?src=qr`). It signs in **once**, as one established worker, and walks every
cell with that session.

So the axis the wave is named for was the one axis not varied:

| persona | rows | what the walk actually showed |
|---|---|---|
| `anon` | 7 (5 banked) | a signed-in worker's view of their own hive — **an anonymous visitor cannot be observed while signed in** |
| `new-user` | 12 (banked) | an established worker with a full hive. A first-timer has **no hive**, so the page they meet is the onboarding path, not this one |
| `adversary` | 8 (banked) | an ordinary worker looking normally. **An adversary is a posture, not a harder look** |
| `worker`, `returner`, `any`, `fleet-supervisor` | 171 | the session genuinely represents these |

**Two of the three are now cast properly, and the third says so.**

- **`anon`** gets a clean context with no session — the only way its own question can be asked.
- **`new-user`** gets a real first-timer. Naming those twelve rows "not answered" was honest but it was not
  the job: **if a cell needs a cast the walk does not have, build the cast.** The platform already holds one
  — `consumer.walk@workhive.test`, **zero memberships and zero logbook entries** — and the walk now signs in
  as that account and deliberately stamps **no hive, no worker, no role**. That absence *is* the first-timer,
  and it means a new-user cell meets the onboarding path the product actually shows a newcomer rather than a
  populated board.
- **`adversary`** stays unanswered, and says why: an adversary is a posture, not a harder look, and it needs
  a probe that actually tries something.

**That costs 8 banked rows their green rather than 20, and it is the honest price.** It is the same shape as the two
lenses retired earlier today and as the 103 function rows given back: evidence gathered by the wrong
instrument is not evidence, and a wave named for a persona has to vary the persona.

### Audit, all nine waves: does each instrument vary the axis its wave is named for?

Three separate findings today had one shape — a wave named for an axis whose instrument never varied it. So
every wave was asked the same question. The answer is not uniform, and that is the useful part:

| wave | the axis it is named for | does the instrument vary it? |
|---|---|---|
| **W3-JN** journeys | vertical, device, language, condition, cast | **partly** — device yes, vertical yes; **language was set and never checked** (254 rows), **two of four conditions were never applied** (40 rows), and the cast's ROLE was never considered (6 hops). All three now fixed |
| **W3-FN** function contracts | refusal, degradation, documented job | **no** — all three graded the first reply, so 128 of 186 rows rested on a complaint about the request. Corrected; 71 re-earned, 103 withdrawn |
| **W3-LC / PG / AR** lifecycle cells | persona × device × entry | **partly** — device and entry per row, **persona never**. `anon` fixed; `new-user` and `adversary` now say they are not answered |
| **W3-SC** shared components | three hosts: phone, desktop, wall | **YES** — 390, 1280 and 1920 are genuinely walked, and the lens reports "its element appeared on 0 of 3 hosts". Clean |
| **W3-LN / CL** learn + calculators | 390, offline, print | **honestly partial** — 390 and a real offline pass (every subresource refused) are exercised; print is not, **and the verdict does not claim it**. A coverage gap, not a false claim |

**The distinction in that last row is the one worth keeping.** A narrow instrument that says exactly what it
measured is sound work; a narrow instrument whose label implies more is the fault this whole wave has been
correcting. `prove_content_ufai` reports *"at 390: no sideways scroll, 0 targets under 40px; still readable
with every subresource refused"* — every clause earned, nothing implied. That is the standard the others
have been brought up to.

**And two waves came back clean**, which matters: this audit was not a search for something to find.

### The landing page cannot be four different lengths

J30 — the RA 11285 energy audit — failed with *"4/8 step(s) did not arrive as themselves"*. The four steps
were its learn articles and its calculator, and the per-step record said each of them had landed on
`index.html`. It also said what each had rendered:

| step | reported landing | characters read |
|---|---|---|
| `learn/ra-11285-…/index.html` | index.html | **15,826** |
| `learn/index.html` | index.html | 3,237 |
| `learn/free-engineering-calculators-…/index.html` | index.html | **14,799** |
| `tools/load-estimation-calculator/index.html` | index.html | 1,965 |

**The landing page cannot be four different lengths.** Every one of those pages had loaded perfectly; the
arrival check was comparing `page.url().split('/').pop()` — the last segment — against a page named
`<slug>/index.html`. Every learn article and every calculator on this platform is `<slug>/index.html`, so
each of them "landed on index.html" and each was recorded as a person who never arrived.

**This is the wrong-end-of-the-path mistake for the second time in one programme.** Earlier it discarded 57
correct readings because the origin carries a `/workhive` prefix and the check compared the wrong end. Here
it discards the directory instead. Both times the fix is one line and the symptom was a confident,
specific-looking failure; both times the number beside it was the tell.

Fixed by comparing the whole path tail rather than the final segment. Four archetypes cross a subpage —
J11, J12, J30 and the Tier-D chain that contains J30 — and all are queued to re-walk.

### "Identity kept" with no identity, and the people the cast could never see

J31 — the OFW portfolio — failed with `resume.html` and `achievements.html` bouncing to the landing page,
and the summary beside it read **`identity kept`**. Both pages are right to bounce: each calls
`whSignInWall()` when there is no worker. The summary was wrong, and wrong in a specific way:

```
const lostAt = story.identity ? steps.filter(…) : [];
const idKept = lostAt.length === 0;
```

**With no identity there is nothing to lose, so a journey walked as nobody reports that its identity
survived.** That is a reassurance produced by an absence — the same shape as an empty string standing for a
zero, and as a busy database read as an empty hive.

**Why it had no identity is the better finding.** `loadCast()` builds the cast by joining **through**
`hive_members`, and J11 and J31 are cast as *a solo technician* and *a solo rider* — operators with **no
hive at all**. The function's own comment says the vertical "names a hive, **or names a person who has
none**"; only the first half was ever written.

The platform has these people. Three auth users hold no active membership, and two of them are exactly the
personas the seed names:

| user | matches |
|---|---|
| `rider.marlonph@auth.workhiveph.com` | *a solo rider with no hive* |
| `rangerowner26@auth.workhiveph.com` | *a solo technician with no hive* |
| `consumer.walk@workhive.test` | nothing — correctly left unused |

Both are cast now, and a story that still finds no one says **`identity NONE CAST`** and records that
nothing it saw is evidence about the story — rather than quietly claiming the identity held.

### A link can exist, be visible, and still be unreachable by the person walking

Seven archetypes routed a signed-in member to `public-feed.html`, and every one of them failed with *"no way
onward at all"* — including four whose path went through `index.html`, which **does** carry two plain
anchors to it. Reading the landing page settles it in one line:

```css
html.wh-signed-in #mkt-wrap { display: none !important; }
```

Both of those anchors live inside `#mkt-wrap`. The whole marketing wrapper is hidden the moment somebody
signs in, and the measurement says the same thing from the other side: **the landing page renders 14,464
characters to a signed-out visitor and 1,197 to a signed-in one.**

**And the product is right.** `nav-hub.js` states the intent in its own words, beside the entry it
deliberately does not create:

> `public-feed.html: public read-only page — linked from index.html, not the app nav`

So the platform means exactly what it does, and **seven journey archetypes were wrong to send a member
there**. Their paths now stop before it, and a dropped destination no longer leaves a page followed by
itself — J31 came out as `resume → index → index → achievements`, and nobody navigates from a page to
itself. 104 rows rewritten across the two passes.

**This is the third distinct way a hop can be unwalkable, and the gate now fails on all three:** no link at
all; a link the cast's own hub mode is not offered; and a link only a signed-out visitor is ever shown. The
first is a broken path, the second and third are a mis-cast — and none of them is a defect in the platform.

### The fix meant to stop a regression very nearly caused one

Building the first-timer cast meant adding a branch that refuses to grade a cell whose persona the walk
cannot represent. It fired on `persona === 'adversary'` — and **eight of the adversary rows are the "take
their record and go" cells**, which had been answered properly a few hours earlier by
`prove_leaving_honesty` (8/8, gate `leaving-honesty`), and whose lens in this same file already **defers to
that gate by name**.

The new branch runs *before* the lens. It would have returned "NOT ANSWERED" over eight rows of real
evidence — **replacing a proven claim with an absence, in the change written specifically to stop that from
happening.**

Caught before it ran, by asking which rows the branch would actually touch. It now skips any row whose lens
already defers to a prover that owns it — **8 rows protected, and no green lost anywhere.**

Asking that question a second time was worth more than the first answer. **The other 33 `adversary` rows are
journey rows (W3-JN), and this prover never touches that wave at all** — so the branch guards zero rows
today and is a guard for a wave that has not been seeded yet. Those 33 are walked by `prove_full_journeys`,
which casts them as the worker, and for *"a person is removed and what remains is honest to those who
stay"*, the departing worker is the right person to be. **There was no gap there to build.**

Two lessons, and the second is the one I nearly skipped: check what a new branch actually touches *before*
believing it protects something, and check it *again* before believing it is needed.

The general form is worth stating, because this session has now hit it from both directions: **a check that
refuses to answer must know which questions somebody else has already answered.** An honest "I cannot say"
is only honest when nobody else has said it.

### The last axis: a moment no hive on this platform has lived

`moment` is the fourth thing the journey grid varies, after vertical, device and language: `month-3` (22
rows), `year-2` (22), and a tier-D `day-1+month-3+year-2` (16). **The word appeared nowhere in the prover
except two unrelated comments.**

It is not like the others. A device is a viewport and a language is a setting — both can be *applied*. A
moment is a fact about how much history the hive HOLDS, so it can only be **verified**. Measured:

| hive | history it holds |
|---|---|
| Lucena Pharmaceutical Mfg. | 544 days |
| Baguio Textile Mills | 130 days |
| Manila Electronics Assembly | 90 days |
| the three fleets | 48 days |

**`year-2` needs about 730 days, and the deepest hive on the platform reaches 544. It is not true of any
hive here.** `month-3` holds in three of six. So 22 rows name a moment nothing in this database has lived,
and 22 more name one that half the cast cannot honour.

The walk now measures the hive's own span and refuses to let a row claim a moment its hive never reached:
*"this row is set at year-2, which needs about 730 days of history; this hive holds 544. The moment it names
is not one this hive has lived, so the walk is about today's data wearing another date."*

**That closes the axis audit.** Of the five things the grid varies — vertical, device, language, condition,
moment — the walk applied two, ignored two, and could never apply the fifth. All five now either hold or say
why they do not.

**A closing note on the prover's own teeth.** Running that self-test while the re-walk chain held the
database made it **crash**: `psql` returns null when it cannot reach the database at all, and the test called
`.slice()` on nothing. The distinction between "a bad answer" and "no answer" is the one this entire prover
is built on, and it was missing from its own self-test. Fixed: a chain that cannot be read now says so.

### The three fleets have no alert lane, and a `least()` could not say so

J2 — breakdown, diagnose, repair, close out — walked clean in the three plant hives and failed in all three
fleet hives with one line: **"the chain is empty in this hive."** That sentence is the finding with the
finding taken out. J2's chain is `least(v_alert_truth, asset_nodes, logbook)`, and a `least()` of three
counts reports a zero without ever naming which of the three produced it.

**The prover now takes a zero apart.** On a zero — and only on a zero, in the same quiet burst that reads
the chains before the browser exists — each link is counted on its own, through the same person, and the
receipt names the one that is missing: *"the missing link is v_alert_truth, while this hive does hold
asset_nodes 6 and logbook 24."* All 18 `least()` chains in the file decompose into balanced, named links.

**What the missing link turned out to be.** It is deducible from the run's own log without asking the
database again: J1's chain is `least(hive_members, asset_nodes, logbook)` and it read 1-3 for every fleet, so
both of J2's other links hold. The zero can only be the alerts.

And the alerts are not seeded — they are **generated**. `v_alert_truth` reads `failure_signature_alerts` and
`anomaly_signals`, neither of which any seeder writes; signature alerts are produced by the
`failure-signature-scan` edge function reading `v_logbook_truth`. The fleets were given a logbook this week
and **the scan has never been run over it**. So this is not a hive that cannot have alerts — it is a lane
whose generator was never pointed at three of the six hives.

That also corrects an assumption I nearly seeded on: `anomaly_alerts` is a real table with a real migration,
and `v_alert_truth` does not read it. Writing rows there would have left the chain at zero and the walk
still failing, with a hive full of alerts nobody's view could see.

### A gate that could not see the page its own class was found on

Chasing the `least()` fault across the toolbox turned up the same shape in a gate. The KPI count-safety
validator catches the class where a page loads `.limit(N)` rows and renders `arr.length` as a count. Its
regex matched **`v_*_truth` views only**, on a reason written into its own docstring: *"raw-table fetches
with limit are usually paginated lists where local .length IS the right count for the page."*

**voice-journal.html disproved that in July, and the gate stayed green through it.** `voice_journal_entries`
is a raw table; `.limit(80)` fed the header; the page printed "80 entries" while the account held 108, and
the search box above filtered only the loaded rows, so a person searching for something said four months ago
was told they had never said it. The narrowing was also **redundant** — the second condition already requires
the length to be rendered as a count — so it bought nothing and cost every raw table on the platform.

Widened to any table, it found two, and the pair is instructive:

| page | what the gate said | what was true |
|---|---|---|
| logbook | `hive_members` limit(500) → `actionable.length` | a false positive: that length is over the offline queue in IndexedDB, not the capped read. The window is character-based, so it paired two unrelated things |
| community | `hive_audit_log` limit(200) → `flagged.length` | **a real defect, at a query the gate did not name** |

**The Mod Queue counted what the page had loaded, not what the queue held.** The community feed is
`.limit(20)` with a load-more cursor, and the supervisor's Mod Queue badge read `flagged.length` over the
posts loaded so far. A supervisor opening Community sees **2** and believes two posts need judging while
thirty sit further down. Under-reporting a moderation queue does not merely mislead: it tells someone the
work is done. Fixed with one head-only count, and the list now says "showing 3 of 30" instead of implying it
is all; where nothing flagged is loaded yet it says so rather than "No flagged posts."

That read carried a marker from a sweep three days ago reading **"cap-ok: rows only — no count or sum is
derived from this read."** A count *was* derived from it. **A cap is only safe while nothing counts it, and
that is a property of every reader, not of the read** — so it cannot be settled by looking at the query.

### The fleet seeder's third and fourth unhonoured claim

Two more journeys measured the fleets empty: J3 (`least(pm_assets, pm_completions)`) and J4
(`least(logbook, hive_audit_log)`), both 0 in Ramos Jeepney Line and Tan Delivery Vans while their schedules
and logbook were full. Same file, same shape as the two claims it was already caught on: it promises to turn
a vehicle registry into an operating fleet, and **a hive whose PMs are never closed and whose actions leave
no trail is a registry again one level up** — it holds the plan and the work, and nothing saying either
happened.

It now writes both. Completions are generated **from `pm_assets` itself** rather than from a list of names,
so every completion closes a schedule that exists; `asset_id` resolves through `asset_nodes` and stays NULL
when nothing matches rather than pointing at a guess; `status` is left NULL because that column's allowed
words have not been read from its CHECK, and a word I bring is exactly what wrote "Completed" into a logbook
that only accepts Open, Closed or Resolved. Audit rows use only verbs the product itself writes
(`register_asset`, `edit_pm_asset`, `edit_part`, collected from the pages' own audit calls), because a row in
a vocabulary the viewer does not know is a row nobody can read. Both are marked and reverted, completions
before the schedules they point at.

### What the decomposition found in its first hour

The change that makes a zero name its own missing link paid immediately, and on something bigger than the
fleets it was written for.

**J7, the knowledge loop, read 0 in all six hives — and the reason is the same sentence six times:**

    the missing link is community_replies, while this hive does hold community_posts 52
                                            ... 32 ... 15 ... 15 ...

**Over a hundred questions on this platform and not one answer.** That is not a journey failing; it is the
whole reputation surface standing on an empty table. `v_community_reputation_truth` derives trust tier and
XP from posts *and* replies, badges hang off participation, and the accepted answer is the event the loop
turns on. None of it has ever had an input. Ruled out first, because it is the cheaper explanation: the
reply read policy is a plain hive-membership check, the same shape as the post policy, and the chain is read
as the person — a member who sees 52 posts would see their replies. The absence is real.

There is no community seeder; the file that looks like one is a UI test flow that asserts against posts and
never writes a reply. So `tools/seed_community_answers.py` now writes them, and two rules shape it. Answers
are chosen by the post's own **category**, because a canned reply pasted under an unrelated question is
incoherent data that teaches a walk to expect something the product would never hold. And every answer comes
from a **different member of the same hive** than the asker, with their real auth id, because a person
answering their own question is not the knowledge loop. Two per hive are accepted answers. There is no
marker column on that table, so the marker is the content itself and `--revert` deletes exactly the
sentences this file writes — narrower than a token, not looser.

**J11 walked both solo stories as nobody.** *"The cast could not sign in: Invalid login credentials"*, then
eight pages of sign-in door. The cast loader picks the solo vertical's people with a keyword sweep over
every hive-less account — leftovers, removed members, whoever matches "rider" or "van" — and none of them
has the password every walk here uses. **A name to cast is not a person to cast.** Two dedicated personas
are now created through the same admin API the product uses, marked so the loader prefers a castable persona
over a leftover; the seeder proves the password works before it reports success. It creates rather than
resets, because overwriting a stranger's password is the one repair here that cannot be undone — the old
password is not knowable, so there would be nothing to put back.

**And J12 did not fail — it crashed, which is worse.** `Cannot access 'problems' before initialization`: two
checks I added push a problem above the line that declares the list. Only the anon-to-member funnel could
reach it, because it is the first story with no hive and no member to cast. A prover that throws reports
nothing about the journeys behind it, so this cost six readings rather than one. `node --check` cannot see a
temporal dead zone, so the fix is verified positionally instead: the declaration is at line 643 and the
first of eighteen uses is at 646.

### Four compliance promises the product never kept, and a gate that certified them by spelling

J13, the AI-assisted day, read 0 in all six hives. Its chain is `select count(*) from ai_audit_log`, and
the chain's own description says the table "is written by voice-handler.js on confirmed actions, and is
never seeded" — so the walk was right to demand it and right to fail. Following that zero to its cause
found something much larger than one journey.

**`voice-handler.js` carries four compliance capabilities, and each name appears in the file exactly twice
— the definition and the export list.** Nothing calls any of them. Measured, not inferred; a search of the
whole repository for callers returns only the export line.

| capability | what the product says | what happens |
|---|---|---|
| `_executeErasure` | the assistant replies *"I can clear your voice + journal history for this hive. Confirm with yes — this cannot be undone"*, and the prompt anchor states *"the scoped DELETE runs on the next confirmed yes"* | on yes, nothing is deleted |
| `_emitAuditEvent` | its own header: *"every confirmed write action (log entry, schedule, alert flag) writes to ai_audit_log so we can replay every voice-driven decision"* | no row is ever written, in any hive |
