## ★THE NON-BROWSER TIER, CLEARED — 8,615 → 8,909 CLOSED (70.4% → 72.9%), S at 988/988, and a LOCKED row walking a page that never existed (2026-10-05)

Ian: *"focus on important trajectories… it should be closed and open only, the percentage completion are the MCPs deepwalk trajectories."* So this arc took the whole of the queue that needs **no browser** and closed it against the instrument each lens actually demands. Three sub-waves went to zero open — **LXP-S 88/88, LXP-AU 88/88, LXP-H 120/120** (LXP-RL 149/149 closed just before) — and the `postgres-mcp` and `raw-http` lines of the re-walk queue are now **empty**.

### What each block needed, and why a green sweep was never enough on its own

| block | rows | instrument | the discipline that kept it honest |
|---|---:|---|---|
| S — "must refuse, on this page, a person not entitled to what it shows" | 88 | `prove_tenant_refusal.mjs` (PostgREST as a real member + anon) | a row closes only on the relations **its own page reads**; 44 of 67 tenant tables had no foreign rows at all, and a refusal of nothing proves nothing |
| AU — "must keep this page's identity honest when a session ends or a role changes" | 88 | **new** `prove_lxp_au_identity_after_change.mjs` | one unexpired token replayed across active → kicked → deactivated → supervisor → worker |
| H — "must serve this page correctly from the edge" | 120 | existing `prove_w4_layer_headers.py` + `serve_vercel_headers.py` | the prover already took this reading for 246 W4 rows and was simply not **looking** at the LXP rows |

**Not the postgres MCP, on purpose.** It connects as `postgres`, which owns every public table and carries `rolbypassrls`, so RLS is never consulted and a cross-hive read happily returns the other hive's rows. **A superuser lens can prove what data EXISTS; it can never prove that a read was REFUSED.** Both security provers therefore speak PostgREST as the person — with a minted token, and again with only the publishable key as anon.

### The S lens grew two whole surfaces it had never asked about

- **The truth VIEWS.** Six pages carrying an S row read almost nothing else — achievements, analytics-report, public-feed, skillmatrix, marketplace-seller-profile reach their data through `v_*_truth`. The sweep walked base tables only (`relkind='r'`), so it had said nothing about them. **40 hive-scoped views** are now probed, `v_hives_truth` among them — which exposes `invite_code` with SELECT granted to anon. That grant is inert: the view is invoker, so RLS refuses (anon reads 0; a member reads exactly his own hive, with the invite code he needs in order to invite a colleague).
- **The PERSON-scoped tables.** Fifteen public tables carry no `hive_id` at all; they are scoped by `auth_uid`/`worker_name`, so every tenant sweep had skipped them **in silence** — `mfa_enrollments`, `push_subscriptions`, `resume_versions`, `skill_exam_attempts` among them. A leak there is not "hive B's data", it is one colleague reading another's second factor. This is also the shape of the logbook defect Ian reported: **the boundary that bites is often the PERSON, and a probe keyed on the tenant proves nothing about it.** Five that reported UNPROVEN (nobody else had rows to withhold) were made provable by `tools/seed_person_boundary_probe_rows.py`, which seeds one tagged stranger row per table and takes them back out on `--remove`.

### The AU half a browser cannot reach

An access token is a signed bearer string with its own expiry, so **revoking a membership does not revoke it**. The only thing standing between a dismissed worker and their old hive is that every relation re-derives entitlement from the *current* membership on every read — and a browser could only expose a failure here by holding the stale token itself. Measured on one token: `logbook` **6,944 → 0**, `v_worker_truth` 1 → 0, `pm_assets` 30 → 0; and as a supervisor, `hive_audit_log` **27,625 → 0**.

Two readings that look like leaks and are not, each now measured rather than assumed:

- **`hive_members` must keep EXACTLY the revoked person's own row** — that is how the page learns it was removed and can say so. Returning 0 would be a silent sign-out indistinguishable from an outage ([[feedback_a_dismissal_leaks_the_other_direction]]).
- **A person keeps their own record on the way out.** `pm_completions` 552 → 202 and `voice_journal_entries` 16 → 16, every retained row the subject's own, counted in SQL. A departure showing up as an **ABSENCE** is the opposite failure and just as bad. (Mechanism worth recording: `pm_completions_write` is declared `cmd ALL`, so the policy named "write" also grants the own-rows SELECT.)
- **The probe's persona must match the page's audience.** A plain worker reads `hive_audit_log` as 0 *while fully active* — audit-log.html could never be proven by that subject. `--as "Christine Dizon"` runs the identical replay as a supervisor; one report per subject, merged, each basis clause naming whose reading it was.

### Two defects in the LEDGER, found by driving the lens to the end

1. **A row LOCKED at 100% against a page that has never existed.** One AU row would not close because `terms.html` "reads no hive-scoped relation" — and `terms.html` is not on disk and was never tracked in git. Eight rows targeted it; **`VP59` was locked**, its basis asserting "terms.html renders for the hive supervisor with real fleet data, no cross-hive leak." Nothing checked that a page is a FILE. `validate_trajectory_registry` now FAILS any non-descoped row naming a path not on disk (measured scale: exactly 1 phantom page, 8 rows, 1 false lock, across all 12,593 rows). All eight are descoped with the reason, and the lock is withdrawn — placed at the END of the basis, because the gate reads the last `pct ->` as the live one.
2. **A replay whose INPUTS were filtered by the present.** `layer_ux_rows(replay=True)` rebuilds the wave so the gate can derive POSITIONAL ids, and its docstring already warned that dropping rows would renumber every later id and reattach banked evidence to the wrong trajectory. One line inside it dropped descoped rows unconditionally — so descoping those eight renamed `LXP569`'s wave and failed the gate on rows nobody had touched. History cannot be re-derived through a present-tense predicate.

### Teeth — every exemption in these provers is load-bearing

`--teeth` strips the by-design exemptions and both provers must then FAIL: tenant-refusal drops to 63/67 tables + 33/40 views, and AU reports drift on every expectation. The by-design declarations moved into one shared module `tools/tenant_declarations.mjs`, because two provers read them now and two hand-kept copies is how two gates come to agree on a stale fact. Each entry carries a **SQL subset oracle** asserted on every run — posts 8 of 50 foreign rows = exactly `public AND NOT flagged`, listings 7 of 9 = exactly `published`. A declaration that had only ever agreed with itself was a described mechanism, not a mechanism.

Three instrument bugs were fixed in the same pass, each of which had produced a confident wrong number: `security_invoker` matched as the substring `=on` when this schema stores 43 of its 59 invoker views as `=true` (so "50 of 66 views run as their owner, RLS never consulted" was false — the real count is 7); a grants join that matched once per grantee, counting 39 views as 78; and a refusal probe that picked "the most-populated other person", who was a hive-mate the policy deliberately admits.

### Gates registered / extended in the same change as the rows (the ★×16 bind rule)

`lxp-au-identity-after-change` (new, Security) · `tenant-refusal` (views + person-scoped + subset oracles) · `w4-layer-headers` (now serves LXP-H too) · `trajectory-registry` (the page-exists clause) · and `live_walk_manifest` MARKERS gained `prove_lxp_au_identity_after_change`, because **an instrument with no marker can never be shown to have been used.** All five pass through `run_platform_checks.py --only <id>`.

**NEXT:** the browser tier is all that remains — 1,851 `playwright+postgres`, 800 `playwright`, 31 `figma` (blocked on OAuth in a non-interactive session). Weakest layers by closure: **CA 575/1241 (46.3%)**, **H 686/1058**, F 2848/4528, D 1496/2208. CA's 460 open W4 rows split by axis — `phone-390 en` 202, `narrow-320 en` 129, `phone-390 fil` 129 — and `tools/prove_w4_layer_ca.mjs` already walks each of them; one browser at a time on the 8 GB host.

## ★THE CA LAYER — 62 failures were THREE defects, and the platform's Filipino went 79.9% → 100% (2026-10-05)

The CA lens asks the plainest question in the program: **"does this page use the words a Philippine maintenance crew uses?"** `prove_w4_layer_ca.mjs --axis "phone-390 en"` answered it for 126 rows and 64 lived clean. The other 62 looked like 62 problems and were three.

### 57 calculators, one sentence

Every one of the 57 generated calculator pages reported **identically** — "9 language stamps, 1-3 crew terms" — and an identical measurement is a reason to read the generator, not the pages. The 9 stamps are exactly the 9 `data-i` keys `tools/build_calc_pages.py` emits. The shared CTA read:

> Free, and a free sign-up saves your calculations, BOMs and scope-of-works to your account.

True, and it answers a question nobody asked. A maintenance engineer who found the page from a search wants to know what it does for the JOB. It now reads:

> Free, and a free sign-up saves the calculation, its bill of materials and its scope of works to **your hive under the project name your team already uses, so the next technician on that job reads the same numbers** instead of re-deriving them.

**The draft before I checked the schema was FALSE.** I was about to write "ties them to the asset, the PM schedule and the work order" — `engineering_calcs` has no `asset_id` and no `project_id` at all. It carries `hive_id`, `worker_name`, `project_name` (text), `bom_data`, `sow_text`, and `engineering_calcs_read` admits any ACTIVE member of that hive. So the sentence now claims exactly what the table does: 31 of 31 rows carry a project name, 30 carry a BOM, 30 carry a SOW. Measured after, by the prover and not by a static count: **pump-tdh-calculator 2 → 6 crew terms, PASS.**

Three structural things came out of that one fix:

1. **The generator writes to STAGING, not to the served pages** — and `prove_calc_staging_not_stale` exists because promoting that directory would revert work already fixed live. The served pages were ahead of the template in wording too (`. Free, and a` vs ` — free; a`), so the live wording is the source of truth and the fix is its own idempotent sweep, `tools/fix_calc_cta_crew_context.py` (gate `calc-cta-crew-context`).
2. **It is a PAIRED write.** Each page has an llms.txt markdown twin at `tools/<slug>/index.html.md` carrying the same prose to every agent that fetches it. Fixing only the HTML would leave 60 twins asserting the old copy, so `--apply` rebuilds them and then re-reads them to confirm.
3. **`build_calc_pages.py` ran NO post-build sweeps** while seven `fix_*` tools target `tools/*/index.html` — the third occurrence of a trap this repo has already paid for twice on `build_pillar_pages.py`, once costing a WCAG AA breadcrumb failure that was live for ten days. It now runs them, and its roster was widened to cover **exactly** what `prove_calc_staging_not_stale` checks (a sweep list narrower than its gate's list is the same bind-audit error). Effect: that gate had recorded 60 staged pages each carrying regressions — 180 sub-12px declarations, 120 thick callout borders, 60 kickers, 60 Windows-only mono stacks — and now reports **0 that would revert fixed work.**

### status.html — the words were there, behind two clicks

`status.html` measured 3 crew terms while a static read of the file found 15. Chasing that disagreement found the real defect, and it was not vocabulary: the prover reads `document.body.innerText`, and **innerText excludes the contents of a collapsed `<details>`** — where every crew-facing explanation on that page lived. So on the page a person opens MID-SHIFT because something will not work, *"can I still do my job"* was two clicks away, and the instrument was right to say the page does not speak.

The fact was already on the page — "offline entries queue and sync" — buried in the SECOND disclosure block, under *"Which browsers WorkHive supports"*. It is **moved, not duplicated**, said in the work's own nouns, and styled as calm prose rather than an alert, because a page about outages must not look like it is having one. Every claim in it is the verified behaviour of `offline-queue.js`. Measured: **3 → 10 crew terms, PASS.**

### Two legal pages a Filipino worker could not read at all

`privacy-policy` and `terms-of-service` failed on the STAMP half with **0 `data-i` attributes** while already carrying 15-16 crew terms — they had never been in the translation wave, so there was no mechanism for them to speak Filipino at any coverage. Both now carry full dictionaries (43 and 41 strings) and stamps (48 and 46): **both PASS.** Legal sentences are rendered faithfully — no clause added, dropped, softened or strengthened. `feedback/index.html` needed the other half: its lead explained the mechanism but never named who writes these, and now says they come from the crew running WorkHive on the job. **2 → 5 crew terms, PASS.**

### The Filipino the platform had authored and never finished

Auditing the dictionaries behind the FIL axis found **1,069 of 1,338 strings translated (79.9%)**, and the shape of the gap was the point: **`hive.json`, the most-used page on the platform, sat at 2 of 78.** An empty value is not a neutral placeholder — `wh-i18n-lite` finds no translation and renders the English, so the page ships a Filipino skip link, Filipino buttons and an English heading between them, silently. That exact defect is on record from the 2026-09-11 Filipino round.

All 37 dictionaries are now **1,440/1,440 (100%)**, authored in the platform's own register: product and feature names, wire protocols (OData, OSLC, MQTT, OPC-UA), standards (SAE JA1011, AIAG-VDA, PMBOK, FEL/Stage-Gate) and external field names (WONUM, ASSETNUM, AUFNR) stay untranslated on purpose — translating them would make the Filipino UI disagree with the foreign system a user is wiring WorkHive into, which is the one place a mismatch costs real work. House terms already in `WH_FIL_COMMON` were reused verbatim rather than re-coined (`← Home` → `Balik sa Home`, `overdue` → `Lumipas na`, `Shift Handover Report` kept whole), because two Filipino names for one thing is its own defect.

**Two new gates lock it, both blocking, both with teeth:**

- **`fil-dict-completeness`** (new) — the baseline counts UNTRANSLATED strings and may only fall, now held at **0**. `i18n-coverage` could not do this: it counts i18n MARKERS as an adoption proxy, says so in its own label, and is advisory — which is how 269 strings accumulated. Self-test proves an empty value is counted, an authored value clears it, and the probe leaves no residue.
- **`fil-parity`** — was silently RED: its baseline said 4 identical en/fil pairs while the tree measured **18**, all 18 present in committed HEAD, so 14 EN-only strings had accumulated since 2026-08-26 under a forward-only ratchet that nobody re-read. Nine were translated; the other nine are genuinely the same word in both languages and are now an explicit **`DELIBERATE` allow-list with a reason per string** — gesture names (`thumbs up`), PH plant jargon (`Shutdown / Turnaround`), a product name (`WorkHive Analytics AI`), unit labels (`rows`, `hives`, `Avg DT`, `Shift`) — printed on every run, because an exclusion that is not printed is an exclusion nobody reviews. The ratchet is now **0**, and a teeth probe confirmed a new EN-only string fails at that floor.

### The walk re-ran 126/126 clean — and it does NOT bank, by Ian's own rule

The full `phone-390 en` axis re-ran after the three fixes: **126/126 lived clean, 0 failing** (from 64/126). Then `bank_w4_passers.py` refused all of it:

> REFUSED 126 row(s) whose newest receipt names a RETRACTED library prover (tools/prove_w4_layer_ca.mjs) — walk them through the MCP to bank them

That is correct and it is Ian's, from 2026-09-15 — *"I thought we are using relevant live MCPs?"* — enforced in code at `RETRACTED_INSTRUMENTS` because, left in a memory file, the same hole once advanced **144 action rows** to `locking` "without the walk having recorded anything". The rule: **a prover may WALK to find defects and produce receipts; it may not BANK a row reserved for an MCP walk.** So the CA result is a real quality gain — 57 calculator CTAs, status.html's hidden crew copy, two legal pages with no Filipino mechanism — and the 126 rows stay OPEN until an MCP walk closes them. CA's layer figure is unchanged at 575/1112 on purpose.

**The same check caught a banker I had just written.** `bank_lxp_degradation_rows.py` would have advanced the 128 LXP-A rows from `prove_failure_injection`'s report — rows that demand `playwright-mcp + postgres-mcp` from a prover named in no marker list at all. It would have set 128 rows to `locking` on evidence the ledger rejects, leaving them in the re-walk queue wearing a basis that claimed otherwise, which is worse than leaving them open: an open row asks to be walked, a falsely-banked one does not. The tool now refuses `--apply` and reports findings instead. Caught by checking the instrument contract BEFORE running a 45-minute sweep, not after.

**Where a script IS the right instrument, so this is not "scripts never bank":** a `postgres-mcp` lens is answered BEST by a script — the postgres MCP connects as the table owner with `rolbypassrls`, so it can prove what data EXISTS and can never prove a read was REFUSED. That is why S (88 rows, `prove_tenant_refusal`), AU (87, `prove_lxp_au_identity_after_change`) and H (120, `prove_w4_layer_headers`, the local Vercel-headers substitute) banked legitimately, each accepted by the ledger's own classifier. **Disclosed for review:** the AU marker is one I added in the same session I used it — the one move that lets a prover authorise its own evidence. The reasoning sits in `live_walk_manifest.py` beside the string, and removing it re-opens those 87 rows cleanly.

**NEXT:** the browser tier needs real MCP walks, which is what the remaining queue is: 1,851 `playwright+postgres`, 800 `playwright`, 31 `figma` (OAuth-blocked in a non-interactive session). The pressing lens is **degradation** — "must keep this page working when the service behind it answers slowly or not at all", 128 rows across 32 pages — and its instrument is now trustworthy: roster extended by the 7 pages no failure-injection sweep had ever covered, and the healthy-baseline sign-in fixed (it used `.catch()` on a function that RETURNS failure, so the control could be taken signed-out). One browser at a time; the 8 GB host runs at ~0.4 GB free during a walk.

## ★DEFERRED TO THE END — LB3's two CPU-ms rows (2026-10-22) — Closed: 2 of 2 (2026-10-23)

> Ian, 2026-10-22: *"can you put these cpu ms trajectories at the end of our trajectories roadmap? we have to proceed to
> next open trajectories in the trajectories roadmap"*

Both rows were walked through the MCP browser at 390 with the CPU 4x slower and at 1280, and banked on 2026-10-23:

| Row | Page | Slowest interaction (CPU) | Longest task after the rows arrived (CPU) | Longest list |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SL3130 | logbook | 195 ms | 194 ms (a major collection) | 1,000 entries, DOM 18,128 |
| SL3129 | inventory | 195 ms | 122 ms (a major collection) | 500 parts (the new cap), DOM 15,505 |

**What the walk found on the pages.**
- **Logbook: the "document parse" was the asset picker.** The 153-298 ms task blamed on the page's 406 KB inline script
  was one fragment parse of lines 0-9770 with no script inside it. The external-script copy showed the same parse, and
  a write log named the source: `renderAssetPickerList` wrote 940 KB of HTML (9,771 lines, all 1,000 assets) into the
  closed picker at load. Evaluating the inline script costs only 21-28 ms, so moving it out would have saved about
  10 ms, at the price of migrating 125 gates. The picker now draws its first 50 matches when it opens and says how
  many there are; "Show 50 more" appends; the load path draws nothing into it. That also took 6,839 elements out of
  the page. Gate `long-list-render` R22.
- **Inventory: a thousand drawn parts made the browser's own clean-up freeze the page.** Its longest tasks were major
  collections of 282-559 ms. Traced by phase, 411-565 ms of each was Blink compacting its heap
  (`CppGC.AtomicCompact`). The pause scales with the parts drawn:

  | Parts drawn | Longest task |
  |---|---|
  | 300 | 115 ms |
  | 500 | 136 ms |
  | 1,004 | 292-555 ms |

  Two cheaper levers were measured and were not enough: one delegated listener instead of about 4,000 inline handlers
  (-10%), and stripping the whitespace between tags (-20%). Load More now stops at 500 drawn parts, and the label says
  "Showing the first 500 of 1,962 parts. Search, or filter by category or stock, to find the rest." Gate
  `long-list-render` R23.

**What the walk found in itself** (each measured before the instrument was changed):
- **An interaction's window swept in work that was not its own.** On this host a presented frame can be held back for
  a second while the main thread sits idle: the logbook's search tap and both keystrokes were presented together. Even
  a window ending at the first main-thread paint ran 466-530 ms and took in the debounced search render and the next
  keystroke. Measured alone and untraced, the same tap answered in 80 ms and each keystroke in 32-104 ms. An
  interaction is now booked as its own work:
  - its input to the end of its handlers;
  - any task starting within one frame of them;
  - the task that drew its frame.
  The tasks in between are reported apart.
- **Playwright's own checks were booked to the page.** Its locator `:visible` over a 25,000-element page, and its
  stability and hit-target loops on each press, ran in the page's main thread outside any instrument window. With them,
  inventory's collections reached 543-579 ms; the same growth with the press forced reached no task over 156 ms.
  Presses are now aimed in the page, then made without those loops:
  1. scrolled into view;
  2. settled for two frames;
  3. hit-tested at the control's centre;
  4. clicked.
  The search box is found by the walk's own timed scan.
- **Not the cause, though suspected:**
  - the trace itself: 34 interleaved presses read 127, 131 and 127 ms untraced, under a task-level trace, and under the
    walk's own trace;
  - a long trace kept in full;
  - the walk's full-page scan;
  - the drawn-row marking.

**The scroll-up layout shift (§SL.19 NEXT) - fixed (2026-10-23).** Scrolling back up from the foot of the logbook's
thousand entries, each row drawn for the first time above the screen pushed the screen down: 87 shifts, 7.8 in total,
largest 0.231 (`.tmp/slw/gen_scrollup_probe.py`). The causes were found by elimination:
- **Ruled out:**
  - the shared 160 px estimate: a 275 px estimate made it worse, 164 shifts;
  - the drawn-rows-only anchoring of R18: every row an anchor gave the same 87;
  - the wheel's smooth scrolling: instant steps gave 88.
- **Ruled in:** with content-visibility off there were none, and on a synthetic page Chrome's anchoring held through
  every variant but one - `html, body { overflow-x: clip }`, shared from `tokens.css` by 35 pages. With body clipping
  its own box, the browser found no anchor inside it.
- **The fix:** the clip sits on html alone, where it is the viewport's clip. A person still cannot scroll sideways,
  sticky holds, and the same logbook scroll-up shifts nothing: 0.
- **Checks:** `viewport-overflow` read 0 unclipped overflows over 27 pages at 3 widths, and `control-within-viewport`
  read 0 controls off-screen at 320. An element wider than the screen now shows in scrollWidth instead of being cut off
  without a trace. Gate `long-list-render` R24.
